docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Route.get('/blogs', BlogController.index); // (1)!

enum Status { active, draft }

@Dto() // (2)!
class BlogFilter {
  final Status status; // ?status=active, else 422
  const BlogFilter({required this.status});
  static const DtoSchema<BlogFilter> schema =
      $BlogFilterDto; // (3)!
}

class BlogController {
  static Future<List<Blog>> index(
    BlogFilter query, // (4)!
  ) async {
    return Blog()
        .where('status', query.status.name)
        .get(); // (5)!
  }
}
  1. A route points at a static method. No reflection, no controller registry.
  2. @Dto() marks an input class. build_runner generates the checks from the fields and their types.
  3. The generated schema. The same schema feeds the OpenAPI docs.
  4. Ask for the DTO as a parameter. Dox reads the query (or the body), checks it, and gives you a typed object. Bad input gets a 422 before your code runs.
  5. The ORM. The same code runs on Postgres, MySQL and SQLite, through native Rust drivers.

docs.title: Fast backendsin Dart
docs.text:
Write in Dart. Serve with Rust.

Dox is a web backend framework for Dart, like Laravel. Routing, an ORM, migrations, validation, auth and a CLI come in one place. It runs one isolate per CPU core and builds to a small native binary.

Build your first API GitHub

docs.title: How fast
docs.text:
1.5× Bun. 2.3× Go. 7× plain Dart.

A real route: read one row from Postgres and return JSON (GET /db). Requests per second on one CPU core, higher is better.

req/s p99 RAM Doxnative server + driver 85,381fastest 5.7 ms 24 MB BunBun.serve + Bun.sql 57,6141.5× slower 6.1 ms 36 MB Gonet/http + pgx 36,7062.3× slower 14.5 ms 18 MB dart:io+ package:postgres 12,1467× slower 47.6 ms 62 MB

Dox 3.0.0-alpha.3 · Bun 1.4 · Go 1.27 · Dart 3.13 · Postgres 18 · 256 connections · wrk · median of 3 runsAll results

Dox also has the lowest p99 (the slowest 1% of requests). Your code is plain Dart. The speed comes from the Rust HTTP server and database drivers. Without a database (GET /json), Bun is faster. See Performance for every route.

You are reading the 3.x docs (alpha)

3.0.0-alpha.x is a preview. Things can still change before the stable release.

docs.title: Run it in two minutes
docs.text:
You need Dart 3.13 or newer. Nothing else: the starter project uses SQLite, so there is no database to install.

dart pub global activate dox ^3.0.0-alpha   # install the CLI
dox create my_app                            # download the starter project
cd my_app
dart pub get
dox s                                        # start the server

Open a second terminal and call the first route:

curl localhost:3000/ping

pong

That is a Dox app. Keep going with the tutorial: it adds a model, a database table, validation, login and a Docker image, one short step at a time.

The CLI is not found?

dart pub global activate puts dox in $HOME/.pub-cache/bin. Add that folder to your PATH. See Installation.

docs.title: Pick your path
docs.text: You are... Start here Then New to Dox Tutorial: build a blog API Routing, Request, Validation Coming from Laravel Coming from Laravel How Dox works Looking for one answer Guides (uploads, auth, Docker, pagination...) Reference Going to production Deployment Docker, Troubleshooting

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Fast by default

    A Rust HTTP server, one isolate per CPU core and streamed bodies. dox build makes one native binary. See Performance.

  • ORM and query builder

    Models, relations, migrations and transactions for Postgres, MySQL/MariaDB and SQLite, with native Rust drivers. See Database.

  • Typed validation

    Write a @Dto class. Dox checks the input and gives your controller a typed object. See Validation.

  • OpenAPI

    OpenAPI 3.1 docs and a Scalar docs page, made from your routes and DTOs. See dox_openapi.

  • File storage

    Local disk and S3 behind one API, with signed URLs. See dox_storage.

  • Cache

    Memory, file and Redis cache with tags and locks. See dox_cache.

  • Real time

    Socket.IO, with Redis for many servers.

  • Security

    JWT authentication, CORS, encryption and hashing.

  • CLI

    Create projects, controllers, models and migrations. Run, build and migrate. See CLI reference.

docs.title: Get help
docs.text:
• Found a bug or have a question? Open an issue on GitHub.
  • Using an AI assistant? Give it llms-full.txt: all of these docs as one plain text file. llms.txt is the page list.
  • Want to help? Read Contribute.

docs.title: Contribute
docs.text:
This page shows how to work on Dox: set up the repo, run the tests, release packages and update the docs.

To send a change, fork the repo and open a pull request.

docs.title: 1. Clone the repo
docs.text: git clone git@github.com:dartondox/dox.git

docs.title: 2. Install melos
docs.text:
The repo is a Dart pub workspace. The melos config is in the root pubspec.yaml (under melos:). Use Dart 3.13 or newer.

dart pub global activate melos

docs.title: 3. Run melos bootstrap
docs.text:
It runs one dart pub get at the root. All local packages are linked. There is one pubspec.lock for the whole repo.

melos bs

docs.title: 4. Useful commands
docs.text:
# Run all tests (not dox_orm).
# Use `melos run test`. `melos test` is a built-in melos command.
melos run test

# Analyze and check format (same as CI)
melos run analyze
melos run format_check

# Run tests for dox_orm with postgres, mysql or sqlite
DB_PORT=5432 melos run test_pg
DB_USER=dox DB_PORT=3306 melos run test_mysql
melos run test_sqlite

# Build the dox cli executable (AOT).
# `dart compile exe` does not work: sqlite3 has a build hook. Use `dart build cli`.
cd packages/dox-cli
dart build cli --target bin/dox.dart --output build

# Run dox cli executable file
build/bundle/bin/dox --version

docs.title: If the project does not run
docs.text:
1. Remove pubspec.lock and .dart_tool at the root.
  2. Remove any old pubspec_overrides.yaml and pubspec.lock in packages/* (left from melos 3).
  3. Run melos bs again.

docs.title: Release (maintainers)
docs.text: The Release GitHub workflow (.github/workflows/publish.yaml) publishes all public packages to pub.dev. It runs when you push a tag like v3.0.0-alpha.5. It uses pub.dev automated publishing, so it needs no token or secret.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
The full guide is RELEASING.md in the repo. In short:

  1. Bump every package with bin/update_versions.sh, and close the ## Unreleased section of each CHANGELOG.md.
  2. Merge the release PR, then push the tag v<version>. This publishes to pub.dev.
  3. Release the matching dox-sample template.

The native packages (dox_http_native, dox_postgres_native, dox_mysql_native) are not in this repo. See Native packages below.

New package only: turn on pub.dev automated publishing for it first. See One-time setup. A new package must first exist on pub.dev, so publish its first version by hand with dart pub publish.

docs.title: What the workflow does
docs.text:
1. It checks that the tag (without v) is the root version, and that every package has this version. If not, it stops. Run bin/update_versions.sh and try again.
  2. It gets the publish order from bin/publish_order.py. Each package comes after the sibling packages it depends on (dependencies and dev_dependencies). Packages with publish_to: none (like dox_app) are left out. New packages are picked up by themselves.
  3. It publishes each package in this order. After each one, it waits until dart pub get can find the new version.

To see the order on your machine:

python3 bin/publish_order.py

A package is skipped when its version is already on pub.dev. So if a run fails halfway, fix the problem and click "Re-run jobs". It continues where it stopped.

docs.title: Dry run
docs.text: Open Actions > Release > "Run workflow". It runs dart pub publish --dry-run for every package and publishes nothing. Warnings (for example a missing CHANGELOG entry) show as yellow warnings. They do not fail the run.

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text:
Do this once for each published package, and for every new package before its first tag. The list of packages is the output of python3 bin/publish_order.py.

On pub.dev:

  1. Open https://pub.dev/packages/<name>/admin.
  2. Under "Automated publishing", click "Enable publishing from GitHub Actions".
  3. Repository: dartondox/dox.
  4. Tag pattern: v{{version}}.
  5. Tick "Require GitHub Actions environment" and set the environment to pub.dev.
  6. Save.

On GitHub, in dartondox/dox > Settings > Environments, there must be an environment named pub.dev. The publish job runs in it. Optional: add yourself as a required reviewer, and allow only tags v*.

docs.title: Native packages
docs.text:
The three native packages live in their own repos:

Package Repo dox_http_native dartondox/dox-http-native dox_postgres_native dartondox/dox-postgres-native dox_mysql_native dartondox/dox-mysql-native

Dox uses them from pub.dev. Their build hooks download ready-built libraries, so you do not need Rust to work on Dox.

To work on a native package and Dox together:

  1. Clone the package next to the Dox repo, like ../dox-http-native.

  2. Add it to the root pubspec_overrides.yaml of the Dox repo. Git ignores this file.

    dependency_overrides:
  dox_http_native:
    path: ../dox-http-native

  3. Run dart pub get.

Each native package is released from its own repo, with its own version. Push a v<version> tag in that repo. Its CI builds the libraries, uploads them, fills the hashes and publishes the package to pub.dev. Then raise the version constraint in the Dox packages that use it.

docs.title: Docs
docs.text:
The docs site is https://dartondox.dev. It is built with MkDocs Material and mike. mike keeps one folder per version on the gh-pages branch.

URL What it is /3.x/... 3.x docs, built from develop /latest/... a copy of the newest version (now 3.x) /2.x/... the old 2.x docs, built from the v2.x branch / redirects to /latest/ old links like /the-basic/routing/ redirect to /latest/the-basic/routing/

docs.title: Write and preview
docs.text:
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install mkdocs==1.6.1 mkdocs-material==9.7.7 mike==2.2.0
.venv/bin/mkdocs serve           # live preview of this branch
.venv/bin/mkdocs build --strict  # the same check as CI. Broken links fail.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
• 3.x deploys by itself. The Docs workflow (.github/workflows/docs.yaml) runs on every push to develop that changes docs/, mkdocs.yml or the workflow. It runs mike deploy --update-aliases 3.x latest.
  • 2.x deploys by hand. Open Actions > Docs > "Run workflow", pick version 2.x. It builds from the v2.x branch (change it with the ref input).
  • After each deploy, the workflow writes small redirect pages for the old root links, the root index.html, a 404.html and the CNAME file. So dartondox.dev and old links keep working.
  • The workflow pushes with the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN. This works because gh-pages is not a protected branch.

docs.title: New major version
docs.text: When 4.x starts, deploy 4.x with mike deploy --update-aliases 4.x latest. Keep a v3.x branch, and add 3.x to the workflow input, so 3.x can still be fixed.

docs.title: Meet Doxie
docs.text: Doxie is the official mascot of Dox. Doxie is a blue dachshund.

docs.title: Why a dachshund
docs.text:
"Doxie" is a common nickname for a dachshund. It sounds like Dox, so the name came first.

A dachshund is small, fast and full of energy. Dox tries to be the same: a small native binary that serves a lot of requests.

docs.title: Logo and mascot
docs.text:
Dox has a logo and a mascot. They have different jobs.

Logo Mascot What A hexagon with a "D" cut out Doxie, the blue dachshund Where The docs header, the favicon, the README, pub.dev The home page, social cards, talks, stickers Files logo.svg (white, for dark backgrounds) mascot.png (transparent background)

Use the logo when the space is small, like an icon or an avatar. Doxie has too much detail to read well at 16 or 32 pixels.

docs.title: Colors
docs.text: Name Hex Used for Sky blue #5CC6FF Doxie's body, links in dark mode Dart blue #0A5FC2 Doxie's ears and collar, links in light mode Navy #0B1B36 The docs header, outlines

docs.title: Use Doxie
docs.text: You are welcome to use Doxie when you write or talk about Dox: blog posts, slides, videos and stickers. Please do not change Doxie's colors, and do not use Doxie to brand another product.

docs.title: Coming from Laravel
docs.text:
This page is for Laravel developers: it shows the Laravel way and the Dox way side by side.

The Laravel code is Laravel 11. The biggest changes are in What is different.

docs.title: Routing
Controllers
docs.text:
Laravel Dox php artisan make:controller BlogController dox make:controller Blog php artisan make:controller BlogController --resource dox make:controller Blog -r public function show(Request $request, int $id) Future<Blog?> show(DoxRequest req, int id) public function store(StoreBlogRequest $request) Future<Blog> store(CreateBlog body) constructor injection by the service container constructor injection by the container: @Inject() above the class method injection filled by type: DoxRequest, one @Dto class, path params, models, container classes implicit route model binding the same: a User user parameter loads {user} by its key

Dox fills a parameter by its type, not by its name. Path params go by position. The container is generated code, not reflection. See Dependency injection. A controller can be a class method, a static method or a plain function.

docs.title: Middleware
Requests and validation
Responses
docs.text: Laravel Dox return 'pong'; return 'pong'; return ['a' => 1]; return <String, int>{'a': 1}; return $blog; (JSON) return blog; (JSON from toJson()) return response($data, 201)->header('X-A', 'b'); return response(data).statusCode(201).header('X-A', 'b'); return response()->json($data); return data; (a Map or List is JSON) return response()->file($path); return File(path); return response()->download($path); return Storage().download(path); ->cookie('theme', 'dark') .cookie(DoxCookie('theme', 'dark')) abort(404, 'Not found'); throw NotFoundHttpException(message: 'Not found'); new BlogResource($blog) BlogSerializer(blog)

docs.title: Eloquent vs Dox Model
Query builder
docs.text:
Laravel Dox DB::table('users')->get() await QueryBuilder.table('users').get() ->where('a', 1)->orWhere('b', 2) .where('a', 1).orWhere('b', 2) ->whereIn('id', [1, 2]) .whereIn('id', <int>[1, 2]) ->whereNull('deleted_at') .whereNull('deleted_at') ->whereRaw('lower(name) = ?', [$n]) .whereRaw('lower(name) = @n', <String, dynamic>{'n': n}) ->select('id', 'name') .select(<String>['id', 'name']) ->orderBy('name', 'desc')->limit(10)->offset(20) .orderBy('name', 'desc').limit(10).offset(20) ->join('posts', 'posts.user_id', '=', 'users.id') .join('posts', 'posts.user_id', 'users.id') ->groupBy('age') .groupBy('age') on QueryBuilder.table() (returns maps) ->count() await ....count() ->paginate(10) .paginate(currentPage: 1, perPage: 10) ->insert([...]) .insertMultiple(<Map<String, dynamic>>[...]) ->update([...]) .update(<String, dynamic>{...}) ->delete() .delete() DB::select('select ...', [$id]) QueryBuilder.query('select ... @id', substitutionValues: {'id': id}) DB::transaction(fn) QueryBuilder.transaction(() async { ... }) ->toSql() .toSql() DB::connection('mysql') .withConnection('mysql')

Values are always bound parameters. Names you pass are quoted. Do not pass user input as a column name or an operator.

docs.title: Migrations and schema
Artisan vs the dox CLI
docs.text:
Laravel Dox laravel new blog dox create blog php artisan serve dox serve (or dox s), with hot restart and build_runner watch php artisan make:resource dox make:serializer php artisan key:generate dox key:generate php artisan route:list not there. Use the OpenAPI docs page at /docs. php artisan tinker not there php artisan optimize dox build (one native binary in build/bundle)

The make:* and migrate commands are in the tables above. Two commands have no Laravel twin: dox build_runner:build makes the generated code, and dox env:generate makes the typed env class. See Dox CLI.

docs.title: Auth
docs.text:
Laravel Dox config/auth.php guards and providers Auth.initialize(AuthConfig(guards: ...)) in a service Auth::attempt(['email' => $e, 'password' => $p]) await Auth().attempt(<String, dynamic>{'email': e, 'password': p}) gives a JWT, or null Auth::login($user) Auth().login(user) gives a JWT Auth::user() req.auth?.user<User>() ->middleware('auth:sanctum') AuthMiddleware() from dox_auth Hash::make($p), Hash::check($p, $hash) Hash.make(p), Hash.verify(p, hash)

Dox auth is a JWT in the Authorization header. There are no sessions, no cookies and no Sanctum tokens table. See Authentication.

docs.title: Cache
docs.text:
Laravel Dox config/cache.php lib/config/cache.dart, CacheConfig(defaultStore:, stores:) Cache::put('k', $v, 600) await Cache().put('k', v, duration: Duration(minutes: 10)) Cache::get('k', 'default') await Cache().get('k', 'default') Cache::remember('k', 600, fn) await Cache().remember('k', Duration(minutes: 10), fn) Cache::forget('k') await Cache().forget('k') Cache::store('redis') Cache().store('redis') Cache::tags(['a']) Cache().tags(<String>['a']) Cache::lock('k', 10) Cache().lock('k', Duration(seconds: 10)) drivers: file, redis, memcached, database, array drivers: file, redis, memory, null

A value must be a JSON type. The memory store is per isolate. See Cache.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Laravel Dox config/filesystems.php disks lib/config/storage.dart, StorageConfig(defaultDisk:, disks:) Storage::put('a.txt', $bytes) await Storage().put('files', bytes, extension: 'txt') (a uuid file name) $request->file('f')->store('avatars') await file.store('avatars') or Storage().putRequestFile('avatars', file) Storage::get($path) await Storage().get(path) Storage::exists($path) await Storage().exists(path) Storage::delete($path) await Storage().delete(path) Storage::url($path) await Storage().url(path) Storage::temporaryUrl($path, now()->addMinutes(10)) await Storage().signedUrl(path, expiresIn: Duration(minutes: 10)) Storage::disk('s3') Storage().disk('s3') Storage::download($path) return Storage().download(path); drivers: local, s3, ftp, sftp drivers: local, s3 (also R2, MinIO, Spaces), memory

See File Storage.

docs.title: Config and .env
docs.text:
Laravel Dox config/*.php files lib/config/*.dart files, put together in AppConfig env('APP_KEY') env.appKey (a getter in lib/config/env.dart) env('APP_PORT', 3000) env.appPort (the default is in the getter: int get appPort => 3000;) config('app.name') env.appName from the typed env class (@DoxEnv()) php artisan config:cache not needed. The typed env is read once, at start.

The typed env class gives you an int for APP_PORT and a build error for a bad type. A missing key stops the app at start, with a list of every missing key. See Environment Variables.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Laravel Dox php artisan test dart test $this->get('/api/ping')->assertStatus(200) (await client.get('/api/ping')).expectStatus(200) with DoxTestClient RefreshDatabase run the migrations in setUpAll, then setUp(refreshDatabase) from package:dox_orm/testing.dart Storage::fake('s3') Dox().storage.fake('s3') Cache::fake() Dox().cache = CacheManager(CacheConfig(...)) with a memory store $this->actingAs($user) client.withToken(token) with the JWT from Auth().login(user)

Dox has no fake HTTP kernel. DoxTestClient.start(appConfig) starts the real server inside the test, on a free port, and sends real requests. See Testing.

docs.title: What is different
docs.text:
• A generated container. Like Laravel, Dox makes your controllers and injects what the constructor asks for. You add @Inject() to the class. build_runner writes lib/container.g.dart with every registration. There are no service providers to write. A singleton is one instance per isolate, not one per request.
  • Isolates, not PHP-FPM workers. One process runs one isolate per CPU core. Each isolate runs your whole app and has its own memory. A static value or a singleton lives once per isolate. A PHP worker starts from zero on each request. A Dox isolate keeps its state between requests, so a memory leak stays. Anything that must be shared goes to the database, Redis or files. See How Dox works.
  • Code generation, not reflection. Laravel reads your classes at run time. Dart has no usable reflection in a compiled app. So build_runner with dox_builder writes the model code, the DTO checks, the env class and the OpenAPI docs into .g.dart files. Run dox build_runner:build after a change, or let dox serve watch for you.
  • One native binary. dox build makes an AOT binary in build/bundle. There is no interpreter, no vendor/ folder and no composer install on the server. The Docker image is about 11 MB.
  • A native HTTP server and native database drivers. Rust parses HTTP and talks to Postgres and MySQL. Your code stays in Dart. They come ready-built, so you do not need Rust.
  • Types everywhere. A DTO is a class with typed fields. A path param is an int. A model field is a String?. The compiler finds many mistakes before you run the app.
  • Async is explicit. Database calls return a Future. You write await. One isolate serves many requests at the same time while it waits for the database.
  • JSON API first. Dox returns text, JSON, files and streams. It has no view layer.

docs.title: What is missing today
docs.text:
Dox does not have these Laravel features yet:

  • queues and jobs, and the task scheduler
  • events and listeners (model events are there)
  • Blade views, mail and notifications
  • sessions (auth uses a JWT; encrypted cookies are there)
  • policies and gates

See What Dox does not have yet for what to use today.

What is there, as separate packages: validation, OpenAPI docs, storage, cache, Socket.IO and auth.

docs.title: Dox and the other Dart backends
docs.text:
This page compares Dox with four other ways to build a backend in Dart: Dart Frog, Serverpod, Shelf (with shelf_router) and Alfred. It lists facts only. Each project is good at different things.

Checked on 2026-10-22

The facts about the other projects come from their own docs, READMEs and pub.dev pages, read on 2026-10-22. Projects change. Check their docs before you decide. Where this page is not sure, the table says "see their docs".

docs.title: What each one is for
docs.text:
• Dox is a full backend framework, in the style of Laravel. It has routes, controllers, typed DTOs, an ORM, migrations, auth, cache, storage and a CLI. It is in 3.0 alpha. The API can still change.
  • Dart Frog is a small backend framework. It is built on Shelf. Routes come from the files in the routes/ folder. It describes itself as "a fast, minimalistic backend framework for Dart".
  • Serverpod is a full-stack framework for Flutter. You write endpoint methods on the server. Serverpod generates a typed Dart client for the Flutter app. It has an ORM, auth, streaming and a hosted service (Serverpod Cloud).
  • Shelf is the request and middleware model from the Dart team. It is a library, not a framework. shelf_router adds a router. You pick every other part yourself.
  • Alfred is a small server in the style of Express.js. Routes, middleware, WebSocket and static files are built in.

docs.title: Feature table
docs.text:
"Not built in" means the project does not ship it. You can still add a package for it.

A separate web server (Relic) has its own routing. Binary: see their docs. Your app is plain Dart. Compile it like any Dart program. Your app is plain Dart. Compile it like any Dart program. Multi-core One isolate per CPU core by default See their docs One isolate per process. Scale with more processes and server roles. serve(..., shared: true) and your own isolates Yes, a multi-isolate mode is in their README HTTP server Native server in Rust (hyper), also for WebSocket Shelf on dart:io Relic (their own) for the web server. API server: see their docs. dart:io HttpServer (shelf_io) dart:io Databases Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, SQLite Not built in Postgres, SQLite (also SQLite on the device). Redis for cache. Not built in Not built in Code sharing with Flutter @Dto classes in a pure Dart package, see Share code with Flutter Plain Dart packages. A generated client is marked "in progress" in their feature list. Generated client package, and shared packages for models Plain Dart packages Plain Dart packages License MIT MIT BSD-3 for most packages. The main serverpod package is SSPL. BSD-3-Clause MIT for the core. Some parts BSD. First release and maturity 3.0 alpha (2026) First on pub.dev in 2022, 1.0 about three years ago First on pub.dev in 2021, now 4.x First on pub.dev in 2014, 1.0 in 2021 First on pub.dev in 2021, 1.x Maintenance (on 2026-10-22) Active Active. Moved to the dart-frog-dev group in 2025. Last dart_frog release: 1.2.6 (November 2025). Active. Release 4.0.4 in October 2026. Active. Published by tools.dart.dev (the Dart team). Last release 1.1.3, about 17 months ago. Unverified uploader.

Sources (checked on 2026-10-22):

  • Dart Frog: dart-frog.dev, github.com/dart-frog-dev/dart_frog (docs in docs/src/content/docs, the roadmap and "The Future of Dart Frog"), pub.dev/packages/dart_frog
  • Serverpod: docs.serverpod.dev, github.com/serverpod/serverpod, github.com/serverpod/serverpod_docs (scalability, streaming, shared packages, database connection), pub.dev/packages/serverpod
  • Shelf: pub.dev/packages/shelf, pub.dev/packages/shelf_router, github.com/dart-lang/shelf, serve API docs

docs.title: Speed
docs.text: This page does not compare speed. Dox's own numbers (hello world and a /db read) are on Performance. To compare, run the same test on your own machine, with each server on the same number of cores.

docs.title: When to pick Dox
docs.text:
• You want a full framework in one place: routes, typed input, ORM, migrations, auth, cache, storage and OpenAPI docs.
  • You know Laravel. See Coming from Laravel.
  • You need MySQL or MariaDB, not only Postgres.
  • You want typed DTOs with the same rules on the server and in a Dart or Flutter client. See Share code with Flutter.
  • You want an OpenAPI document made from your code, for clients that are not written in Dart.
  • You can accept an alpha: the API can change before 3.0 is stable. See Status and roadmap.

docs.title: When to pick something else
docs.text:
• You need a stable API today. Dox is alpha. Dart Frog, Serverpod and Shelf have had 1.0 or later for years.
  • You want a hosted service. Serverpod has Serverpod Cloud. Dox has no hosted service. You deploy it yourself (a binary or Docker).
  • Your app is Flutter only, and you want the client made for you. Serverpod generates a typed client for every endpoint. Dox does not generate a Dart client. It generates an OpenAPI document.
  • You want a small tool with few parts. Dart Frog is simpler. You add only what you need.
  • You want to build your own stack. Shelf gives you the base parts, and the Dart team publishes it.
  • You need features Dox does not have yet, like queues, a scheduler or mail. See What Dox does not have yet.

docs.title: How Dox works
docs.text: This page explains what happens inside Dox when a request comes in, how isolates work and what each folder of an app is for.

docs.title: The life of a request
docs.text:
Dox has two parts:

  • A native server, written in Rust (dox_http_native). It owns the sockets and parses HTTP.
  • Your app, written in Dart. Routes, middleware, DTOs, controllers and the ORM all run here.

A request goes through these steps:

  1. Rust accepts the connection and reads the request. It parses the HTTP request line, the headers and the body. A bad request gets 400. Headers over 16 KB get 431. A body over the size limit gets 413. Dart never sees these requests.
  2. Rust hands the requests to Dart in a batch. One message holds many requests.
  3. Dart finds the route. It matches the method, the Host (for domain routes) and the path. A plain path is a map lookup. A path with {params} is a pattern match. No match gives 404. A CORS preflight (OPTIONS) gets 204.
  4. Dart adds the CORS headers of the route.
  5. Dart reads the body, only when the request has a Content-Type. A request without a body skips this step.
  6. Dart runs the middleware list of the route, in this order: global middleware, router middleware, group middleware, route middleware. A middleware returns the request to go on. Anything else is sent as the response, and the controller does not run.
  7. Dart fills the controller parameters. Path params are converted first. A value that does not fit its type (abc for int id) gets 404. Then the DTO is read and checked. Bad input gets 422. A body that is not JSON gets 400. A content type Dox can not read gets 415.
  8. The controller runs and returns a value.
  9. The responseHandler from AppConfig runs, when you set one. It can change every response.
  10. Dox turns the value into the response: a String is text, a Map or model is JSON, a File is streamed.
  11. Dart sends the answers of the batch back to Rust in one call. Rust writes the bytes to the socket.

When a step throws, Dox catches the error. An IHttpException (like NotFoundHttpException) gives its own status. Any other error gives 500 and goes to the report method of the ExceptionHandler in AppConfig.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant R as Rust (dox_http_native)
    participant D as Dart isolate
    participant M as Middleware
    participant K as Controller

    C->>R: TCP connection, HTTP request
    R->>R: parse request, check size limits
    R->>D: batch of requests (one message)
    D->>D: router: method, host, path
    D->>D: CORS headers, read body
    D->>M: global, router, group, route middleware
    M-->>D: request (go on) or a response
    D->>D: path params, DTO check
    D->>K: call with typed parameters
    K-->>D: return value
    D->>D: responseHandler, build the response
    D->>R: batch of answers (one call)
    R->>C: bytes

No reflection

Dox reads the parameter types of every controller once, at start. It does not use dart:mirrors. DTOs come from a generated list (lib/dtos.g.dart). This is why dox build can make a native (AOT) binary.

docs.title: Where things are decided
docs.text:
Step Code What it decides Route match lib/routes/*.dart, Route.get(...) which controller runs Middleware AppConfig(globalMiddleware:), Router.middleware, Route.middleware(...), the route list go on, or answer early Input a @Dto class in lib/app/http/dtos/ what the controller gets, or 422 Output the return value, response(...), responseHandler status, headers, body Errors IHttpException, AppConfig(exceptionHandler:) the error response, logging

See Routing, Middleware, Validation and Response.

docs.title: Isolates
docs.text: Dart runs code on isolates. An isolate is like a thread, but it has its own memory. Dox starts one isolate per CPU core (Platform.numberOfProcessors). Every isolate runs the full app.

docs.title: One port, many isolates
docs.text:
Every isolate runs its own HTTP server on the same port. The operating system spreads the connections.

System Native server Linux one socket per isolate (SO_REUSEPORT) macOS the isolates share one socket Windows only one isolate serves HTTP

Each isolate also has its own Rust network thread. DOX_HTTP_THREAD=shared puts all isolates on one thread. Leave it off unless you measure a gain.

docs.title: What each isolate gets
docs.text:
Before it starts an isolate, Dox copies three things to it:

  • the AppConfig,
  • the list of services,
  • the routes you added before startServer().

Then each isolate does this, once:

  1. It runs setup() of every service, in list order. This is where a database pool is opened.
  2. It registers the routes of your routers.
  3. It reads the parameter types of every controller.
  4. It starts its HTTP server.

Nothing in this list runs per request.

Because the config and the services are copied, they must not hold open sockets or pools. Open these in setup(). See Services.

docs.title: Each isolate has its own memory
docs.text:
• A static value or a singleton exists once per isolate. A change in one isolate is not seen in the others.
  • The memory cache store is per isolate. Use the redis store to share cache data.
  • To share data between isolates, use the database, Redis or files.
  • Dox().isolateId tells you which isolate runs the code. The first one is 1.

docs.title: When an isolate crashes
docs.text:
• An error in a request is caught. Dox answers 500 and keeps going.
  • An async error outside a request is caught and passed to the ExceptionHandler. The isolate keeps running.
  • When a worker isolate still dies, Dox prints [dox] isolate N exited, restarting and starts a new one after 1 second.
  • When the first (main) isolate dies, the process exits with a non-zero code. A supervisor (Docker restart:, systemd Restart=always) must start it again.

docs.title: How many isolates
docs.text: Set totalIsolate in AppConfig, or APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE in .env. In code, Dox().totalIsolate(2) before startServer() wins over the config. Use 1 in tests. See Isolate.

docs.title: Where the database pools live
docs.text:
The ORM is started in a service (ORMService). Every isolate runs setup(), so every isolate opens a pool. The native drivers live in Rust. There, isolates that open the same settings get the same pool.

Driver Per isolate Per process Postgres native (dox_postgres_native) nothing one pool of maxConnectionCount connections per settings, and one Rust runtime (extra['threads'], default 1) MySQL native (dox_mysql_native) nothing one pool of maxConnectionCount connections per settings, and one Rust runtime SQLite one connection nothing shared

So for Postgres and MySQL, the app opens at most maxConnectionCount connections, for any number of isolates. The pool size is always your choice. Set it below the max_connections of the database.

The pool closes when the last isolate that uses it closes it. See Native Postgres driver.

Postgres and MySQL have only the native drivers. When the native library does not load, the app stops with an error that says why and how to fix it. See Database.

docs.title: The layout of a Dox app
docs.text:
dox create my_app copies the dox-sample template. It looks like this:

my_app/
├── bin/
│   └── server.dart          # starts the app
├── db/
│   └── migration/           # migrations (.dart with a registry, or .sql)
├── lib/
│   ├── app/
│   │   ├── http/
│   │   │   ├── controllers/     # *.controller.dart
│   │   │   ├── dtos/            # *.dto.dart, typed and checked input
│   │   │   ├── middleware/      # *.middleware.dart
│   │   │   ├── serializers/     # *.serializer.dart, custom JSON shapes
│   │   │   └── response_handler.dart
│   │   └── models/              # one folder per model, *.model.dart
│   ├── config/
│   │   ├── app.dart             # AppConfig: port, isolates, middleware
│   │   ├── cache.dart           # cache stores
│   │   ├── cors.dart
│   │   ├── database.dart        # DatabaseConfig: connections
│   │   ├── env.dart             # typed env class (@DoxEnv), optional
│   │   ├── logger.dart
│   │   └── storage.dart         # storage disks
│   ├── routes/
│   │   ├── api.dart             # ApiRouter, prefix `api`
│   │   └── web.dart             # WebRouter
│   ├── services/
│   │   └── orm_service.dart     # opens the database in every isolate
│   ├── container.g.dart         # generated: @Inject classes, routers, services
│   ├── dtos.g.dart              # generated: the list of DTOs
│   └── openapi.g.dart           # generated: the OpenAPI docs
├── storage/                     # local disk, file cache, uploads
├── test/
├── .env                         # local settings, not in git
├── .env.example
├── Dockerfile
├── docker-compose.yml
└── pubspec.yaml
Folder What goes there bin/ server.dart calls Dox().initialize(appConfig), runs the migrations, then Dox().startServer(). dox make:migration adds migrate.dart. db/migration/ Your migrations. Dart migrations are listed in migrations.dart, which the CLI writes. lib/app/http/ Everything about HTTP: controllers, DTOs, middleware, serializers. lib/app/models/ One folder per model. build_runner writes the .g.dart file next to it. lib/config/ One file per config object. app.dart puts them together in AppConfig. lib/routes/ One Router class per file. Dox finds each router by itself. lib/services/ Classes that implement DoxService. Their setup() runs in every isolate. lib/*.g.dart Generated files. Do not edit them. Run dox build_runner:build to make them again. storage/ Files the app writes: uploads, the file cache, SQLite files.

build_runner with dox_builder makes the model classes, the DTO checks, the typed env class and the OpenAPI docs.

docs.title: Status and roadmap
docs.text:
This page shows what works in Dox today, what is missing and what is planned.

Checked on 2026-10-25, for version 3.0.0-alpha.7.

Dox 3.0 is an alpha. You can build with it, but the API can still change between alpha versions. All packages share one version number.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
What the states mean:

  • May change: works and has tests. Names and options can still change before 3.0 is stable.
  • Experimental: new code. It changed in a breaking way during the alphas, or it has a known gap.

No package is marked "stable API" yet. That comes with 3.0 stable.

Package What it does State Tests dox_core Routes, middleware, controllers, request and response, isolates, config May change 36 test files. CI runs them on the native server. dox_orm Query builder, models, relations, transactions, drivers May change 26 test files. CI runs them on Postgres, MariaDB, MySQL 8.4 and SQLite. dox_validation @Dto rules, fluent schemas, JSON Schema, Standard Schema May change 6 test files dox_builder Code generator for models, DTOs, env classes and OpenAPI May change 4 test files dox_annotation Annotations used by the generator May change 1 small test file. Mostly tested through dox_builder. dox (CLI) dox create, dox serve, dox build, make:*, migration:* May change 8 test files dox_migration Migrations for Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite May change 4 test files. CI runs them on each database. dox_auth JWT auth guard and middleware May change 2 test files dox_cache Memory, file and Redis cache, tags, locks May change 4 test files, with Redis in CI dox_storage Local disk and S3 (and S3-compatible) storage May change 7 test files, with MinIO in CI dox_openapi OpenAPI 3.1 document and a docs page May change 4 test files dox_socketio Socket.IO v4 server with a Redis adapter May change 8 test files, with the real socket.io-client in CI dox_http_native Native HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket server (Rust hyper). Dox has no other server. Experimental 3 Dart test files and Rust tests dox_postgres_native Native Postgres client (Rust tokio-postgres), the Postgres driver. Has TLS (sslmode). Experimental 5 Dart test files, plus the dox_orm tests dox_mysql_native Native MySQL and MariaDB client (Rust mysql_async), the MySQL driver. Has TLS. Experimental 1 Dart test file, plus the dox_orm tests

Hash (bcrypt password hashing) is in dox_core.

About test coverage

The repo does not measure line coverage. The "Tests" column counts test files and says where CI runs them. The CI setup is in .github/workflows/test.yaml. The three native packages live in their own repos, with their own CI.

docs.title: What Dox does not have yet
docs.text:
These were checked by searching the code in packages/*/lib with rg.

Feature Status What to do today Queues and jobs Not there Use a database table, Redis or a separate worker process. See Background work. Task scheduler Not there Use cron or a systemd timer to call a route or a Dart script. Mail Not there Use a Dart mail package or an HTTP mail API. Notifications Not there Send them from your own service class. Events and listeners Not there Model events are there. See Model events. Views and templates Not there Dox is for APIs. Serve the front end on its own. Sessions and password reset Not there Auth uses JWT. req.httpRequest.session throws UnsupportedError. Policies and gates Not there Check the user in a middleware or in the controller. Database factories and seeders Not there Write a Dart script, or a migration with data. Localization Not there Keep your own message maps.

docs.title: Planned
docs.text:
This is a plan, not a promise. Open an issue to discuss.

Items come from the code (ponytail: notes in packages/*/lib) and from the owner. There are no dates.

New package: github.com/dartondox/dox-queue. dox_scheduler Run tasks on a schedule. New package: github.com/dartondox/dox-scheduler. 3.0 stable After the alpha API settles

docs.text:

  • Notifications

The package CHANGELOGs have an Unreleased section when changes wait for the next version.

docs.title: How to help
docs.text:
• Try the alpha and open an issue when something breaks or is missing.
  • Pick an item above and open an issue first, so the design can be discussed.
  • See Contribute to set up the repo and run the tests.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
Connect Dox to Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB or SQLite with the dox_orm package.

  • Query builder: build SQL with methods.
  • Models: one class per table.
  • Transactions: many queries that succeed or fail together.
  • Migration and Schema: create and change tables.

This is how a query travels from your code to the database:

flowchart LR
    M["Model or QueryBuilder"] --> S["SQL text<br>quoted names, @values"]
    S --> D{"Driver"}
    D --> N["Native Rust pool<br>dox_postgres_native, dox_mysql_native"]
    D --> T["sqlite3"]
    N --> DB[("Database")]
    T --> DB

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The query builder and the models are in the dox_orm package.

dart pub add dox_orm

import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

docs.title: Supported databases
docs.text:
Database Driver Driver Pool Good for Postgres Driver.postgres dox_postgres_native Yes Production MySQL 8+ and MariaDB Driver.mysql dox_mysql_native Yes Production SQLite Driver.sqlite sqlite3 No, one connection per isolate Development, tests, small apps

Native drivers

Postgres and MySQL use a native (Rust) driver. There is no other driver. When the native library can not load, the app stops with an error. See the Postgres and MySQL pages.

docs.title: Config
docs.text:
Put the connections in lib/config/database.dart. connection is the name of the default connection.

lib/config/database.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: env.dbConnection,
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.postgres,
      host: 'localhost',
      port: 5432,
      user: 'postgres',
      password: 'postgres',
      database: 'postgres',
      extra: <String, dynamic>{'maxConnectionCount': 10},
      debug: false,
    ),
    'mysql': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.mysql, // also for MariaDB
      host: 'localhost',
      port: 3306,
      user: 'root',
      password: 'password',
      database: 'dox',
      extra: <String, dynamic>{'maxConnectionCount': 10},
      debug: false,
    ),
    'sqlite': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.sqlite,
      database: 'storage/app.db', // file path, or ':memory:'
      debug: false,
    ),
  },
);
  • debug: true prints each SQL query and its values.
  • user, password, host and port are not used by SQLite.

Start the ORM in a service. Each isolate runs the service. Isolates with the same settings share one pool, so maxConnectionCount is for the whole process.

lib/services/orm_service.dart
class ORMService implements DoxService, DoxShutdown {
  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig);
  }

  /// Close the database connections when the server stops.
  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await SqlQueryBuilder.close();
  }
}

docs.title: .env
docs.text:
The app config and the migration commands read these values.

.env
DB_CONNECTION=postgres # postgres, mysql or sqlite
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432           # 3306 for mysql
DB_NAME=dox            # for sqlite: the file path, like storage/app.db
DB_USERNAME=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=postgres

docs.title: DATABASE_URL
docs.text:
Many hosts (Fly, Render, Heroku and others) give you one database url. Dox reads it from the DATABASE_URL environment variable.

The rule: when DATABASE_URL is set, it wins. It replaces the config of the default connection (DatabaseConfig.connection). That config still gives debug, printer and extra. Other named connections do not change.

DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:s%40cret@db.example.com:5432/blog?sslmode=require
Form Database postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db or postgresql://... Postgres mysql://user:pass@host:3306/db or mariadb://... MySQL, MariaDB sqlite:///abs/path.db, sqlite://db/dox.sqlite, sqlite::memory:, file:db/dox.sqlite SQLite
  • The user, password and database name are url-decoded. Write @ in a password as %40.
  • No port: 5432 for Postgres, 3306 for MySQL.
  • For Postgres, sslmode works like libpq (disable, prefer, require, verify-ca, verify-full). require does not check the certificate. Use verify-full when your host supports it. See Postgres TLS.
  • For MySQL, ssl=true (or sslmode=require) turns TLS on, and it checks the certificate. Add verifyCertificate=false to skip the check, only for a self-signed certificate in development.
  • host=/path (or socket=/path) connects to a Unix socket, like host=/cloudsql/project:region:instance. See Unix socket.
  • Any other option goes to extra, like ?maxConnectionCount=20. A number becomes an int, true and false a bool.

The ORM reads DATABASE_URL from the real environment, not from .env. To use a url from .env, or any other url, give it yourself:

DatabaseConfig(
  connection: 'postgres',
  connections: {...},
  url: Env.get<String?>('DATABASE_URL'),
);

An empty url (url: '') turns DATABASE_URL off. To make one ConnectionConfig from a url, use ConnectionConfig.fromUrl(url). Migrations read DATABASE_URL too, also from .env.

docs.title: Unix socket
docs.text:
A host that starts with / is a Unix socket. Google Cloud SQL on Cloud Run uses /cloudsql/PROJECT:REGION:INSTANCE.

DB_HOST=/cloudsql/my-project:europe-west1:blog
# or
DATABASE_URL=postgres://blog:secret@/blog?host=/cloudsql/my-project:europe-west1:blog

Postgres: the host is the socket folder, like in libpq. The driver uses the socket file <folder>/.s.PGSQL.<port>. A host that already ends with /.s.PGSQL.5432 works too.

MySQL and MariaDB: the host is the socket file itself. The port is not used. On Cloud SQL, the socket file is /cloudsql/PROJECT:REGION:INSTANCE. A local server often uses /var/run/mysqld/mysqld.sock or /tmp/mysql.sock.

DB_CONNECTION=mysql
DB_HOST=/var/run/mysqld/mysqld.sock
# or
DATABASE_URL=mysql://app:secret@/app?socket=/var/run/mysqld/mysqld.sock

?socket= and ?host= do the same thing.

docs.title: extra options
docs.text:
extra is a map in ConnectionConfig for driver options.

Key Database Default What it does maxConnectionCount Postgres, MySQL 10 Most connections in the pool. threads Postgres, MySQL 1 Rust threads of the native driver. maxConnectionAge MySQL 12 hours A connection older than this is opened again. preparedStatementCacheSize MySQL, SQLite 100 Prepared statements kept per connection. sslMode Postgres disable TLS mode: disable, prefer, require or verify-full. sslRootCert Postgres none Path of a PEM file with the CA certificates to trust for verify-full. verifyCertificate MySQL true false skips the TLS certificate check. Only for development. timeZone Postgres UTC Time zone of the session. applicationName Postgres none Name of the app in pg_stat_activity. busyTimeout SQLite 5000 Milliseconds a query waits for a lock.

docs.title: Table and column names are quoted
docs.text:
Table and column names you pass to select, where, join, groupBy, orderBy, insert and update are quoted. Postgres and SQLite use "name". MySQL uses `name`. So names like order or key work.

  • table.column, table.*, * and column as alias are quoted in the right way.
  • Anything else (for example count(*) as total) throws an ArgumentError. So user input can not add SQL.
  • For expressions, use the raw methods (selectRaw, whereRaw, orderByRaw, groupByRaw, joinRaw).
  • On Postgres, a quoted name is case sensitive. userId is not the same column as userid.

docs.title: Raw queries
docs.text:
QueryBuilder.query() runs SQL on the default connection. Use @name for values. The values are sent as bound parameters.

List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.query(
  'select * from blog where id = @id',
  substitutionValues: <String, dynamic>{'id': 1},
);

Pass connection to run it on another connection.

await QueryBuilder.query('select 1', connection: 'mysql');

docs.title: Other connections
docs.text:
Use withConnection() with a connection name from the config.

List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('blog')
    .withConnection('mysql')
    .get();

A model keeps its connection. save() and delete() use it. Models that a query returns use the connection of the query.

Blog blog = Blog()..withConnection('mysql');
blog.title = 'Hello';
await blog.save(); // saved on 'mysql'

docs.title: MySQL and MariaDB
docs.text:
• The driver is dox_mysql_native. Its page lists how values are converted.
  • CREATE, ALTER and DROP are saved right away. A transaction can not undo them.

docs.title: SQLite
docs.text:
SQLite is good for development, tests and small apps. For a busy production app, use Postgres or MySQL.

How it runs

The sqlite3 package calls SQLite directly (FFI). A query blocks the isolate while it runs. Each isolate has one connection. The file uses WAL mode, so readers do not wait for the writer. busyTimeout makes a query wait for a lock from another isolate, instead of failing. Foreign keys are on. Before each SELECT, the driver checks PRAGMA schema_version to see if a table changed.

Types

SQLite has no bool, JSON or date type. Dox converts them for you:

  • boolean() is saved as 0/1 and read back as bool.
  • json() is saved as text and read back as Map or List.
  • Dates are saved as ISO text in UTC and read back as DateTime.

The driver uses the column type in CREATE TABLE. It finds the table by the table names in the query. So it works on tables made by Schema, or by SQL with the same type names (BOOLEAN, JSON, TIMESTAMP, DATE, DATETIME). A column with an alias (active as is_active) is not converted.

Limits

  • Schema limits (change(), dropColumn, NOT NULL columns) are in SQLite notes.
  • dropColumn does not work on a primary key column.
  • insertMultiple with rows that have different keys inserts the rows one by one, because SQLite has no DEFAULT in VALUES.
  • SQLite before 3.39 has no RIGHT JOIN.

Native library

The sqlite3 package (v3) bundles SQLite with a build hook. You do not install a system library. For the AOT binary, use dox build. It puts the library in build/bundle/lib/, next to build/bundle/bin/server. Keep the two folders together. dart compile exe does not work with build hooks. See Deployment.

docs.title: Factories
docs.text: A factory makes models with sample data. Use it in tests and in seeders.

docs.title: Create a factory
docs.text:
dox make:factory User

This makes db/factories/user.factory.dart:

db/factories/user.factory.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/factory.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class UserFactory extends Factory<User> {
  @override
  User definition() {
    User user = User();
    user.name = 'Jane';
    user.email = 'jane@example.com';
    return user;
  }
}

definition() gives one new model with the default values. It runs once for each model, so random values are new each time.

docs.title: Make and create
State
docs.text:
state() changes each model after definition().

User admin = await UserFactory()
    .state((User u) => u..isAdmin = true)
    .createOne();

You can add more than one state. They run in the order you add them.

A factory method makes a state easy to use again:

class UserFactory extends Factory<User> {
  @override
  User definition() => User()..name = 'Jane';

  UserFactory admin() {
    state((User u) => u..isAdmin = true);
    return this;
  }
}

List<User> admins = await UserFactory().admin().count(3).create();

Call your own methods first. count() and state() return a Factory<User>, not a UserFactory.

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
sequence() is a state that also gets the index of the model: 0, 1, 2 and so on.

List<User> users = await UserFactory()
    .count(3)
    .sequence((User u, int i) => u..email = 'user$i@example.com')
    .create();
// user0@example.com, user1@example.com, user2@example.com

To switch between a few values, use the index:

List<String> roles = <String>['admin', 'editor'];
await UserFactory()
    .count(4)
    .sequence((User u, int i) => u..role = roles[i % roles.length])
    .create();

docs.title: Belongs to
docs.text:
Set the parent key with a state:

User user = await UserFactory().createOne();

await PostFactory()
    .count(3)
    .state((Post p) => p..userId = user.id)
    .create();

docs.title: Has many
docs.text:
has() creates child models for each saved model. The second argument sets the parent on each child.

List<User> users = await UserFactory()
    .count(2)
    .has(PostFactory().count(3), (Post p, User u) => p..userId = u.id)
    .create();
// 2 users, each with 3 posts

has() only works with create() and createOne(). make() saves nothing, so it makes no children.

docs.title: Fake data
docs.text:
Dox has no fake data generator. The faker package works well with factories:

dart pub add faker
db/factories/user.factory.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/factory.dart';
import 'package:faker/faker.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class UserFactory extends Factory<User> {
  @override
  User definition() {
    return User()
      ..name = faker.person.name()
      ..email = faker.internet.email();
  }
}

docs.title: Use in tests
docs.text:
A factory needs the ORM. Set it up first, the same as in your app.

import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/factories/user.factory.dart';

void main() {
  test('lists users', () async {
    await UserFactory().count(3).create();
    // call your route and check the result
  });
}

See Testing with a database.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Each call like count() or state() changes the factory and returns it. Make a new factory for each set of models.
  • Import factories from package:dox_orm/factory.dart. The main dox_orm import does not include them.

docs.title: Migration
docs.text:
A migration changes your database schema step by step, with an up method that makes the change and a down method that undoes it.

Write migrations in Dart with the schema builder. The same migration then works on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. Plain .sql migrations work too.

docs.title: Create a migration
docs.text:
dox make:migration create_users_table

This makes db/migration/2026_10_21_120000_create_users_table.dart. The numbers are the date and time when you run the command.

db/migration/2026_10_21_120000_create_users_table.dart
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

class CreateUsersTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.create('users', (Table table) {
      table.id();
      table.timestamps();
    });
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.dropIfExists('users');
  }
}

Add your columns in up, for example table.string('email').unique();. See Schema for all column types.

The name of the migration decides what the new file contains:

Name The file has create_users_table schema.create('users', ...) in up, and dropIfExists('users') in down add_avatar_to_users_table (also _from_, _in_, _on_) schema.table('users', ...) in up and down any other name empty up and down
  • create:migration does the same.
  • dox make:model Blog -m makes the model and a create_blogs_table migration.

Raw SQL and data in a Dart migration

schema.driver runs raw SQL on the same connection and transaction: await schema.driver.execute("UPDATE users SET role = 'admin' WHERE id = 1"); Do not use models or QueryBuilder in a migration. They use another connection.

docs.title: The registry
docs.text:
An AOT build can not load a file at run time. So Dox keeps a list of your Dart migrations in db/migration/migrations.dart:

// Made by `dox make:migration` and the `dox migration:*` commands.
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import '2026_10_21_120000_create_users_table.dart' as m1;

final List<MigrationEntry> migrations = <MigrationEntry>[
  MigrationEntry(
    '2026_10_21_120000_create_users_table',
    m1.CreateUsersTable(),
  ),
];
  • dox make:migration and every dox migration:* command write this file again. You do not edit it.
  • It lists each file named YYYY_MM_DD_HHMMSS_name.dart and its class ... extends Migration.
  • The name of a migration is its file name without .dart. The order is by name.

The first dox make:migration also makes bin/migrate.dart in your app:

import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await Migrator(migrations: migrations).run(args);
}

The dox migration:* commands run dart run bin/migrate.dart <command>. So your migrations run as part of your app code.

docs.title: Run migrations
docs.text:
Command What it does dox migration:run Run the migrations that did not run yet. Short name: dox migrate. dox migration:rollback Undo the last batch. dox migration:rollback --step=2 Undo the last 2 migrations, even across batches. dox migration:reset Undo all migrations. dox migration:refresh Undo all migrations, then run them again. dox migration:fresh Drop all tables, then run all migrations. It also drops tables that no migration made. dox migration:status Show each migration, its batch, and if it ran.

migrate:rollback, migrate:reset, migrate:refresh, migrate:fresh and migrate:status are short names.

Add --seed to migration:run, migration:refresh or migration:fresh to run the seeders after it.

A batch is the group of migrations that ran in one migration:run. Migrations are undone newest first. The ran migrations are saved in the dox_db_migration table.

When a migration fails, the error shows its name, and the command exits with code 1. The failed migration is not saved, and the later ones do not run.

You can also run dart run bin/migrate.dart run (or rollback --step=2, reset, refresh, status) yourself.

docs.title: Run on server start
docs.text:
The AOT server binary can run the migrations, because the registry is compiled in. The new app template already does this:

bin/server.dart
import 'package:dox_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() async {
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);
  await Migrator(migrations: migrations).migrate();
  await Dox().startServer();
}

Keep the db/migration folder next to the binary if you also have .sql migrations.

docs.title: Database settings
docs.text:
The migrations read the .env file and the environment variables. A real environment variable wins over .env, the same as Env.get().

When DATABASE_URL is set, it wins over all DB_* keys. See DATABASE_URL.

.env
DB_CONNECTION=postgres # or mysql (also MariaDB), or sqlite
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
DB_NAME=postgres
DB_USERNAME=admin
DB_PASSWORD=password

For SQLite, only two variables are needed:

.env
DB_CONNECTION=sqlite
DB_NAME=storage/app.db # file path, made if missing
  • DB_DATABASE works too, in place of DB_NAME.
  • The default port is 5432 for Postgres and 3306 for MySQL.
  • One run opens one driver and closes it at the end. Each migration runs on one connection.
  • A DB_HOST that starts with / is a Unix socket.
  • Migrations use TLS only with a DATABASE_URL that has sslmode (Postgres) or ssl (MySQL), like ?sslmode=require. The url options are on the Database page.

You can also give the database yourself:

  • Migrator(migrations: migrations, config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig()) opens this config, and closes it at the end.
  • Migrator(migrations: migrations, connection: SqlQueryBuilder().dbDriver) runs on a driver that is already open. The migrator does not close it.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
Each migration runs in one transaction. On Postgres and SQLite, a failed migration undoes all its changes.

MySQL

On MySQL and MariaDB, CREATE, ALTER and DROP save right away. So if a migration fails half way, these changes stay. Only data changes are undone. Keep each MySQL migration small: one table change per migration.

To run a migration without a transaction (for example CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on Postgres):

class AddSearchIndex extends Migration {
  @override
  bool get withinTransaction => false;

  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.driver.execute(
      'CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY posts_title_index ON posts (title)',
    );
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.driver.execute('DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY posts_title_index');
  }
}

SQLite foreign keys

On SQLite, foreign key checks are off while a migration runs. This lets Dox make a table again (see SQLite notes). Before the end, Dox checks all foreign keys. The migration fails if one is broken.

docs.title: SQL migrations
docs.text:
Use a .sql migration for SQL that only one database understands.

dox make:migration create_blog_table --sql

-- up
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS blog (
    id serial PRIMARY KEY,
    title VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL
);

-- down
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS blog
  • Put the up SQL under a line -- up, and the down SQL under a line -- down. Each of these lines must be on its own line. Other -- lines are normal SQL comments.
  • Statements are split on ;. A ; inside quotes, comments or a postgres $$ ... $$ body does not split.

SQLite ids

In SQLite, id serial PRIMARY KEY does not make an auto increment id. The id stays NULL. Use id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT for SQLite. table.id() in Dart does this for you.

docs.title: Dart and SQL in one folder
docs.text:
Both kinds can live in db/migration. They run in file name order (the timestamp).

  • With bin/migrate.dart: the Migrator runs the Dart migrations from the registry and reads the .sql files from the folder, merged by name.
  • Without bin/migrate.dart (a project with only .sql files): dox runs the .sql files itself.
  • A Dart and a .sql migration with the same name is an error.

docs.title: Native MySQL driver
docs.text:
dox_mysql_native is the MySQL and MariaDB driver of the Dox ORM, written in Rust.

You use it through your models and queries. It needs no extra config. Rust (mysql_async) owns the connections and the pool. Each connection keeps its prepared statements. It works with MySQL 8.4 (the default caching_sha2_password login) and MariaDB 11.

Alpha

This driver is new. If you see a problem, please open an issue.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text: A find-by-id query takes about 65 µs alone, and about 10 µs each with 32 queries in flight (AOT build, local MySQL 8.4 or MariaDB 11, Apple M-series). See Performance: database drivers.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
dox_orm depends on dox_mysql_native. You do not add it yourself. Add it only to use MysqlNativePool without the ORM:

dart pub add dox_mysql_native

You do not need Rust. The build hook downloads a ready-built library for your system.

The package lives in its own repo: dartondox/dox-mysql-native.

docs.title: When the library does not load
docs.text:
MySQL has no other driver in Dox. When the native library does not load, SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig (and every other place that opens a MySQL connection) throws an UnsupportedError like this:

dox_mysql_native did not load: <reason>.
Dox needs it to talk to MySQL. Fix: run the app with `dart run` or `dart build cli`. ...

To fix it:

  • Run the app with dart run, dart test or dart build cli. They run the build hook. dart compile exe does not.
  • Or install Rust. The build hook then builds the library from source.
  • When you set lib_path in pubspec.yaml, check that the file is there and is built for your system.

A driverFactory on the connection wins over all of this: the ORM uses your driver.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
The driver reads the normal fields of the ConnectionConfig (host, port, user, password, database, useSSL) and these keys from extra:

Key Default What it does maxConnectionCount 10 Most connections in the pool. maxConnectionAge 12 hours A connection older than this is closed and opened again. preparedStatementCacheSize 100 Prepared statements kept per connection. threads 1 Rust threads for all pools of the process. Only the first pool sets it. One thread is the fastest for most apps. verifyCertificate true With useSSL, TLS checks the server certificate. Set it to false only for a self-signed certificate in development.

Isolates that open a pool with the same settings share one pool in Rust. So maxConnectionCount is for the whole process, not per isolate. You can also give driver.pool.handle (an int) to another isolate and use MysqlNativeDriver(MysqlNativePool.fromHandle(handle)) there. MysqlNativeDriver comes from package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart.

A request (pool slot, connect and query) fails after 300 s with no answer. A transaction that gets no request for 300 s is rolled back, so its connection goes back to the pool.

docs.title: Use it without the ORM
docs.text:
MysqlNativePool pool = MysqlNativePool.open(
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'root',
  password: 'password',
  database: 'app',
);

MysqlNativeResult result = await pool.query(
  'SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id = ?',
  parameters: <Object?>[1],
);
print(result.rows); // [{id: 1, name: Ada}]

MysqlNativeResult insert = await pool.query(
  'INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (@name)',
  parameters: <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Bob'},
);
print(insert.insertId); // the new AUTO_INCREMENT id
print(insert.affectedRows); // 1

int tx = await pool.begin();
await pool.execute('UPDATE users SET name = ?', parameters: <Object?>['Cy'], transaction: tx);
await pool.commit(tx); // or pool.rollback(tx)
  • parameters is a list for ?, or a map for @name.
  • execute is like query, but the rows are not sent back to Dart.
  • A transaction runs on one connection. Its queries run in the order you send them.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
MySQL / MariaDB Dart TINYINT(1) (boolean()) bool TINYINT, SMALLINT, INT, BIGINT, YEAR int FLOAT, DOUBLE, DECIMAL double CHAR, VARCHAR, TEXT, ENUM String DATE, DATETIME, TIMESTAMP DateTime in UTC TIME String, like 12:34:56 JSON the decoded JSON value BLOB, BINARY, VARBINARY Uint8List NULL null

MariaDB keeps JSON columns as LONGTEXT. So on MariaDB, TEXT that is a JSON object or array comes back decoded.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Every error throws MysqlException. For an error from the server, code is the MySQL error number (eg. 1062 for a duplicate key) and sqlState is the 5 letter SQLSTATE. For other errors (eg. the server is down) both are null. MysqlException comes from package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart.

try {
  await QueryBuilder.table('users').insert(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
} on MysqlException catch (error) {
  if (error.code == 1062) print('taken');
}

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• The timeZone, collation, serverPublicKey and timeoutMs keys are not read. The connection uses utf8mb4.
  • A login with sha256_password (not the default) does not work. The default caching_sha2_password and mysql_native_password work.

docs.title: Native Postgres driver
docs.text:
dox_postgres_native is the Postgres driver of the Dox ORM, written in Rust.

You use it through your models and queries. It needs no extra config. Rust (tokio-postgres) owns the connections and the pool. Each connection keeps its prepared statements.

Alpha

This driver is new. If you see a problem, please open an issue.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text: A find-by-id query takes about 60 µs alone, and about 12.5 µs each with 64 queries in flight (AOT build, local Postgres 14, Apple M-series). See Performance: database drivers.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
dox_orm depends on dox_postgres_native. You do not add it yourself. Add it only to use PgNativePool without the ORM:

dart pub add dox_postgres_native

You do not need Rust. The build hook downloads a ready-built library for your system.

The package lives in its own repo: dartondox/dox-postgres-native.

docs.title: When the library does not load
docs.text:
Postgres has no other driver in Dox. When the native library does not load, SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig (and every other place that opens a Postgres connection) throws an UnsupportedError like this:

dox_postgres_native did not load: <reason>.
Dox needs it to talk to Postgres. Fix: run the app with `dart run` or `dart build cli`. ...

The reason tells what went wrong, for example no library for your system. To fix it:

  • Run the app with dart run, dart test or dart build cli. They run the build hook. dart compile exe does not.
  • Or install Rust. The build hook then builds the library from source.
  • When you set lib_path in pubspec.yaml, check that the file is there and is built for your system.

A driverFactory on the connection wins over all of this: the ORM uses your driver.

docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
Set the TLS mode with useSSL or extra['sslMode'], or with sslmode in the DATABASE_URL:

Mode What it does disable No TLS. The default. prefer TLS when the server has it. No certificate check. require TLS. No certificate check, like libpq. useSSL: true gives this mode. verify-ca TLS. The certificate is checked, the host name is not. verify-full TLS. The certificate and the host name are checked. It uses the Mozilla roots and the roots of the system. 
ConnectionConfig(
  driver: Driver.postgres,
  // ... host, user, password, database as before
  extra: <String, dynamic>{'sslMode': 'verify-full'},
  debug: false,
),

To trust your own CA (for example the CA bundle of your cloud database, or a self-signed CA in development), give the path of a PEM file in extra['sslRootCert'], or with sslrootcert in the url. Then verify-full trusts only the certificates in that file. prefer and require do not use it.

extra: <String, dynamic>{
  'sslMode': 'verify-full',
  'sslRootCert': '/etc/ssl/certs/db-ca.pem',
},

DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:secret@db.example.com/blog?sslmode=verify-full&sslrootcert=/etc/ssl/certs/db-ca.pem

A missing file, or a file with no valid certificate, throws PgException when the pool opens.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
The driver reads these keys from extra of the ConnectionConfig:

Key Default What it does maxConnectionCount 10 Most connections in the pool, for the whole process. sslMode disable TLS mode, see TLS. sslRootCert none Path of a PEM file with the CA certificates to trust for verify-full, see TLS. timeZone UTC Time zone of the session. applicationName none Name of the app in pg_stat_activity. threads 1 Rust threads for all pools of the process. 0 is one thread with a single-thread runtime. Only the first pool sets it.

Isolates that open a pool with the same settings share one pool in Rust. So maxConnectionCount is for the whole process, not per isolate. The pool closes when the last isolate closes it. You can also give driver.pool.handle (an int) to another isolate and use PostgresNativeDriver(PgNativePool.fromHandle(handle)) there. PostgresNativeDriver comes from package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart.

Each connection keeps up to 512 prepared statements. When it is full, it drops the one used longest ago. A request (pool slot, connect and query) fails after 300 s with no answer. A transaction that gets no request for 300 s is rolled back.

docs.title: Use it without the ORM
docs.text:
PgNativePool pool = PgNativePool.open(
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'postgres',
  password: 'postgres',
  database: 'postgres',
);

PgNativeResult result = await pool.query(
  'SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id = @id',
  parameters: <String, dynamic>{'id': 1},
);
print(result.rows); // [{id: 1, name: Ada}]

int tx = await pool.begin();
await pool.query('UPDATE users SET name = @n', parameters: <String, dynamic>{'n': 'Bob'}, transaction: tx);
await pool.commit(tx); // or pool.rollback(tx)
  • parameters is a map for @name, or a list for $1, $2.
  • A transaction runs on one connection. Its queries run in the order you send them.
  • PgNativePool.fromUrl('postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db?sslmode=require') makes a pool from a url.

docs.title: Values
docs.text:
You send plain Dart values: null, bool, int, double, String, DateTime, Duration (an interval), Uint8List (bytea), Map (json) and List (an array, eg. for int4[]).

  • The server picks the type. When it can not, add a cast in the SQL, eg. @id::int8.
  • A List is an array, not json. On insert and update the ORM sends a List as json text, so a List in a json column works. With the pool alone, send jsonEncode(list) for a json column.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Postgres Dart int2, int4, int8 int float4, float8 double numeric String text, varchar, char String bool bool timestamp, timestamptz, date DateTime in UTC infinity dates the text 'infinity' or '-infinity' time String, eg. '13:45:01.5' interval Duration (a month is 30 days) json, jsonb the decoded JSON value uuid String bytea Uint8List arrays of most types above List NULL null

Other types come back as Uint8List.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A server error throws PgServerException. It has code (the SQLSTATE, eg. 23505 for a unique violation), severity, message, and detail, hint, schema, table, column and constraint when the server sends them. Other errors (eg. the server is down, a TLS error, a timeout) throw PgException. Both come from package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart.

try {
  await QueryBuilder.table('users').insert(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
} on PgServerException catch (error) {
  if (error.code == '23505') print('taken: ${error.constraint}');
}

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text: • maxConnectionAge and queryTimeout are not read.

docs.title: Query Builder
docs.text:
The query builder makes SQL from chained methods and runs it with bound values on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite.

Set up the database first. See Database.

docs.title: Start a query
docs.text:
There are two ways to start a query.

// with a model: the result is a list of Actor models
List<Actor> actors = await Actor().where('age', '>=', 23).get();

// with a table name: the result is a list of maps, one map per row
List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('actor')
    .where('age', '>=', 23)
    .get();

The examples on this page use an Actor model on the table actor. The SQL in the examples is for Postgres. MySQL quotes names with ` instead of ".

Start each query with a new object

A query object keeps its where, orderBy and other parts. Use Actor() (or QueryBuilder.table(...)) again for each new query.

docs.title: get
docs.text:
Runs the query and returns all rows that match.

List<Actor> actors = await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').get();
// SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "name" = @name_p0

docs.title: all
docs.text:
Returns all rows of the table. all() ignores where, join, orderBy and limit. Use get() for those.

List<Actor> actors = await Actor().all();
// SELECT * FROM "actor"

docs.title: find
docs.text:
Returns one row, or null when there is no match.

// by primary key
Actor? actor = await Actor().find(1);
// SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "id" = @id_p0 LIMIT 1

// by another column
Actor? byName = await Actor().find('name', 'John Wick');
// SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "name" = @name_p0 LIMIT 1

docs.title: getFirst
docs.text:
Returns the first row of the query, or null.

Actor? actor = await Actor().where('age', '>', 60).orderBy('age').getFirst();
// SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "age" > @age_p0 ORDER BY "age" LIMIT 1

docs.title: count
docs.text:
Returns the number of rows as an int.

int total = await Actor().count();
int adults = await Actor().where('age', '>=', 18).count();
// SELECT count(*) as total FROM "actor" WHERE "age" >= @age_p0
  • count() ignores limit, offset and orderBy.
  • With groupBy, count() returns the number of groups.

docs.title: paginate
docs.text:
Returns one page of rows and the page info. It runs a count() query and a get() query.

Pagination<Actor> page = await Actor()
    .where('age', '>=', 18)
    .paginate(currentPage: 2, perPage: 10);

List<Actor> actors = page.data;
print(page.total);    // rows that match
print(page.lastPage); // number of pages

page.toJson() gives total, per_page, last_page, current_page and data. So you can return a Pagination from a controller.

docs.title: where
docs.text:
// equal
await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').get();
// WHERE "name" = @name_p0

// other operator
await Actor().where('age', '>=', 23).get();
await Actor().where('name', '!=', 'John Wick').get();
await Actor().where('name', 'like', 'John%').get();

// null
await Actor().where('deleted_at', null).get();
// WHERE "deleted_at" IS NULL

Many where calls are joined with AND.

Info

The operator must be one of =, !=, <>, <, >, <=, >=, like, not like or ilike (any case). Any other value throws an ArgumentError. The column must be a plain name. Use whereRaw for expressions.

docs.title: orWhere
docs.text:
await Actor().where('name', 'John Doe').orWhere('name', 'John Wick').get();
// WHERE "name" = @name_p0 OR "name" = @name_p1

await Actor().where('age', '<', 18).orWhere('age', '>', 60).get();

docs.title: whereIn and whereNotIn
docs.text:
await Actor().whereIn('id', <int>[1, 2]).get();
// WHERE "id" IN (@id_p0,@id_p1)

await Actor().whereNotIn('id', <int>[1, 2]).get();
await Actor().where('age', 60).orWhereIn('id', <int>[1, 2]).get();
await Actor().where('age', 60).orWhereNotIn('id', <int>[1, 2]).get();
  • On Postgres, a list of only int or only String values is sent as one array parameter: "id" = ANY(@id_p0) (<> ALL for whereNotIn).
  • An empty list matches no rows for whereIn, and all rows for whereNotIn.

docs.title: whereNull and whereNotNull
docs.text:
await Actor().whereNull('deleted_at').get();
await Actor().whereNotNull('deleted_at').get();
await Actor().where('age', 60).orWhereNull('deleted_at').get();
await Actor().where('age', 60).orWhereNotNull('deleted_at').get();

docs.title: whereRaw and orWhereRaw
docs.text:
Write the condition yourself. Put values in a map, and use @key in the SQL. The column names are not quoted.

await Actor().whereRaw('name = @name', <String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Wick'}).get();

await Actor()
    .where('age', 60)
    .orWhereRaw('lower(name) = @name', <String, dynamic>{'name': 'john wick'})
    .get();

Warning

Never put user input into the SQL text. Always send it in the map.

docs.title: Select
docs.text:
select sets the columns. Each call replaces the columns of the call before.

// a list
await Actor().select(<String>['id', 'name']).get();
// SELECT "id","name" FROM "actor"

// comma separated
await Actor().select('id, name, age').get();

// with an alias
await Actor().select('name as actor_name').get();

// raw: nothing is quoted
await Actor().selectRaw('DISTINCT name').get();
await QueryBuilder.table('actor').selectRaw('count(*) as total, name').groupBy('name').get();
