Each part must be a plain name: name, table.name, table.*, * or name as alias. Anything else, like count(*), throws an ArgumentError. Use selectRaw for it.

Info

A model loaded with select() only has the selected fields. save() on it only updates the fields it has.

docs.title: orderBy
docs.text:
await Actor().orderBy('name').get();
await Actor().orderBy('name', 'desc').get();
await Actor().orderBy('name', 'asc').orderBy('id', 'desc').get();
// ORDER BY "name" asc,"id" desc
  • The direction must be asc or desc. Any other value throws an ArgumentError.
  • The column must be a plain name. Anything else throws an ArgumentError.
  • For an expression, use orderByRaw('count(*) desc'). Nothing is quoted there, so never put user input in it.

docs.title: limit, take and offset
docs.text:
limit and take do the same thing.

await Actor().limit(10).get();
await Actor().take(10).get();
await Actor().limit(10).offset(20).get();
// LIMIT @dox_limit OFFSET @dox_offset

The numbers are sent as bound parameters.

docs.title: groupBy
docs.text:
Takes one column, or a list of columns.

List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('actor')
    .selectRaw('count(*) as total, age')
    .groupBy('age')
    .get();

For an expression, use groupByRaw('date(created_at)'). Nothing is quoted there.

Info

Use QueryBuilder.table() for groupBy. A group row is a map, not a model. On a model, get() gives models (List<Actor>), so a groupBy there throws a StateError. count() with groupBy works on a model too.

docs.title: Join
docs.text:
await Actor().join('actor_info', 'actor_info.actor_id', 'actor.id').get();
// JOIN "actor_info" on "actor_info"."actor_id" = "actor"."id"

await Actor().leftJoin('actor_info', 'actor_info.actor_id', 'actor.id').get();
await Actor().rightJoin('actor_info', 'actor_info.actor_id', 'actor.id').get();

// with an operator
await Actor().join('actor_info', 'actor_info.actor_id', '=', 'actor.id').get();

For other join conditions, use the raw methods. Nothing is quoted. Values go in the map, like in whereRaw.

await Actor().joinRaw('actor_info on actor_info.actor_id = actor.id').get();
await Actor().leftJoinRaw('actor_info on actor_info.actor_id = actor.id').get();
await Actor().rightJoinRaw(
  'actor_info on actor_info.actor_id = actor.id and actor_info.type = @type',
  <String, dynamic>{'type': 'main'},
).get();

Note

SQLite before 3.39 has no RIGHT JOIN.

docs.title: create and insert
docs.text:
create and insert do the same thing. They insert one row, then read it back and return it.

Actor actor = await Actor().create(<String, dynamic>{
  'name': 'John Wick',
  'age': 60,
});
print(actor.id);
  • On a model, the result is the model. On QueryBuilder.table(...), the result is a map.
  • It works with any primary key type, for example a uuid string.
  • On a model with events, create calls save(), so the hooks run.

docs.title: insertMultiple
docs.text:
Inserts many rows in one query. It does not return models. On Postgres it returns the new ids, like [{id: 4}, {id: 5}]. On MySQL it returns only one id.

await Actor().insertMultiple(<Map<String, dynamic>>[
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Wick', 'age': 60},
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Doe', 'age': 25},
]);

The columns are the keys from all rows. When a row does not have a key, that column gets its default value.

docs.title: Update
docs.text:
Updates all rows that match the where part.

await Actor()
    .where('id', 3)
    .where('status', 'active')
    .update(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'Updated AJ', 'age': 120});
// UPDATE "actor" SET "name" = @name_p2,"age" = @age_p3
//   WHERE "id" = @id_p0 AND "status" = @status_p1

Warning

update without where changes every row of the table. A query update does not set updated_at and fires no model events. To do that, load the model, change it and call save().

docs.title: delete
docs.text:
Deletes all rows that match the where part.

await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').delete();
// DELETE FROM "actor" WHERE "name" = @name_p0

On a model with softDelete: true, delete sets deleted_at and keeps the row.

docs.title: forceDelete
docs.text:
On a model with softDelete: true, forceDelete really deletes the rows. It also deletes rows that are already soft deleted, so you do not need withTrash().

await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').forceDelete();

docs.title: withTrash
docs.text:
A model with softDelete: true hides soft deleted rows. withTrash() shows them too. On a model without soft deletes it does nothing.

List<Actor> actors = await Actor().withTrash().where('name', 'John Wick').get();

docs.title: truncate
docs.text:
Deletes all rows of the table and resets the id counter.

await Actor().truncate();
await Actor().truncate(resetId: false); // keep the id counter on Postgres and SQLite

On Postgres it runs TRUNCATE TABLE ... RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE. On SQLite it runs DELETE FROM.

docs.title: toSql
docs.text:
Returns the SQL of the query with the values filled in. The values are not quoted or escaped, so use it only to read the query.

String sql = Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').toSql();
print(sql); // SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "name" = John Wick

docs.title: debug
docs.text:
Prints the SQL and the values of the query when it runs.

await Actor().debug(true).where('age', 60).get();

To print all queries, set debug: true in the ConnectionConfig. See Database.

docs.title: Schema builder
docs.text:
The schema builder creates, changes and drops tables with Dart code that works on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite.

You mostly use it inside a migration.

await schema.create('posts', (Table table) {
  table.id();
  table.foreignId('user_id').constrained().cascadeOnDelete();
  table.string('title');
  table.text('body').nullable();
  table.enumeration('status', <String>['draft', 'published']).defaultTo('draft');
  table.timestamps();
});

docs.title: Get a schema
docs.text:
In a migration, up and down get a Schema. It runs on the migration connection.

Outside a migration, Schema() uses the query builder connection. You can also give a driver: Schema(driver).

Schema schema = Schema();
await schema.dropIfExists('posts');

docs.title: Tables
docs.text: Method What it does create('t', (Table table) {...}) Create table t. It fails when the table exists. table('t', (Table table) {...}) Change table t: add columns, change columns, keys. drop('t') Drop table t. It fails when the table is missing. dropIfExists('t') Drop table t when it exists. rename('from', 'to') Rename a table. hasTable('t') true when the table exists. hasColumn('t', 'c') true when the column exists. getColumnListing('t') The column names, in order.

docs.title: Column types
docs.text:
Method Postgres MySQL / MariaDB SQLite id() / bigIncrements('id') BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT increments('id') SERIAL PRIMARY KEY INT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT string('c', [255]) VARCHAR(n) VARCHAR(n) VARCHAR(n) char('c', [255]) CHAR(n) CHAR(n) CHAR(n) text('c') TEXT TEXT TEXT mediumText('c') TEXT MEDIUMTEXT TEXT longText('c') TEXT LONGTEXT TEXT integer('c') INTEGER INT INTEGER bigInteger('c') BIGINT BIGINT INTEGER smallInteger('c') SMALLINT SMALLINT INTEGER tinyInteger('c') SMALLINT TINYINT INTEGER unsignedInteger('c') (and unsignedBigInteger, unsignedSmallInteger, unsignedTinyInteger) signed type ... UNSIGNED INTEGER float('c') REAL FLOAT FLOAT double('c') DOUBLE PRECISION DOUBLE DOUBLE decimal('c', [8], [2]) DECIMAL(p, s) DECIMAL(p, s) DECIMAL(p, s) boolean('c') BOOLEAN TINYINT(1) BOOLEAN date('c') DATE DATE DATE dateTime('c') TIMESTAMP DATETIME DATETIME dateTimeTz('c') TIMESTAMPTZ DATETIME DATETIME time('c') TIME TIME TIME timestamp('c') TIMESTAMP TIMESTAMP TIMESTAMP timestampTz('c') TIMESTAMPTZ TIMESTAMP TIMESTAMP json('c') / jsonb('c') JSONB JSON JSON uuid(['uuid']) UUID CHAR(36) TEXT binary('c') BYTEA BLOB BLOB enumeration('c', ['a', 'b']) VARCHAR(255) + CHECK ENUM('a', 'b') VARCHAR(255) + CHECK foreignId('user_id') BIGINT BIGINT UNSIGNED INTEGER foreignUuid('user_id') UUID CHAR(36) TEXT

Helpers:

  • timestamps(): nullable created_at and updated_at (timestampTz).
  • softDeletes(['deleted_at']): nullable deleted_at (timestampTz), for models with softDelete: true.
  • rememberToken(): nullable remember_token VARCHAR(100).
  • morphs('owner'): owner_id (unsigned big integer), owner_type (string) and one index on both columns.

JSON on SQLite

SQLite has no JSON type. The column is declared as JSON, so the SQLite driver knows to decode it when you read it.

docs.title: Modifiers
docs.text:
Modifiers come after the column type. They can be chained: table.string('email').nullable().unique().

Modifier What it does Notes nullable() Allow NULL. Columns are NOT NULL by default. nullable(false) makes it NOT NULL again. defaultTo(value) Default value. Strings are escaped, so any text is safe. bool, numbers, null, Map/List (saved as JSON) and DateTime work too. withDefault does the same. defaultRaw('sql') Default as raw SQL. It is not escaped. Put expressions in ( ): defaultRaw('(1 + 1)'). MySQL and SQLite need it. useCurrent() Default to the current time. Same as defaultRaw('CURRENT_TIMESTAMP'). useCurrentOnUpdate() Set the current time on each update. MySQL only. Postgres and SQLite ignore it. Set the time in your code there. unique() Add a unique index {table}_{column}_unique. index() Add an index {table}_{column}_index. primary() Make the column the primary key. unsigned() UNSIGNED. MySQL only. Others ignore it. comment('text') Column comment. Postgres and MySQL. SQLite ignores it. after('column') Put the new column after another one. MySQL only, only in schema.table. Others add it at the end. change() Change an existing column (in schema.table). See Change columns.

MySQL defaults on TEXT and JSON

MySQL only allows a default on TEXT, BLOB and JSON as an expression. The schema builder writes it as DEFAULT ('value') for you.

docs.title: Change a table
docs.text:
await schema.table('users', (Table table) {
  table.string('avatar').nullable().after('email'); // add
  table.string('name', 100).nullable().change();    // change
  table.renameColumn('bio', 'about');
  table.dropColumn('age');
  table.dropColumns(<String>['a', 'b']);
});

A column in schema.table is added. Add .change() to change a column that exists.

docs.title: Change columns
docs.text:
change() sets the full new column: type, null, default and comment. Give every modifier you want to keep.

// before: string('title') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'x'
table.string('title', 500).nullable().defaultTo('x').change();

How it runs:

Driver SQL Postgres One ALTER TABLE: ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE ... USING col::type, SET/DROP NOT NULL, SET/DROP DEFAULT, and the enum CHECK again. MySQL ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN <full column>. SQLite SQLite can not change a column. Dox makes the table again (see below).

change() with unique() or index() adds the index. It fails when the index already exists.

docs.title: Indexes and keys
docs.text:
columns is a column name or a list of names.

table.index(<String>['state', 'created_at']);  // posts_state_created_at_index
table.unique('slug');                          // posts_slug_unique
table.primary(<String>['post_id', 'tag_id']);  // composite primary key

table.dropIndex(<String>['state', 'created_at']); // by columns
table.dropUnique('posts_slug_unique');            // or by name

Index names are {table}_{columns}_{index|unique|foreign}. You can give your own name as the last argument: table.unique('slug', 'my_name').

docs.title: Foreign keys
docs.text:
table.foreignId('user_id').constrained().cascadeOnDelete();
// same as:
table.foreignId('user_id');
table.foreign('user_id').references('id').on('users').onDelete('cascade');
  • constrained([table], [column = 'id']) guesses the table from the column: user_id becomes users, category_id becomes categories. Dox models use singular table names by default (User is user). If your table is singular, give it: constrained('user').
  • Actions: onDelete('cascade' | 'set null' | 'restrict' | 'no action'), onUpdate(...), and the short ones cascadeOnDelete(), nullOnDelete(), restrictOnDelete(), cascadeOnUpdate().
  • Put nullable() before constrained(): table.foreignId('editor_id').nullable().constrained('users').
  • Drop it: table.dropForeign(<String>['user_id']) or table.dropForeign('posts_user_id_foreign').

Same type on both sides

id() is a big integer. foreignId() is a big integer too, so they match. If the parent uses increments() (a normal integer), use unsignedInteger() for the child on MySQL.

docs.title: SQLite notes
docs.text:
SQLite ALTER TABLE can only add, rename and drop columns. For these changes, Dox makes the table again:

  • change() of a column,
  • foreign(...) on an existing table,
  • dropForeign(...).

It makes a new table with the change, copies the rows, drops the old table and renames the new one. It keeps the columns, primary key, AUTOINCREMENT, foreign keys, indexes and enum checks. All of it runs in one transaction. It fails on tables with other CHECK constraints or with generated columns.

Other SQLite limits:

  • primary(...) on an existing table is not supported.
  • A new column that is NOT NULL needs a default. A new column can not default to CURRENT_TIMESTAMP.
  • dropColumn fails when the column is in an index or a foreign key. Drop those first.

docs.title: Per driver notes
docs.text: Feature Postgres MySQL / MariaDB SQLite comment COMMENT ON COLUMN inline COMMENT ignored add/drop foreign key on a table ALTER TABLE ALTER TABLE table rebuild schema changes in a transaction yes no, saved right away yes index name length 63 64 no limit

docs.title: See the SQL
docs.text:
Every change is a Table blueprint. A grammar turns it into SQL, without a database:

Table table = Table('users', creating: true)
  ..id()
  ..string('email').unique();
print(table.toSql(PostgresGrammar()));
// [CREATE TABLE "users" ("id" BIGSERIAL NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, "email" VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL),
//  CREATE UNIQUE INDEX "users_email_unique" ON "users" ("email")]

Grammars: PostgresGrammar, MysqlGrammar and SqliteGrammar. On SQLite, the changes that need a table rebuild only run on a database.

docs.title: Seeders
docs.text: A seeder puts data in your database. Use it for sample data in development, or for data your app needs, like a list of countries.

docs.title: Create a seeder
docs.text:
dox make:seeder UserSeeder

This makes three files:

File What it is db/seeders/user.seeder.dart the new seeder db/seeders/seeders.dart the list of all seeders. Dox writes it again on each make:seeder and db:seed. Do not edit it. bin/seed.dart the script that runs a seeder. It is made only when it is missing. db/seeders/user.seeder.dart
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import '../factories/user.factory.dart';

class UserSeeder extends Seeder {
  @override
  Future<void> run() async {
    await UserFactory().count(10).create();
  }
}

Use factories, models or the query builder in run().

docs.title: DatabaseSeeder
docs.text:
dox db:seed runs DatabaseSeeder by default. Use it to call your other seeders.

dox make:seeder DatabaseSeeder
db/seeders/database.seeder.dart
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import 'post.seeder.dart';
import 'user.seeder.dart';

class DatabaseSeeder extends Seeder {
  @override
  Future<void> run() async {
    await call(<Seeder>[UserSeeder(), PostSeeder()]);
  }
}

call() runs the seeders one after another, in the list order.

docs.title: Run seeders
docs.text:
Command What it does dox db:seed Run DatabaseSeeder. dox db:seed --class=UserSeeder Run one seeder. dox migration:fresh --seed Drop all tables, run all migrations, then run DatabaseSeeder. dox migration:refresh --seed Undo all migrations, run them again, then run DatabaseSeeder. dox migration:run --seed Run new migrations, then run DatabaseSeeder.

migrate:fresh and migrate:refresh are short names, so dox migrate:fresh --seed works too.

The database comes from .env, the same as the migrations: DATABASE_URL, or DB_CONNECTION, DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD and DB_NAME.

Warning

migration:fresh drops every table of the database, also tables that no migration made. Do not run it on a production database.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
A seed runs in one transaction. When a seeder throws an error, nothing is saved, and the command exits with code 1.

On MySQL and MariaDB, CREATE, ALTER and DROP TABLE save right away. A rollback can not undo them. Keep schema changes in migrations.

A very large seed can turn the transaction off:

class BigSeeder extends Seeder {
  @override
  bool get withinTransaction => false;

  @override
  Future<void> run() async {
    // ...
  }
}

Only the seeder you run says if there is a transaction. For dox db:seed it is DatabaseSeeder.

docs.title: bin/seed.dart
docs.text:
dox db:seed runs dart run bin/seed.dart. You can run it yourself too, for example in a deploy script:

dart run bin/seed.dart
dart run bin/seed.dart --class=UserSeeder
bin/seed.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import '../db/seeders/seeders.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SeederRunner(seeders: seeders).run(args);
}

SeederRunner sets up the ORM, runs the seeder and closes the ORM. Pass config: to use your app's database config instead of .env:

import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SeederRunner(
    seeders: seeders,
    config: databaseConfig,
  ).run(args);
}

docs.title: Use in tests
docs.text:
A seeder is a normal class. Call run() after you set up the ORM:

await DatabaseSeeder().run();

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
A transaction runs many queries as one unit, so either all of them are saved or none of them.

QueryBuilder.transaction() takes a function:

  • It commits when the function ends.
  • It rolls back when the function throws. Then the error is thrown again.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
// a transaction
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  Actor actor = Actor();
  actor.name = 'John Wick';
  await actor.save();
  await QueryBuilder.table('actor_info').insert(<String, dynamic>{
    'actor_id': actor.id,
  });
});

// return a value
int? id = await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  Actor actor = Actor();
  actor.name = 'John Wick';
  await actor.save();
  return actor.id;
});

// on another connection
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  // ...
}, connection: 'mysql');
  • All queries and models inside the function use the transaction. You do not pass a transaction object around.
  • A transaction inside another transaction uses a savepoint. See Nested transactions.

MySQL

On MySQL and MariaDB, CREATE, ALTER and DROP TABLE are saved right away. A rollback can not undo them.

docs.title: Nested transactions
docs.text:
A transaction inside another transaction uses a savepoint. It runs on the same connection as the outer one.

  • When the inner function ends, its work stays in the outer transaction. It is saved when the outer one commits.
  • When the inner function throws, only its work is undone. Then the error is thrown again.
  • If you catch that error, the outer transaction goes on and can still commit.
  • If you do not catch it, the outer transaction rolls back too.
  • When the outer transaction rolls back, the inner work is undone too.
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await Actor().create(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Wick'});
  try {
    await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
      await Actor().create(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'Bad row'});
      throw StateError('stop');
    });
  } on StateError {
    // only 'Bad row' is undone
  }
});
// 'John Wick' is saved

This works on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. You can nest many levels.

  • Run nested transactions one after another, not at the same time (for example in Future.wait). They share one connection.
  • On MySQL and MariaDB, a CREATE, ALTER or DROP TABLE inside a nested transaction saves the outer work and ends the savepoint. Do not change the schema there.

docs.title: Connections
docs.text:
• Postgres and MySQL use a connection pool. Set the size with maxConnectionCount in the extra map of the connection.
  • A transaction uses one connection of the pool. Other queries use the other connections.
  • SQLite has one connection per isolate. While a transaction is open, the other queries of that isolate wait.
  • When a model has more than one relation to load (preload or eager), the relation queries run at the same time outside a transaction. Inside a transaction, they run one after another on its connection.
  • A query runs in a transaction only when you use QueryBuilder.transaction().

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
A model is a Dart class for one database table, used to read, create, change and delete its rows.

A model has all the query builder methods too.

docs.title: Create a model
docs.text:
dox make:model Blog      # only the model
dox make:model Blog -m   # the model and a migration for the table `blogs`

This makes lib/app/models/blog/blog.model.dart. create:model is another name for the same command.

The model code uses a generated class (BlogGenerator). Run the generator after you make or change a model:

dart run build_runner build

dart run build_runner watch runs the generator again each time you save a file.

docs.title: A model
Model options
docs.text:
All options go in @DoxModel(...).

Option Default What it does table class name in snake_case The table name. primaryKey 'id' The primary key column. primaryKeyType int The Dart type of the primary key, like String for a UUID. createdAt 'created_at' The column that keeps the create time. updatedAt 'updated_at' The column that keeps the last update time. timestamps true false turns off createdAt and updatedAt. softDelete false delete() sets deleted_at and keeps the row.

docs.title: table
docs.text:
The default table name is the class name in snake_case, and singular. Blog uses blog, and BlogPost uses blog_post.

@DoxModel(table: 'blogs')
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}

Info

dox make:model Blog -m sets table: 'blogs' for you, because the migration makes the plural table blogs.

docs.title: primaryKey
docs.text:
@DoxModel(primaryKey: 'uid')
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}

The field name is the key in camelCase. With primaryKey: 'blog_id', the field is blogId.

docs.title: primaryKeyType
docs.text:
The primary key field is int? by default. Use primaryKeyType for another type, like a UUID string.

@DoxModel(primaryKey: 'uuid', primaryKeyType: String)
class Device extends DeviceGenerator {}

Device device = Device();
device.uuid = '0b6f2c1e-1a2b-4c3d-8e9f-001122334455';
await device.save(); // insert

save() inserts a new model, also when you set the key yourself. It updates a model that was read from the table or saved before. model.exists tells which one it is.

docs.title: createdAt and updatedAt
docs.text:
save() sets these columns to the current UTC time. Use the options when your columns have other names.

@DoxModel(createdAt: 'created', updatedAt: 'modified')
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}

Read the values with blog.createdAt and blog.updatedAt.

docs.title: timestamps
docs.text:
Set timestamps: false when the table has no created_at and updated_at columns.

@DoxModel(timestamps: false)
class Setting extends SettingGenerator {}

To turn off only one of them, set it to null, like @DoxModel(updatedAt: null).

docs.title: softDelete
docs.text:
@DoxModel(softDelete: true)
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}

The table needs a nullable deleted_at column. In a migration, add table.softDeletes();.

  • delete() sets deleted_at to the current time. The row stays in the table.
  • Queries do not return soft deleted rows. Use withTrash() to get them too.
  • forceDelete() really deletes the row.
  • restore() sets deleted_at back to NULL.

docs.title: Field types
docs.text:
The field type tells Dox how to read the value.

Field type Column String? text, varchar int? integer types double? float, double. MySQL also gives DECIMAL as double. Postgres gives numeric as String. bool? boolean, or a number like tinyint (0 is false) DateTime? date, datetime, timestamp Map<String, dynamic>? or List<dynamic>? JSON an enum, like Status? text with the enum name

For other conversions, use a cast, or beforeSave and beforeGet.

docs.title: beforeSave and beforeGet
docs.text:
These options take a static function of the model class. The function gets a map and returns the value.

  • beforeSave runs before a save. It gets the model values (column name => value). It returns the value to save in this column.
  • beforeGet runs when a row is read. It gets the row from the database. It returns the value for this field.
@DoxModel()
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  // beforeSave: make the slug from the title
  @Column(beforeSave: makeSlug)
  String? slug;

  // beforeGet: old rows have no status, show them as draft
  @Column(beforeGet: readStatus)
  String? status;

  static String? makeSlug(Map<String, dynamic> map) {
    return map['title']?.toString().toLowerCase().replaceAll(' ', '-');
  }

  static String? readStatus(Map<String, dynamic> map) {
    return map['status'] as String? ?? 'draft';
  }
}

docs.title: Save
docs.text:
save() inserts a new model, or updates a model that has an id.

// insert
Blog blog = Blog();
blog.title = 'My first blog';
await blog.save();
print(blog.id); // the new id

// update
Blog? found = await Blog().find(1);
found?.title = 'New title';
await found?.save();

// set a field to null
found?.slug = null;
await found?.save(); // slug is now NULL in the database

// create from a map
Blog created = await Blog().create(<String, dynamic>{
  'title': 'My first blog',
  'status': 'draft',
});
  • On insert, null fields are not sent, so the database default is used.
  • On update, only the fields that changed are sent. A field is compared to its value from the last load or save. A Map or List field is always sent, because it can change in place.
  • When nothing changed, save() runs no query, and updated_at stays as it is.
  • On update, a field is set to NULL only when it had a value before (loaded from the database, or saved). Fields that were not loaded, for example with select(), are not changed.
  • save() returns false when a model event cancels it.

docs.title: Mass assignment
docs.text:
create(), insert() and update() take any key of the map. So User().create(req.body) with {"is_admin": 1} makes an admin. Set fillable or guarded to stop this.

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  // only these keys are taken from a map
  @override
  List<String> get fillable => <String>['name', 'email'];

  // or: these keys are never taken from a map
  @override
  List<String> get guarded => <String>['is_admin'];
}
  • Keys that are not allowed are dropped. They do not throw.
  • Both lists are empty by default. Then every key is taken.
  • save() is not changed. Fields you set in code are always saved.

docs.title: Delete
docs.text:
// delete a record
Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);
await blog?.delete(); // deletes only this record

// force delete
Blog? trashed = await Blog().withTrash().find(1);
await trashed?.forceDelete(); // deletes the row, also with softDelete

// restore
Blog? deleted = await Blog().withTrash().find(1);
await deleted?.restore(); // sets deleted_at back to NULL

save(), delete(), forceDelete() and restore() fire model events.

docs.title: Convert to a map or JSON
docs.text:
Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);

Map<String, dynamic>? map = blog?.toMap();  // all columns and computed values
Map<String, dynamic>? json = blog?.toJson(); // the same, without hidden fields
Map<String, dynamic>? row = blog?.toMap(original: true); // the raw database row

jsonEncode(blog) uses toJson(). So you can return a model, or a list of models, from a controller.

docs.title: Hide fields
docs.text:
Fields in hidden are left out of toJson(). Use the column names.

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>['password', 'remember_token'];
}

docs.title: Computed values
docs.text:
A computed value is a getter that is added to toJson() and toMap(). Add @Computed() to the getter, then run dart run build_runner build.

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column(name: 'first_name')
  String? firstName;

  @Column(name: 'last_name')
  String? lastName;

  @Computed() // json key: full_name
  String get fullName => '$firstName $lastName';

  @Computed(name: 'initials') // custom json key
  String get shortName => '${firstName?[0]}${lastName?[0]}';
}

User? user = await User().find(1);
print(user?.toJson());
// {id: 1, first_name: John, last_name: Wick, ..., full_name: John Wick, initials: JW}
  • The default key is the getter name in snake_case (fullName becomes full_name).
  • A computed value is never a column. It is not read from the database, and it is not sent in INSERT or UPDATE.
  • hidden also hides computed values. Use the json key, for example ['full_name'].
  • Computed values of loaded relations are in the nested JSON too.
  • toMap(original: true) returns the raw database row, so it has no computed values.
  • A getter runs each time toJson() or toMap() is called, so keep it fast.

docs.title: New query
docs.text:
A model object keeps the parts of its query (where, orderBy, ...). query() gives a new, empty model, so you can start another query.

Blog blog = Blog();
List<Blog> active = await blog.where('status', 'active').get();

// a new query, without the where above
List<Blog> deleted = await blog.query().where('status', 'deleted').get();

docs.title: Debug
docs.text:
debug(true) prints the SQL of this model in the terminal.

Blog blog = Blog();
blog.debug(true);
blog.title = 'John Wick';
await blog.save();

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
A model can load related models. See HasOne, HasMany, BelongsTo and ManyToMany.

The relationship pages use these tables:

erDiagram
    user ||--o| user_info : "HasOne"
    user ||--o{ post : "HasMany"
    user ||--o{ comment : "BelongsTo, from comment"
    artist ||--o{ artist_song : "ManyToMany"
    song ||--o{ artist_song : "ManyToMany"
    user {
        int id PK
        string name
    }
    user_info {
        int id PK
        int user_id FK
        string address
    }
    post {
        int id PK
        int user_id FK
        string title
    }
    comment {
        int id PK
        int user_id FK
        string content
    }
    artist_song {
        int id PK
        int artist_id FK
        int song_id FK
    }

docs.title: Attribute casts
docs.text:
A cast changes a column value between the database and Dart. For example, it reads JSON text as a map, or saves an enum by its name. Casts work the same on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite.

Set a cast with cast on @Column(). Then run dart run build_runner build.

enum Status { draft, live }

enum Level { low, mid, high }

@DoxModel()
class Item extends ItemGenerator {
  @Column(cast: JsonCast())
  Map<String, dynamic>? meta;

  @Column(cast: ListCast<String>())
  List<String>? tags;

  @Column()
  bool? active; // gets BoolCast()

  @Column()
  Status? status; // gets EnumCast(Status.values)

  @Column(cast: EnumCast<Level>(Level.values, byIndex: true))
  Level? level;
}

The cast runs when a row is read (get(), find() and others), when the model is saved, and in toJson().

docs.title: Built-in casts
docs.text:
Cast Dart value Database value JsonCast() a map or a list JSON, or JSON in a text column ListCast<E>() a typed list, like List<String> JSON, or JSON in a text column BoolCast() bool boolean, or a number like tinyint (0 is false), or the text 1, 0, true, false, t, f EnumCast<E>(E.values) an enum text with the enum name EnumCast<E>(E.values, byIndex: true) an enum a number, the enum index

You do not need cast for two field types:

  • A bool field gets BoolCast().
  • An enum field gets EnumCast(values), so it is saved by its name.

DateTime fields need no cast either. Dox reads them on every database.

Info

A cast changes the values of a model. It does not change a where() value. Use the database value there, like where('status', Status.live.name).

docs.title: Your own cast
docs.text:
Extend Cast<T>. get() gets the database value and returns the Dart value. set() gets the Dart value and returns the value to save. The class needs a const constructor.

class Money {
  final int cents;
  const Money(this.cents);
}

class MoneyCast extends Cast<Money> {
  const MoneyCast();

  @override
  Money? get(dynamic value) => value == null ? null : Money(value as int);

  @override
  dynamic set(Money? value) => value?.cents;
}

@DoxModel()
class Product extends ProductGenerator {
  @Column(cast: MoneyCast())
  Money? price;
}

A cast can take const arguments, like EnumCast does. The generator copies the cast code into the generated file, so the names in it must be imported in the model file.

A column with beforeGet does not use its cast.

docs.title: Counting relations
docs.text:
withCount() adds the number of related rows to each model. It does not load the rows. It adds a subquery to the select, so you get the counts with the same query.

It works with hasOne, hasMany and manyToMany relations.

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @HasMany(Post)
  List<Post> posts = <Post>[];
}

List<User> users = await User().withCount('posts').get();

users.first.countOf('posts'); // 3
users.first.toJson();         // {..., "posts_count": 3}

The key is the relation name in snake_case and _count, like posts_count. Use the relation name (the field name) in withCount() and countOf().

docs.title: Count only some rows
docs.text:
Give a function to add conditions to the related rows. Use as to give the count its own key.

List<User> users = await User()
    .withCount('posts')
    .withCount('posts as published_count', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
      q.where('published', true);
    })
    .get();

users.first.countOf('posts');               // all posts
users.first.aggregate('published_count');   // published posts

The global scopes and soft deletes of the related model are used in the count.

docs.title: With other query methods
docs.text:
withCount() works with where(), orderBy(), find(), getFirst(), paginate() and with preload() or eager relations:

User? user = await User().preload('posts').withCount('posts').find(1);
user?.posts;              // the posts
user?.countOf('posts');   // the number of posts

docs.title: Sum and max
docs.text:
withSum() and withMax() work the same way, on one column of the related rows. The value is null when there is no related row.

User? user = await User()
    .withSum('posts', 'views')
    .withMax('posts', 'views')
    .find(1);

user?.aggregate('posts_sum_views');
user?.aggregate('posts_max_views');

Info

withCount() is not for belongsTo relations. It throws an UnsupportedError. A relation from a table to the same table is not supported.

docs.title: Model events
docs.text:
A model fires events when you save, delete or restore it, and you can run your own code on them.

There are two ways to listen:

  • Hooks: methods in the model class. Use them for code that belongs to the model, like filling a value.
  • Observers: separate classes. Use them for code that needs other services, like a mailer.

docs.title: Hooks in the model
docs.text:
Override an on... method in the model. Then run dart run build_runner build.

lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
@DoxModel()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  String? slug;

  @override
  Future<void> onSaving() async {
    slug = title?.trim().toLowerCase().replaceAll(' ', '-');
  }
}

Post post = Post()..title = 'Hello World';
await post.save(); // onSaving runs first, so slug is 'hello-world'

All hooks come in pairs: one runs before the query, one after it.

Before hook After hook Run on onSaving onSaved every save(): a new or a loaded model onCreating onCreated save() or create() on a new model (INSERT) onUpdating onUpdated save() on a loaded model (UPDATE) onDeleting onDeleted delete() onForceDeleting onForceDeleted forceDelete(): really removes a soft-deleted row onRestoring onRestored restore(): brings back a soft-deleted row
  • A before hook runs before the query. The row is not written yet. You can change values, or cancel the operation.
  • An after hook runs after the query. The row is written, and a new model has its id. Use it for side effects.
  • Declare the hooks in the model class itself. The generator looks there.

docs.title: Order of events
docs.text:
Call Events, in order save() on a new model saving → creating → INSERT → created → saved save() on a loaded model saving → updating → UPDATE → updated → saved create({...}) the same as save() on a new model delete() deleting → DELETE or soft delete → deleted forceDelete() forceDeleting → deleting → DELETE → deleted → forceDeleted restore() restoring → UPDATE deleted_at = NULL → restored
  • The model hook runs first. Then the observers run, in the order you added them.
  • When a model has events, create({...}) saves only the @Column fields.

Query updates and deletes fire no events

Events fire only on one model instance. Post().where('draft', true).update({...}), Post().where(...).delete() and insertMultiple() run one query and fire no events.

docs.title: Set a value only on create
docs.text:
onCreating runs only for a new row. Updates do not change the value again.

@override
Future<void> onCreating() async {
  status ??= 'draft';
  publicId = Uuid().v4(); // from package:uuid
}

docs.title: Stop an operation
docs.text:
Throw CancelModelEvent in a before hook. The query does not run, and the call returns false.

lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
@override
Future<void> onDeleting() async {
  if (status == 'published') {
    throw CancelModelEvent('unpublish the post first');
  }
}
lib/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart
Future<Map<String, String>> destroy(DoxRequest req, int id) async {
  Post? post = await Post().find(id);
  if (post == null) throw NotFoundHttpException();

  bool deleted = await post.delete();
  if (!deleted) {
    throw BadRequestException(message: 'Unpublish the post first');
  }
  return <String, String>{'message': 'deleted'};
}
  • save(), delete(), forceDelete() and restore() return false when a hook cancels.
  • create({...}) returns the unsaved model. Its id is null.
  • Any other error from a hook is thrown to the caller.

docs.title: Do something after a change
docs.text:
After hooks are for side effects. The row is already in the database.

@override
Future<void> onSaved() async {
  await Cache().forget('post:$id'); // the next read gets the new data
}

@override
Future<void> onDeleted() async {
  if (coverPath != null) {
    await Storage().delete(coverPath!); // remove the file of the post
  }
}

docs.title: Observers
docs.text:
An observer is a class that listens to one model. Use it when the code needs other objects, like a mailer, or when you do not want it in the model.

The methods have the same names as the hooks. Each one gets the model. Override only the ones you need.

Before method After method Run on onSaving(T model) onSaved(T model) every save(): a new or a loaded model onCreating(T model) onCreated(T model) save() or create() on a new model (INSERT) onUpdating(T model) onUpdated(T model) save() on a loaded model (UPDATE) onDeleting(T model) onDeleted(T model) delete() onForceDeleting(T model) onForceDeleted(T model) forceDelete() onRestoring(T model) onRestored(T model) restore()

A before method can stop the operation with CancelModelEvent, like a before hook.

lib/app/observers/user.observer.dart
class UserObserver extends ModelObserver<User> {
  final Mailer mailer;

  UserObserver(this.mailer);

  @override
  Future<void> onCreated(User user) async {
    await mailer.sendWelcome(user.email!);
  }
}

Add it in the setup() of a service. Observers live in memory, and each isolate has its own memory, so every isolate must add them.

lib/services/observer_service.dart
class ObserverService implements DoxService {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Model.observe<User>(UserObserver(Mailer()));
  }
}

Dox finds ObserverService by itself, like every DoxService. Run dart run build_runner build after you add it.

  • You can add more than one observer to a model.
  • Model.forgetObservers<User>() removes the observers of User. Model.forgetObservers() removes all.

docs.title: Skip events
docs.text:
Use this for imports, seed data or tests.

await user.saveQuietly(); // save without events

await Model.withoutEvents(() async {
  await user.save();
  await post.delete();
});

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
save() does not start a transaction. If an after hook throws, the row stays written. To undo the row when a hook fails, wrap the call in QueryBuilder.transaction():

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await user.save(); // if onCreated() throws, the INSERT is rolled back
});

A model with no hooks and no observers does no event work.

docs.title: Query scopes
docs.text: A scope is a query part that you use again and again, like "only active users". You write it once in the model. Then you call it like a query method.

docs.title: Local scopes
docs.text:
Add a static method with @Scope() to the model. It takes the query first and returns the query. Then run dart run build_runner build.

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column()
  bool? active;

  @Column()
  int? age;

  @Scope()
  static QueryBuilder<User> isActive(QueryBuilder<User> q) {
    return q.where('active', true);
  }

  @Scope()
  static QueryBuilder<User> olderThan(QueryBuilder<User> q, int age) {
    return q.where('age', '>', age);
  }
}

The generator adds each scope as a method on the query of the model:

List<User> users = await User().isActive().get();

List<User> adults = await User()
    .where('name', 'like', 'a%')
    .isActive()
    .olderThan(18)
    .get();

A scope can take more arguments: required, optional ([...]) and named ({...}). The generated method takes the same arguments, without the query.

Pick a free name

The scope name must not be a field or a method of the model. For example, a scope active next to a field active does not work. Use isActive. A scope named like a query method (count, get) is never called.

docs.title: Global scopes
docs.text:
@Scope(global: true) adds the scope to every query of the model. This includes get(), find(), all(), count(), paginate(), query updates and deletes, and relation queries.

@DoxModel()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  bool? archived;

  /// every query leaves out archived posts
  @Scope(global: true)
  static QueryBuilder<Post> notArchived(QueryBuilder<Post> q) {
    return q.where('archived', false);
  }
}

await Post().get(); // ... WHERE ("archived" = false)

The global scope goes in brackets, and your own conditions too. So an orWhere() in your query can not skip the scope.

Remove a global scope for one query with withoutGlobalScope(), or remove all of them with withoutGlobalScopes():

await Post().withoutGlobalScope('notArchived').get();
await Post().withoutGlobalScopes().find(1);

The name of a global scope is the method name.

Info

save(), delete() and restore() on a model instance work on that one row. They do not use the global scopes. Soft deletes are not a global scope. Use withTrash() for them.

docs.title: BelongsTo
docs.text:
Use BelongsTo when this table keeps the foreign key to another table. For example, a comment belongs to a user. The comment table has the column user_id.

BelongsTo is the other side of HasOne and HasMany.

docs.title: Define it
docs.text:
Add a field with @BelongsTo(...) to the model. The field type is the related model, nullable.

lib/app/models/comment/comment.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../user/user.model.dart';

part 'comment.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Comment extends CommentGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId; // column user_id

  @Column()
  String? content;

  @BelongsTo(User)
  User? user;
}
lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @Column()
  String? status;
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add a relationship.

docs.title: Load it
docs.text: The relation is not loaded by default. Load it in one of these ways. Use the field name ('user') as the relation name.

docs.title: preload
docs.text:
Use it when you load the models with a query.

List<Comment> comments = await Comment().preload('user').all();
for (Comment comment in comments) {
  print(comment.user?.name);
}

preload works with find, get, all and getFirst. It runs one query for all comments, not one query per comment.

docs.title: $getRelation
docs.text:
Use it when you already have the model.

Comment? comment = await Comment().find(1);
await comment?.$getRelation('user');
print(comment?.user?.name);

Do not call it in a loop over many models. Use preload for a list.

docs.title: related
docs.text:
Use it when you need more conditions on the related row.

Comment? comment = await Comment().find(1);
User? activeUser = await comment
    ?.related<User>('user')
    ?.where('status', 'active')
    .getFirst();

It does not set comment.user.

docs.title: eager
docs.text:
Use it when every query of Comment should load the relation.

@BelongsTo(User, eager: true)
User? user;

You do not call preload.

The load runs this SQL:

SELECT * FROM "user"
  WHERE "user"."id" IN (@userid_p0, ...)

Each user is read once, also when it has many comments. Comments of the same user get the same User object.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default What it is foreignKey {related model}_id, like user_id The column in this table that points to the related model. localKey the primary key of the related model The column in the related table that foreignKey points to. onQuery none A static function that changes the query. eager false Load the relation on every query.

The default foreignKey uses the class name of the related model in snake_case. User gives user_id, also when the table is users.

docs.title: foreignKey and localKey
docs.text:
@BelongsTo(User, foreignKey: 'author_id', localKey: 'id')
User? author;

docs.title: onQuery
docs.text:
onQuery is a static function in the same model class. It gets the query of the related model and returns it.

@DoxModel()
class Comment extends CommentGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId;

  @BelongsTo(User, onQuery: onlyActive)
  User? activeUser;

  static QueryBuilder<User> onlyActive(User q) {
    return q.where('status', 'active');
  }
}

docs.title: In JSON
docs.text:
• A relation with eager: true is always in toJson().
  • A relation loaded with preload is in toJson() of that query.
  • The JSON key is the field name in snake_case: user.

Known issue: names with more than one word

For a relation without eager: true, toJson() looks for the snake_case name in the preload list. But preload needs the field name ('activeUser'). So a preloaded activeUser is on the model, but it is not in toJson(). Use a one word field name, or eager: true, when you need it in JSON.

docs.title: HasMany
docs.text: Use HasMany when one row of this table has many rows in another table. For example, a user has many posts. The other table keeps the foreign key (post.user_id).

docs.title: Define it
docs.text:
Add a field with @HasMany(...) to the model. The field type is a list of the related model. Start it as an empty list.

lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../post/post.model.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @HasMany(Post)
  List<Post> posts = <Post>[];
}
lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'post.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId; // column user_id

  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  String? status;
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add a relationship.

docs.title: Load it
docs.text: The relation is not loaded by default. Load it in one of these ways. Use the field name ('posts') as the relation name.

docs.title: preload
docs.text:
Use it when you load the models with a query.

User? user = await User().preload('posts').find(1);
print(user?.posts.length);

List<User> users = await User().preload('posts').get();

preload works with find, get, all and getFirst. For a list of users, it runs one query for all of them. A user without posts gets an empty list.

docs.title: $getRelation
docs.text:
Use it when you already have the model.

User? user = await User().find(1);
await user?.$getRelation('posts');
print(user?.posts.length);

docs.title: related
docs.text:
Use it when you need more conditions on the related rows.

User? user = await User().find(1);
List<Post> activePosts = await user
        ?.related<Post>('posts')
        ?.where('status', 'active')
        .orderBy('id', 'desc')
        .get() ??
    <Post>[];

It does not set user.posts.

docs.title: eager
docs.text:
Use it when every query of User should load the relation.

@HasMany(Post, eager: true)
List<Post> posts = <Post>[];

You do not call preload.

The load runs this SQL:

SELECT *, "user_id" as "_owner_id" FROM "post" WHERE "user_id" IN (@user_id_p0, ...)

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default What it is foreignKey {this model}_id, like user_id The column in the related table that points to this model. localKey the primary key of this model The column in this table that foreignKey points to. onQuery none A static function that changes the query. eager false Load the relation on every query.

The default foreignKey uses the class name in snake_case. User gives user_id, also when the table is users.

docs.title: foreignKey and localKey
docs.text:
@HasMany(Book, foreignKey: 'author_code', localKey: 'code')
List<Book> books = <Book>[];

docs.title: onQuery
docs.text:
onQuery is a static function in the same model class. It gets the query of the related model and returns it. You can have two fields on the same model with different queries.

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @HasMany(Post)
  List<Post> posts = <Post>[];

  @HasMany(Post, onQuery: onlyActive)
  List<Post> activePosts = <Post>[];

  static QueryBuilder<Post> onlyActive(Post q) {
    return q.where('status', 'active').orderBy('id', 'desc');
  }
}

docs.title: In JSON
docs.text:
• A relation with eager: true is always in toJson().
  • A relation loaded with preload is in toJson() of that query.
  • The JSON key is the field name in snake_case.

Known issue: names with more than one word

For a relation without eager: true, toJson() looks for the snake_case name in the preload list. But preload needs the field name ('activePosts'). So a preloaded activePosts is on the model, but it is not in toJson(). Use a one word field name, or eager: true, when you need it in JSON.

docs.title: HasOne
docs.text: Use HasOne when one row of this table has one row in another table. For example, a user has one user info row. The other table keeps the foreign key (user_info.user_id).

docs.title: Define it
docs.text:
Add a field with @HasOne(...) to the model. The field type is the related model, nullable.

lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../user_info/user_info.model.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @HasOne(UserInfo)
  UserInfo? userInfo;
}
lib/app/models/user_info/user_info.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user_info.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class UserInfo extends UserInfoGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId; // column user_id

  @Column()
  String? address;
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add a relationship.

docs.title: Load it
docs.text: The relation is not loaded by default. Load it in one of these ways. Use the field name ('userInfo') as the relation name.

docs.title: preload
docs.text:
Use it when you load the models with a query.

User? user = await User().preload('userInfo').find(1);
print(user?.userInfo?.address);

preload works with find, get, all and getFirst. For a list of users, it runs one query for all of them.

docs.title: $getRelation
docs.text:
Use it when you already have the model.

User? user = await User().find(1);
await user?.$getRelation('userInfo');
print(user?.userInfo?.address);

docs.title: related
docs.text:
Use it when you need more conditions on the related row.

User? user = await User().find(1);
UserInfo? info = await user
    ?.related<UserInfo>('userInfo')
    ?.where('address', '!=', '')
    .getFirst();

It does not set user.userInfo.

docs.title: eager
docs.text:
Use it when every query of User should load the relation.

@HasOne(UserInfo, eager: true)
UserInfo? userInfo;

You do not call preload.

The load runs this SQL:

SELECT *, "user_id" as "_owner_id" FROM "user_info" WHERE "user_id" IN (@user_id_p0)

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default What it is foreignKey {this model}_id, like user_id The column in the related table that points to this model. localKey the primary key of this model The column in this table that foreignKey points to. onQuery none A static function that changes the query. eager false Load the relation on every query.

The default foreignKey uses the class name in snake_case. User gives user_id, also when the table is users.

docs.title: foreignKey and localKey
docs.text:
@HasOne(UserInfo, foreignKey: 'owner_id', localKey: 'id')
UserInfo? userInfo;

docs.title: onQuery
docs.text:
onQuery is a static function in the same model class. It gets the query of the related model and returns it.

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @HasOne(UserInfo, onQuery: onlyActive)
  UserInfo? userInfo;

  static QueryBuilder<UserInfo> onlyActive(UserInfo q) {
    return q.where('status', 'active');
  }
}

docs.title: In JSON
docs.text:
• A relation with eager: true is always in toJson().
  • A relation loaded with preload is in toJson() of that query.
  • The JSON key is the field name in snake_case: user_info.

Known issue: names with more than one word

For a relation without eager: true, toJson() looks for the snake_case name in the preload list. But preload needs the field name ('userInfo'). So a preloaded userInfo is on the model, but it is not in toJson(). Use a one word field name (like info), or eager: true, when you need it in JSON.

docs.title: ManyToMany
docs.text:
Use ManyToMany when rows on both sides can have many rows on the other side. For example, an artist has many songs, and a song has many artists.

The link is kept in a third table, the pivot table. It has one foreign key to each side.

docs.title: Tables
Define it
docs.text:
Add a field with @ManyToMany(...) to each model that needs it. The field type is a list of the related model. Start it as an empty list.

lib/app/models/artist/artist.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../song/song.model.dart';

part 'artist.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Artist extends ArtistGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @ManyToMany(Song)
  List<Song> songs = <Song>[];
}
lib/app/models/song/song.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../artist/artist.model.dart';

part 'song.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Song extends SongGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  @ManyToMany(Artist)
  List<Artist> artists = <Artist>[];
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add a relationship.

docs.title: Load it
docs.text: The relation is not loaded by default. Load it in one of these ways. Use the field name ('songs') as the relation name.

docs.title: preload
docs.text:
Use it when you load the models with a query.

Artist? artist = await Artist().preload('songs').find(1);
print(artist?.songs.length);

List<Song> songs = await Song().preload('artists').get();

preload works with find, get, all and getFirst. For a list of models, it runs one query for all of them. A model without links gets an empty list.

docs.title: $getRelation
docs.text:
Use it when you already have the model.

Artist? artist = await Artist().find(1);
await artist?.$getRelation('songs');
print(artist?.songs.length);

docs.title: related
docs.text:
Use it when you need more conditions on the related rows.

Artist? artist = await Artist().find(1);
List<Song> songs = await artist
        ?.related<Song>('songs')
        ?.orderBy('song.title')
        .get() ??
    <Song>[];

It does not set artist.songs. The query joins the pivot table, so write table.column for column names.

docs.title: eager
docs.text:
Use it when every query of Artist should load the relation.

@ManyToMany(Song, eager: true)
List<Song> songs = <Song>[];

You do not call preload. Do not set eager: true on both sides. Each side would load the other side again and again.

The load runs this SQL:

SELECT "song".*, "artist_song"."artist_id" as "_owner_id" FROM "song"
  LEFT JOIN "artist_song" on "artist_song"."song_id" = "song"."id"
  WHERE "artist_song"."artist_id" IN (@artist_songartist_id_p0, ...)

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
The examples are for @ManyToMany(Song) in the Artist model.

Option Default Example value What it is pivotTable the two model names in A-Z order, joined with _ artist_song The pivot table. pivotForeignKey {this model}_id artist_id The pivot column that points to this model. pivotRelatedForeignKey {related model}_id song_id The pivot column that points to the related model. localKey the primary key of this model id The column in artist that pivotForeignKey points to. relatedKey the primary key of the related model id The column in song that pivotRelatedForeignKey points to. onQuery none A static function that changes the query. eager false Load the relation on every query.

The defaults use the class names in snake_case, not the table names. So @DoxModel(table: 'artists') does not change them.

  • Artist and Song give artist_song.
  • Blog and Category give blog_category.
  • BlogPost and Tag give blog_post_tag.

docs.title: Set all keys
docs.text:
@ManyToMany(
  Song,
  pivotTable: 'artist_song',
  pivotForeignKey: 'artist_id',
  pivotRelatedForeignKey: 'song_id',
  localKey: 'id',
  relatedKey: 'id',
)
List<Song> songs = <Song>[];

docs.title: onQuery
docs.text:
onQuery is a static function in the same model class. It gets the query of the related model and returns it.

@DoxModel()
class Artist extends ArtistGenerator {
  @ManyToMany(Song, onQuery: onlyPublished)
  List<Song> songs = <Song>[];

  static QueryBuilder<Song> onlyPublished(Song q) {
    return q.where('song.status', 'published');
  }
}

docs.title: In JSON
docs.text:
• A relation with eager: true is always in toJson().
  • A relation loaded with preload is in toJson() of that query.
  • The JSON key is the field name in snake_case: songs.

Known issue: names with more than one word

For a relation without eager: true, toJson() looks for the snake_case name in the preload list. But preload needs the field name, like 'topSongs'. So a preloaded topSongs is on the model, but it is not in toJson(). Use a one word field name, or eager: true, when you need it in JSON.

docs.title: Cache
docs.text:
Cache() keeps data that is slow to make, so the next request can read it fast.

It runs on dox_cache, which is built into dox_core.

docs.title: Drivers
docs.text:
Driver Where the data is Shared between isolates Locks file files in a folder (default storage/cache) yes, on the same machine no memory a map inside the isolate no yes redis a Redis server yes, also between machines yes null nowhere. It stores nothing - no

Many isolates

Dox runs one isolate per CPU core. Each isolate has its own memory store. So a value you put in one isolate is missing in the others. Use redis when all isolates and servers must see the same data.

docs.title: Config
docs.text:
Without a config, Dox has a file store (the default) and a memory store. To change the stores, make lib/config/cache.dart:

lib/config/cache.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

CacheConfig cache = CacheConfig(
  defaultStore: env.cacheStore,
  stores: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    'file': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'file', 'path': 'storage/cache'},
    'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory', 'max_size': 10000},
    'redis': <String, dynamic>{
      'driver': 'redis',
      'host': env.redisHost,
      'port': env.redisPort,
      'prefix': 'app_cache:',
    },
  },
);

Redis needs two keys that a new project does not have yet. Add them to lib/config/env.dart and run dart run build_runner build:

lib/config/env.dart
  String get redisHost => '127.0.0.1';

  int get redisPort => 6379;

Then pass it to AppConfig(cache: cache) in lib/config/app.dart. Each store is made once per isolate, the first time you use it.

docs.title: Store options
docs.text:
Driver Options file path (default storage/cache), prefix memory max_size: the most items. When it is full, the item that was used least recently is removed. No limit by default. Expired items are removed when read, and by a sweep every few thousand writes. Also prefix. redis host (default 127.0.0.1), port (default 6379), username, password, db (default 0), tls (true/false), pool_size (default 10), prefix

The default prefix is dox_cache:. You rarely need pool_size: the cache sends no blocking commands, so each isolate uses about one Redis connection.

docs.title: Values are JSON
docs.text: A value must be a JSON type: Map, List, String, num, bool or null. A Map comes back as Map<String, dynamic>. A List comes back as List<dynamic>.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
// no duration: the value stays forever
await Cache().put('foo', 'bar');
await Cache().put('foo', 'bar', duration: Duration(minutes: 10));

await Cache().get('foo');             // 'bar', or null when missing
await Cache().get('foo', 'default');  // 'default' when missing
await Cache().has('foo');             // true
await Cache().forget('foo');          // remove one key
await Cache().forever('settings', <String, dynamic>{'theme': 'dark'});
await Cache().flush();                // remove all items of the store

docs.title: remember
docs.text:
remember reads the value from the cache. When it is missing, the function runs and its result is stored.

List<dynamic> posts = await Cache().remember(
  'posts',
  Duration(minutes: 5),
  () => Post().all(),
);

rememberForever(key, fn) does the same with no expiry.

docs.title: getRaw
docs.text:
getRaw gives the stored JSON text as it is. Send it as a response with no decode and no encode:

String? json = await Cache().getRaw('posts');
if (json != null) {
  return response(json).contentType(ContentType.json);
}

A missing key gives null. A stored String comes back as JSON, with its quotes: "bar". The memory driver also keeps JSON text, so get decodes on every hit there too.

docs.title: Another store
docs.text:
store(name) uses a store from the config instead of the default store:

await Cache().store('redis').put('foo', 'bar');
await Cache().store('memory').get('foo');

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Put items under a tag. Then you can remove only the items of that tag:

await Cache().tag('users').put('u1', 'Ann');
await Cache().tag('users').flush(); // removes only the items of this tag

tags(['a', 'b']) uses many tags.

docs.title: Locks
docs.text:
A lock makes sure only one request (or one server) runs some code at a time. The memory and redis stores support locks. Use redis when many isolates must share the lock.

CacheLock lock = Cache().store('redis').lock('report', Duration(seconds: 30));
if (await lock.get()) {
  try {
    await buildReport();
  } finally {
    await lock.release();
  }
}
  • get() tries once. It is true when you got the lock.
  • block(Duration(seconds: 5)) tries again and again until the time is over.
  • The lock is freed after its ttl, even if you never call release().

docs.title: More methods
docs.text:
Method What it does add(key, value, duration:) store only when the key is missing. true when it was stored pull(key) get the value and remove it increment(key, [by]) / decrement(key, [by]) change an integer. A missing key starts at 0 repository the dox_cache CacheStore, for everything else

See dox_cache for custom drivers.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: To use a memory store in tests, see Testing.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
This page shows how to build a Dox app for production and run it safely.

Never run production with dart run

dart run (and dox serve) uses the JIT compiler. It is made for development. It uses about 25x more memory at start (around 390 MB instead of 16 MB) and starts slower. Always build an AOT binary for production.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
dox build

This makes a build/bundle/ folder:

File What it is build/bundle/bin/server the native binary. No Dart SDK needed to run it build/bundle/lib/ native libraries from build hooks (eg. SQLite) build/bundle/db/ your migrations build/bundle/.env.example copy it to build/bundle/.env, or use env variables

dox build runs build_runner (when your app uses it), then dart build cli --target bin/server.dart --output build. It exits with code 1 when a step fails, so CI can stop.

Not dart compile exe

dox_orm depends on sqlite3 v3. It bundles SQLite with a build hook. dart compile exe does not run build hooks, so it stops with an error. dart build cli is the same AOT compiler and runs the hooks. Keep bin/ and lib/ together: the binary loads the libraries from ../lib.

Start it:

cd build/bundle
./bin/server

The binary reads .env and db/ from the folder you start it in. A real environment variable wins over the .env file.

A new Dox app runs the migrations in bin/server.dart, before the server starts. So the database is up to date when the first request comes in.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
A new Dox app has this multi-stage Dockerfile. The final image is FROM scratch: only the Dart AOT runtime, the bundle, db/ and an empty /tmp.

FROM dart:stable AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY pubspec.* ./
RUN dart pub get
COPY . .
RUN dart pub get --offline
RUN dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
RUN dart build cli --target bin/server.dart --output build
RUN mkdir -p /out/app/storage /out/tmp \
  && chmod 1777 /out/tmp \
  && cp -r build/bundle/. /out/app/ \
  && cp -r db /out/app/db

FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /runtime/ /
COPY --from=build /out/ /
WORKDIR /app
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["/app/bin/server"]

The image has no .env file, so secrets stay out of it. Pass config as environment variables:

docker build -t my-app .
docker run -p 3000:3000 -e APP_PORT=3000 -e APP_KEY=... -e DB_HOST=... my-app

Or use env_file: .env in docker-compose.yml.

docs.title: HTTPS: put a proxy in front
docs.text:
Do not serve HTTPS from Dart. TLS in Dart's HttpServer is slow (a known Dart SDK issue). Dox has no bindSecure.

Run Dox on plain HTTP on a private port. Put Caddy or nginx in front of it. The proxy does TLS, HTTP/2 and gzip.

flowchart LR
    C["Client"] -->|HTTPS| X["Caddy or nginx<br>TLS, HTTP/2, gzip, body size limit"]
    X -->|"plain HTTP on 127.0.0.1:3000"| D["Dox binary<br>bin/server, one isolate per core"]
    D -->|"one shared pool"| DB[("Database")]
    M["Migrations<br>bin/server.dart runs them once, before the server starts"] --> DB

Then tell Dox to trust the proxy, so req.ip() and req.scheme() show the real client:

AppConfig(
  /// the proxy's IP, or a range like '10.0.0.0/8', or '172.16.0.0/12' for docker
  trustedProxies: <String>['127.0.0.1', '::1'],
);
  • req.ip() reads X-Forwarded-For. Dox walks the list from the right and skips your proxies, so a fake value from the client is ignored.
  • req.scheme() reads X-Forwarded-Proto (http or https). req.isSecure() is true for https.
  • trustedProxies is empty by default. Then Dox ignores those headers, because any client can send them.
  • ['*'] trusts any direct client. Only use it when the app port is not reachable from outside. With *, req.ip() is the right-most X-Forwarded-For hop, the one your proxy added. If you have two proxies in a row, list their IPs or ranges instead.

docs.title: Caddy
docs.text:
Caddy gets a certificate for you and sets X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto. Websockets work with no extra config.

example.com {
  encode gzip
  reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:3000
}

docs.title: Nginx
docs.text:
upstream dox {
  server 127.0.0.1:3000;
  keepalive 64;
}

map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
  default upgrade;
  ''      '';
}

server {
  listen 443 ssl http2;
  server_name example.com;

  ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem;
  ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem;

  # match maxMultipartSize in AppConfig
  client_max_body_size 100m;

  gzip on;
  gzip_types application/json text/plain text/css application/javascript;

  location / {
    proxy_pass http://dox;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;

    # websocket upgrade
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;

    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

    # stream uploads to Dox, do not buffer them in nginx first
    proxy_request_buffering off;
  }
}

server {
  listen 80;
  server_name example.com;
  return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
}

docs.title: Keep it running
docs.text:
When a worker isolate dies, Dox starts it again. When the main isolate dies, the process exits with a non-zero code (see Isolate). Let a supervisor restart it: restart: unless-stopped in Docker compose, or Restart=always in systemd.

# /etc/systemd/system/dox.service
[Service]
WorkingDirectory=/srv/app/build/bundle
ExecStart=/srv/app/build/bundle/bin/server
EnvironmentFile=/srv/app/build/bundle/.env
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

docs.title: Graceful shutdown
docs.text:
On SIGTERM (docker stop, Kubernetes, Cloud Run, Fly, systemd) or SIGINT (Ctrl+C), Dox stops gracefully, in every isolate:

  1. It stops taking new connections at once.
  2. Open requests can finish. Each keep-alive connection closes after its current answer.
  3. After shutdownTimeout (default 8 seconds), it closes the connections that are still open.
  4. It runs shutdown() of each service that implements DoxShutdown (see Services). The ORMService of a new project closes the database connections here.
  5. It closes the cache stores of Cache(), eg. the Redis connections.
  6. The process exits with code 0.

A second SIGINT or SIGTERM stops the process at once.

Set the timeout in lib/config/app.dart:

AppConfig(
  shutdownTimeout: Duration(seconds: 20),
  ...
)

Keep it shorter than the time your platform waits before it kills the process:

Platform Waits Change it with docker stop 10 seconds docker stop -t 30, or stop_grace_period in compose Kubernetes 30 seconds terminationGracePeriodSeconds Cloud Run 10 seconds can not be changed Fly.io 5 seconds kill_timeout in fly.toml systemd 90 seconds TimeoutStopSec

In code, await Dox().stop() does steps 1 to 4 and does not exit.

docs.title: Many processes or machines
docs.text:
One Dox process already uses every core. You only need more processes to run on more machines, or to restart one process without downtime. Run each one on its own port (or machine) and list them in the proxy:

upstream dox {
  server 10.0.0.11:3000;
  server 10.0.0.12:3000;
  keepalive 64;
}

Socket.IO rooms then need a shared adapter (like Redis), because each process has its own memory.

docs.title: Dox CLI
docs.text:
The dox CLI creates projects and files, runs the dev server, builds for production and runs migrations.

Every make:* command also answers to its create:* name. Run dox help to see all commands. Run dox help <command> for one command.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
dart pub global activate dox ^3.0.0-alpha

Add the pub bin folder to your PATH

If your shell can not find dox, add this line to ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc, and open a new terminal:

export PATH="$PATH":"$HOME/.pub-cache/bin"

To remove the CLI:

dart pub global deactivate dox

docs.title: All commands
docs.text: Command What it does dox create <name> [--version <v>] create a new project dox serve (or dox s) start the dev server with build_runner watch dox build build the native (AOT) bundle into build/bundle dox build_runner:watch / dox build_runner:build run the code generator dox make:controller <name> [-r] create a controller dox make:middleware <name> create a middleware dox make:dto <name> create a DTO (typed, checked input) dox make:serializer <name> create a serializer dox make:model <name> [-m] (old name create:model) create a model, and with -m its migration dox make:migration <name> [--sql] (old name create:migration) create a Dart migration, or a .sql one with --sql dox migration:run (or dox migrate) run new migrations dox migration:rollback [--step=N] undo the last batch, or the last N migrations dox migration:reset undo all migrations dox migration:refresh undo all, then run all again dox migration:fresh (or migrate:fresh) drop all tables, then run all migrations dox migration:status show which migrations ran, and their batch dox make:factory <model> create a model factory in db/factories, see Factories dox make:seeder <name> create a seeder in db/seeders, see Seeders dox db:seed [--class=<name>] run DatabaseSeeder, or another seeder dox make:job <name> create a queue job in lib/app/jobs (and bin/queue.dart) dox queue:work [--queue=a,b] [--concurrency=N] [--once] [--tries=N] [--timeout=S] [--sleep=S] [--stop-when-empty] run the queue worker dox queue:failed list the failed jobs dox queue:retry <id\|all> put a failed job (or all) back on the queue dox queue:forget <id> delete one failed job dox queue:flush delete all failed jobs dox schedule:work run the scheduler and keep it running dox schedule:run run the tasks that are due now, once dox schedule:list list the scheduled tasks dox schedule:test <name> run one scheduled task now dox key:generate make a new APP_KEY dox env:generate make lib/config/env.dart (the typed env class) from .env.example, see Environment Variables dox env:check check the env against lib/config/env.dart. Prints every missing or bad key (exit code 1) dox openapi:generate [dir] write openapi.json and openapi.yaml (default storage/openapi), see OpenAPI dox update update the CLI dox version (or dox -v) show the CLI version dox help [command] show help

docs.title: Create a project
docs.text:
dox create new_blog
dox create new_blog --version v3.0.0-alpha.5

dox create copies the dox-sample template from GitHub. Without --version, it uses the newest template release with the same major version as the CLI.

docs.title: Run the dev server
docs.text:
dox serve                         # or: dox s
dox s --ignore-build-runner       # do not run build_runner watch

dox serve runs dart run bin/server.dart and restarts it when a .dart file changes. It also runs build_runner watch, so generated files stay up to date.

docs.title: Build for production
docs.text:
dox build
cd build/bundle
./bin/server

See Deployment.

docs.title: Create files
docs.text:
dox make:controller Blog        # lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart
dox make:controller Blog -r     # resource controller
dox make:middleware Auth
dox make:dto CreateBlog         # lib/app/http/dtos/create_blog.dto.dart
dox make:serializer Blog
dox make:model Blog -m          # model and its create_blogs_table migration
dox make:migration create_blogs_table          # .dart file (default)
dox make:migration create_blogs_table --sql    # .sql file
  • -r adds the methods index, create, store, show, edit, update and destroy.
  • Word breaks are kept. BlogPost makes blog_post.controller.dart with the class BlogPostController.
  • After make:dto, run dox build_runner:build. See Validation.
  • The table of a model is its name in plural snake case: BlogPost makes blog_posts. The model gets @DoxModel(table: 'blog_posts').

docs.title: Database settings
docs.text:
The migration commands read the database settings from the .env file and the real environment. A real environment variable wins.

.env
# postgres, mysql or sqlite
DB_CONNECTION=postgres
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
# for sqlite: the file path
DB_NAME=postgres
DB_USERNAME=admin
DB_PASSWORD=password
  • DB_CONNECTION defaults to postgres. The default port is 5432 for postgres and 3306 for mysql.
  • DB_DATABASE works too, in place of DB_NAME.
  • Put comments on their own line. A # after a value becomes part of the value.

All keys are in the Env reference.

docs.title: Run and undo migrations
docs.text:
dox migration:run                # or: dox migrate
dox migration:status
dox migration:rollback           # undo the last batch
dox migration:rollback --step=2  # undo the last 2 migrations
dox migration:reset              # undo all migrations
dox migration:refresh            # undo all migrations, then run them again
dox migration:fresh              # drop all tables, then run all migrations

migrate:rollback, migrate:reset, migrate:refresh, migrate:fresh and migrate:status also work. Add --seed to migration:run, migration:refresh or migration:fresh to run the seeders after it.

  • A failed migration stops the run, and the CLI exits with code 1.
  • On MySQL, statements like CREATE, ALTER and DROP save right away. So when a migration fails half way, these changes are not undone.

docs.title: Update the CLI
docs.text: dox update installs the newest version with the same major version as your CLI, previews included. To pick the version yourself, run the install command again.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Declare your env keys once, in a typed class.

Then env.appPort is an int, your IDE suggests every key, and a missing key stops the app at startup.

docs.title: The typed env class
docs.text:
A new project already has lib/config/env.dart. Its keys are listed in the Env reference. This example shows the kinds of getters you can write:

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'env.g.dart';

enum LogLevel { debug, info, error }

@DoxEnv()
abstract class AppEnv {
  static AppEnv load([EnvReader? reader]) {
    return _$AppEnv.load(reader);
  }

  String get appName;                       // APP_NAME, required
  String get appKey;                        // APP_KEY, required
  int get dbPort => 5432;                   // DB_PORT, default 5432
  bool get appDebug => false;               // APP_DEBUG, default false
  LogLevel get logLevel => LogLevel.info;   // LOG_LEVEL=debug
  Duration get cacheTtl => const Duration(minutes: 5); // CACHE_TTL=5m
  List<String> get corsOrigins => <String>[];          // CORS_ORIGINS=a.com,b.com

  @EnvKey('AWS_BUCKET')
  String? get s3Bucket;                     // optional, null when not set
}

/// The env of the app. Read and checked once, on first use.
final AppEnv env = AppEnv.load();

Run dart run build_runner build after each change to the class. It writes env.g.dart. Then use env anywhere:

import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: 'postgres',
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(port: env.dbPort /* int */, ...),
  },
);
