docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
• Key: the getter name in UPPER_SNAKE case. appName reads APP_NAME, s3Bucket reads S3_BUCKET. Use @EnvKey('X') for another name.
  • Default: the getter body. It can be any expression, like Platform.numberOfProcessors. It runs only when the key is missing. A default can not read another env getter.
  • Optional: a nullable getter with no body (String? get s3Bucket;). It is null when the key is missing.
  • Required: any other getter with no body. A missing key stops the app.
  • Empty: an empty value (or the text null) counts as missing.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Type Value in .env String any text int, double, num 3000, 0.5 bool true/false, 1/0, yes/no, on/off (any case) Uri https://dox.dev Duration a number and a unit: 500ms, 30s, 5m, 2h, 1d. A plain number is seconds: 300 is 5 minutes. an enum the name of a value, any case: debug List<String> comma separated: a, b, c. Empty items are dropped.

Any other type is a build error.

docs.title: Fail fast
docs.text:
AppEnv.load() reads every key one time. Then it checks them all, and throws one EnvException that lists every missing or bad key:

EnvException: the env is not valid
  - APP_KEY is missing
  - DB_PORT must be an int, not "abc"

This happens once, when the app starts. After that, env.dbPort is a plain field read.

docs.title: Where values come from
docs.text:
Dox reads values from two places:

  1. Real environment variables (set in the shell, Docker or systemd).
  2. The .env file in the folder where you start the app. It is optional.

The environment wins

A real environment variable wins over the .env file. So you can keep .env for development and use real variables in production.

docs.title: The .env file
docs.text:
.env
APP_NAME=dox
APP_KEY=change-me
DB_PORT=5432
  • One KEY=value per line.
  • Quotes around a value are removed. So APP_NAME="My app" gives My app. Use ", ' or `.
  • A = inside the value is kept: TOKEN=a=b gives a=b.
  • A line that starts with # is a comment.
  • A # after a space starts a comment: APP_PORT=3000 # dev gives 3000.
  • A # with no space before it is kept: DB_PASSWORD=abc#123 gives abc#123.
  • A # inside quotes is kept: DB_PASSWORD="abc # 123" gives abc # 123.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
dox env:generate   # make lib/config/env.dart from .env.example
dox env:check      # load the env and print every missing or bad key

dox env:generate reads .env.example:

  • digits become an int with that default: APP_PORT=3000 gives int get appPort => 3000;
  • true/false become a bool with that default
  • an empty value becomes an optional String?
  • any other value becomes a required String. The example value is never a default, so a secret in the example can not leak into the code.
  • # comment lines above a key become its doc comment

It does not overwrite an existing lib/config/env.dart. Run dox build_runner:build after it.

dox env:check exits with code 1 when a key is missing or bad. Use it in CI or before a deploy.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: To pass your own values in a test, see Testing.

docs.title: Env.get: the low-level way
docs.text:
Env.get() reads one key by name. Use it for a key you only know at run time. For normal config, use the typed class.

Env.get<String>('APP_KEY');             // '' when missing
Env.get('APP_KEY', 'default_value');
Env.get<int>('APP_PORT', 3000);
Env.get<bool>('SOCKETIO_ENABLED', false); // true, 1, yes, on
Env.get<String?>('AWS_BUCKET');          // null when it is not set

A missing or empty key gives the default. With no default:

  • String gives an empty string ''. It is never the text "null".
  • String? and dynamic give null. With no type, like Env.get('KEY'), the type is dynamic, so you get null.
  • int, num, double and bool throw an ArgumentError with the key name. A value that is not a number throws too.

Env.get() looks up and converts the value on every call. Do not call it on a hot path.

APP_KEY

When APP_KEY is missing, not 32 characters, or a public sample key, Dox().startServer() stops with an error. When APP_ENV is development, local or test, it only logs a warning. Make a key with dox key:generate.

docs.title: File Storage
docs.text:
Storage() saves and reads files on a disk: the local folder, AWS S3 (and R2, MinIO, Spaces), or memory.

It runs on dox_storage, which is built into dox_core.

Route.post('/avatar', (DoxRequest req) async {
  RequestFile file = req.input('avatar');
  String path = await Storage().putRequestFile('avatars', file);
  return <String, String>{'path': path}; // /avatars/<uuid>.png
});

docs.title: Config
docs.text:
Without a config, Dox has one disk: local, in the storage folder. To add disks, make lib/config/storage.dart:

lib/config/storage.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

StorageConfig storage = StorageConfig(
  defaultDisk: env.storageDisk,
  disks: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    'local': <String, dynamic>{
      'driver': 'local',
      'root': 'storage',
      'url': 'https://app.test/files', // for url() and signedUrl()
    },
    's3': <String, dynamic>{
      'driver': 's3',
      'bucket': env.awsBucket,
      'region': env.awsDefaultRegion,
      'key': env.awsAccessKeyId,
      'secret': env.awsSecretAccessKey,
      'endpoint': env.awsEndpoint, // R2, MinIO, Spaces
    },
    'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory'},
  },
);

The s3 disk reads five keys that a new project does not have yet. Add them to lib/config/env.dart and run dart run build_runner build. They are nullable, so the app starts without them:

lib/config/env.dart
  String? get awsBucket;

  String get awsDefaultRegion => 'us-east-1';

  String? get awsAccessKeyId;

  String? get awsSecretAccessKey;

  /// R2, MinIO or Spaces. Null for AWS.
  String? get awsEndpoint;

Then pass it to AppConfig(storage: storage) in lib/config/app.dart.

Driver Options local root (default storage), url, app_key (default: your APP_KEY), visibility s3 bucket, region, key, secret, token, endpoint, path_style (MinIO), url (CDN), visibility, acl, batch_delete memory none. For tests

The s3 disk needs bucket, key and secret. When one is missing, the first use of the disk throws an ArgumentError that names the setting.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
// save with a new uuid file name, returns '/images/<uuid>.png'
String path = await Storage().put('images', bytes, extension: 'png');
String path2 = await Storage().putRequestFile('images', file);

Uint8List? bytes = await Storage().get(path);  // null when missing
bool found = await Storage().exists(path);
await Storage().delete(path);

String url = await Storage().url(path);         // needs the disk `url` option
String signed = await Storage().signedUrl(path, expiresIn: Duration(minutes: 10));

// another disk
await Storage().disk('s3').put('reports', bytes, extension: 'pdf');

putRequestFile on the local disk moves the upload temp file. It does not read it into memory.

putRequestFile and file.store() take the extension from the file name. When the bytes are a known format (png, jpg, pdf, zip, ...) that does not match the name, the extension of the bytes is used. So a png sent as a.html is saved as .png and is never served as a web page.

docs.title: stream and download
docs.text:
Route.get('/photo', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().stream(req.input('path'));    // shown in the browser
});

Route.get('/report', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().disk('s3').download('reports/2024.pdf'); // saved as a file
});

Both read the file as a stream, from any disk, with Content-Length. A big file is never loaded into memory. A missing file answers 404.

docs.title: Full disk API
docs.text: Storage().use('s3') returns the dox_storage Disk: copy, move, listAll, getMetaData, putStream, setVisibility and more. See dox_storage.

docs.title: Serve local signed URLs
docs.text:
// lib/routes/web.dart
Route.files('files');                    // GET /files/{key*}, signed URLs only
Route.files('public', signed: false);    // any file of the disk
Route.files('docs', disk: 'memory');     // another disk than the default
Route.files('uploads', download: true);  // every file is a download

An html, svg, xml or javascript file is always sent as a download in a sandbox, so its script does not run on your site. Every file has X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.

String url = await Storage().signedUrl('invoices/1.pdf'); // https://app.test/files/invoices/1.pdf?expires=...&signature=...

A missing, wrong or expired signature answers 403. Set the disk url option to the full URL of the route (https://app.test/files).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: To swap a disk with a memory disk in tests, see Testing.

docs.title: Your own driver
docs.text:
Implement DriverContract from package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart. Register it in a service, so every isolate has it:

Dox().storage.register('dropbox', DropboxDriver());
await Storage().disk('dropbox').put('notes', bytes, extension: 'txt');

docs.title: Health check
docs.text: A health route tells a load balancer, Docker or Kubernetes if the app can serve requests.

docs.title: Add the route
Check the database and the cache
docs.text:
Give named checks. Each check is a function:

lib/routes/web.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

Route.health(
  '/health',
  checks: <String, HealthCheckFunction>{
    'database': () => QueryBuilder.query('select 1'),
    'cache': HealthCheck.cache(),
  },
);

When all checks pass, the answer is 200:

{"status": "ok", "checks": {"database": "ok", "cache": "ok"}}

When one check fails, the answer is 503 Service Unavailable:

{"status": "fail", "checks": {"database": "fail", "cache": "ok"}}

A check fails when it:

  • throws an error,
  • returns false,
  • or takes longer than timeout (default 5 seconds).

The checks run at the same time.

  • HealthCheck.cache() writes a key to the default cache store and reads it back. HealthCheck.cache('redis') checks the store with that name.
  • Any other check is your own function, like a call to another API.

docs.title: Error details
docs.text:
The error of a failed check is passed to exceptionHandler.report(), so you see it in your logs.

The answer has the error text (in errors) only when APP_ENV is development or local. In other envs the text is left out, because it can show hosts or user names.

docs.title: Change the timeout
docs.text:
Route.health(
  '/health',
  timeout: Duration(seconds: 2),
  checks: <String, HealthCheckFunction>{
    'database': () => QueryBuilder.query('select 1'),
  },
);

Tip

A route in a router gets the middleware of that router and the global middleware. Put Route.health in a router with no auth middleware, or the health check gets 401.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Docker for a health check in the image
  • Deployment

docs.title: Isolate
docs.text: This page explains how Dox runs your app on many isolates (threads), and what that means for your code.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Dox starts many isolates. Each one runs its own native server on the same port. The operating system spreads the connections between them.

  • Linux: each isolate has its own socket (SO_REUSEPORT).
  • macOS: the isolates share one socket.
  • Windows: only one isolate serves HTTP.

Each isolate has its own Rust acceptor on the port:

flowchart TD
    OS["Port 3000<br>the OS spreads the connections"] --> A1["Rust acceptor"]
    OS --> A2["Rust acceptor"]
    OS --> A3["Rust acceptor"]
    A1 --> I1["Isolate 1, main<br>own memory cache"]
    A2 --> I2["Isolate 2<br>own memory cache"]
    A3 --> I3["Isolate N<br>own memory cache"]
    I2 -. "crash: started again after 1 second" .-> I2
    I1 -. "crash: the process exits" .-> S["Supervisor restarts the process<br>Docker, systemd"]

With the Postgres and MySQL drivers, all isolates share one database pool in Rust. See How Dox works.

docs.title: How many isolates
docs.text:
By default Dox starts one isolate per CPU core (Platform.numberOfProcessors).

To change it, set totalIsolate in lib/config/app.dart. A new app reads it from APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  totalIsolate: env.appTotalIsolate ?? Platform.numberOfProcessors,
);

You can also set it in code, before startServer(). This wins over the config:

bin/server.dart
Dox().initialize(appConfig);
Dox().totalIsolate(2);
await Dox().startServer();

Use fewer isolates when:

  • the machine also runs the database or other heavy work, or
  • you use Socket.IO rooms without the Redis adapter. A room only reaches clients on the same isolate. Use 1, or see Socket.IO.

docs.title: Each isolate has its own memory
docs.text:
Isolates do not share memory:

  • A static value or a singleton exists once per isolate. When you change it in one isolate, the others do not see it.
  • The memory cache store is per isolate. See Cache.
  • To share data between isolates or servers, use a database, Redis or files.

Dox().isolateId tells you which isolate runs the code. The first isolate is 1.

docs.title: What each isolate does at start
docs.text:
Dox copies the AppConfig, the services and the routes you added before startServer() to each new isolate. Then every isolate:

  1. runs setup() of each service (for example, it opens the database pool),
  2. registers the routes of your routers,
  3. reads the parameter types of each controller once,
  4. starts its HTTP server.

Because the config and services are copied, they must not hold open sockets or database pools. Open these in setup(). See Services.

docs.title: When an isolate crashes
docs.text:
• An error in a request is caught. Dox sends a 500 and keeps going.
  • An async error outside a request (for example a future that nobody awaits) is caught and passed to the report method of the exception handler. The isolate keeps running.
  • If a worker isolate still dies, Dox prints [dox] isolate N exited, restarting to stderr. It starts a new isolate after 1 second.
  • If the first (main) isolate dies, the process exits with a non-zero code. Let a supervisor start it again, like Docker restart: or systemd Restart=always. See Deployment.

docs.title: Native server
docs.text:
Dox runs on a native HTTP server from the package dox_http_native.

You do not need to set anything. Every app uses it, also an app with WebSocket or Socket.IO routes.

  • Rust (hyper) owns the sockets and parses HTTP.
  • All your code stays in Dart: routes, controllers, DTOs, middleware, ORM.
  • It is much faster than the dart:io server. In a hello world test on one core it served about 5 times more requests. See Performance.

You do not need Rust. The package downloads a ready-built library for your system when you build the app.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Rust reads the requests from the sockets.
  2. It sends the requests to Dart in batches (one message per batch).
  3. Dart runs your handlers.
  4. Dart sends all answers back to Rust in one call.

The native server has the same API as the dart:io HttpServer. So req.httpRequest, HttpResponse and code written for dart:io keep working.

Each isolate runs its own server on the same port. See Isolate. The OS spreads connections, not requests. A keep-alive connection stays on one isolate. So a few busy connections (eg. from one proxy or a load test with few connections) can keep some isolates idle. Use more connections than isolates.

docs.title: When the library does not load
docs.text:
Dox stops at start, before any isolate runs. The error says why and how to fix it:

Unsupported operation: dox_http_native did not load: <reason>.
Fix: install Rust (cargo, see https://rustup.rs), then run the app again ...

<reason> is for example native library ABI 4, expected 5: the library on disk is from another version of the package. See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: WebSocket
docs.text:
Rust also does the WebSocket upgrade and the WebSocket protocol.

  1. Rust marks a request that asks for an upgrade.
  2. Dart runs the route, the middleware and the Origin check, like for any request. A normal answer (eg. 403) refuses the upgrade.
  3. When Dart accepts, Rust sends the 101 answer. From then on Rust answers pings, does the close handshake, checks that text is UTF-8 and checks the size of each message.

  4. Dart gets whole messages, in the same batches as requests. It sends messages back the same way as answers.

  5. A message or frame over the size limit closes the socket with code 1009. Dart never reads it. NativeWebSocket.upgrade takes maxMessageSize. Socket.IO uses maxHttpBufferSize.

  6. Compression (permessage-deflate) is never agreed. A small compressed message could grow very big in memory.
  7. On a graceful stop (SIGTERM), every open WebSocket gets close code 1001.
  8. In your own code, use NativeWebSocket.upgrade(request) from dox_http_native. It gives a dart:io WebSocket.

docs.title: Threads
docs.text: Each isolate has its own Rust network thread. DOX_HTTP_THREAD=shared puts all isolates on one thread. It is off by default: on 2 cores the one thread was the limit and req/s fell by a quarter. Leave it off unless you measure a gain.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Max size of the request line plus headers: 16 KB. Bigger gets 431.
  • A bad request gets 400.
  • A multipart form over maxMultipartSize, or any other body over maxBodySize, gets 413 from Rust. When Content-Length is too big and the client sent Expect: 100-continue, the 413 comes before the body is sent. Else Rust reads and drops the body first, so the client sees the 413. Dart checks the limits again.
  • A client that sends no body bytes for 120 seconds (idle time) gets 408. A slow but steady upload is fine.
  • A small response is sent in one piece when it is closed. A streamed response (a file, a download, any Stream) over 64 KB goes out in parts: the client gets the first bytes early. At most 1 MB of it waits in memory. Dart reads more of the file only when the client has read what was sent. When the client leaves, Dart stops reading.
  • A request body of 64 KB or more goes to Dart without a copy.
  • compress: true works: Rust gzips the body on another thread, so the isolate does not wait. A streamed response is not compressed.

docs.title: Where the library comes from
docs.text:
The build hook of dox_http_native (hook/build.dart) picks the first one that works:

  1. A path you give in the root pubspec.yaml of your app:

    hooks:
  user_defines:
    dox_http_native:
      lib_path: /path/to/libdox_http_native.so

  2. A local build in native/target/release of the package (for work on the package itself).

  3. The ready-built library from the GitHub release, checked with sha256. There are builds for macOS (arm64, x64), Linux (x64, arm64) and Windows (x64).
  4. A build from source with cargo, when Rust is installed.

When none works, the app still builds, but it stops at start with the error above. Install Rust and run it again, so step 4 works.

Use dart build cli

dart compile exe does not run build hooks. Use dox build or dart build cli. See Deployment.

docs.title: Work on the native code
docs.text:
dox_http_native lives in its own repo: dartondox/dox-http-native. The Rust code is in its native folder.

cd dox-http-native/native
cargo build --release   # the hook uses this build from now on
cargo test
cd .. && dart test --concurrency=1

To use your local copy in the Dox repo, or to release the package, see Contribute.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
This page shows how fast Dox is, and how to keep your app fast in production.

The short version:

  1. Build with dox build and run the AOT binary. Never dart run in production.
  2. Put Caddy or nginx in front for HTTPS and gzip.
  3. Keep the default isolates (one per CPU core).
  4. Keep the body limits on. Uploads stream to disk.

docs.title: Benchmark
docs.text:
A "hello world" test. Each server answers GET / with the plain text Hello World. Dox is a small real Dox app with one route.

Hello world only measures framework overhead. A real app spends most of its time on the database, JSON and your own code, so the gaps are much smaller there.

docs.title: 1 core
docs.text:
Server req/s p99 ms CPU % peak MB Dox, native server 171,042 0.92 100 9 Dox, dart:io server 33,154 5.48 101 39 Bun 1.4.3 181,162 1.13 101 14 Node 24.22.0 81,909 2.26 101 54 Pure Rust hyper (the ceiling) 254,349 0.47 100 5

On one core, Dox with the native server is about as fast as Bun (0.94x). It is 5x faster than Dox on dart:io.

How it was run:

  • Docker on an Apple M2 (8 CPUs in the Docker VM), linux/arm64.
  • The server and wrk run in two containers, pinned to different CPUs: server on CPU 0, wrk on CPUs 2-7.
  • wrk 4.2.0, 100 connections (the tables) and 256 connections. 5 seconds warm-up, then 3 runs of 10 seconds. The tables show the median.
  • CPU % and peak memory come from docker stats. 100% = one core.
  • Dart 3.13.6, Rust 1.99.1. Dox is built with dart build cli (this is what dox build does). The build hook of dox_http_native builds the Rust library with cargo.
  • The dart:io row is the same Dox app on a dart:io HttpServer, for comparison.

docs.title: App benchmark
docs.text: A small real app, the same in each language: GET /json returns a map, GET /db reads one row by id from Postgres, GET /queries?n=20 reads 20 rows one after another. The table has 10,000 rows. Each server runs alone on one or two pinned CPUs, Postgres 18 and wrk on other CPUs, 256 connections, 4 database connections per core, 3 runs of 10 seconds, median. Versions: Dox 3.0.0-alpha.3 (native server, dox_postgres_native), Go 1.27 (net/http + pgx), Bun 1.4 (Bun.serve + Bun.sql), Node 24 (node:http + pg), dart:io (HttpServer + package:postgres).

docs.title: 1 core
docs.text:
1 core: 1.5× Bun, 2.3× Go

GET /db: read one row from Postgres. Requests per second, higher is better.

req/s p99 RAM Doxnative server + driver 85,381fastest 5.65 ms 24 MB BunBun.serve + Bun.sql 57,6141.5× slower 6.11 ms 36 MB Gonet/http + pgx 36,7062.3× slower 14.49 ms 18 MB dart:io+ package:postgres 12,1467.0× slower 47.62 ms 62 MB

Dox 3.0.0-alpha.3 · Bun 1.4 · Go 1.27 · Dart 3.13 · Postgres 18 · 256 connections · wrk · median of 3 runs

Route Dox Bun Go dart:io /json req/s 157,036 176,148 79,884 33,670 /db req/s 85,381 57,614 36,706 12,146 /queries req/s 9,745 10,097 3,810 966 /db p99 ms 5.65 6.11 14.49 47.62 /db peak MB 24 36 18 62

docs.title: 2 cores
docs.text:
2 cores: still the fastest

GET /db on 2 CPU cores. Dox runs one isolate per core; Bun and Node one worker process per core.

req/s p99 RAM Dox2 isolates 138,514fastest 3.62 ms 51 MB Bun2 workers 128,9981.1× slower 5.61 ms 57 MB Node2 workers + pg 61,6112.2× slower 8.06 ms 297 MB Gonet/http + pgx 49,3932.8× slower 8.53 ms 22 MB

Dox 3.0.0-alpha.3 · Bun 1.4 · Go 1.27 · Node 24 · Postgres 18 · 256 connections · wrk · median of 3 runs

2 cores: 20 queries per request

GET /queries?n=20: 20 reads from Postgres, one after another, in one request.

req/s Dox2 isolates 12,902fastest Bun2 workers 11,0061.2× slower Node2 workers + pg 5,8702.2× slower Gonet/http + pgx 5,1342.5× slower

Dox 3.0.0-alpha.3 · Bun 1.4 · Go 1.27 · Node 24 · Postgres 18 · 256 connections · wrk · median of 3 runs

Route Dox Bun Go Node /json req/s 251,427 385,553 175,009 156,389 /db req/s 138,514 128,998 49,393 61,611 /queries req/s 12,902 11,006 5,134 5,870 /db p99 ms 3.62 5.61 8.53 8.06 /db peak MB 51 57 22 297

Dox runs one isolate per core, Bun and Node one worker process per core. On the database routes Dox is ahead of all of them on 2 cores, and its p99 is the lowest. On /json Bun is faster: its server is C++ and calls the JavaScript handler on the same thread, while Dox hands each batch of requests from the Rust thread to the Dart isolate.

Dox on dart:io with the Dart postgres driver is 4 to 10 times slower than Dox with the native server and driver. Keep both on.

docs.title: Dart VM flags
docs.text: We tried a bigger young generation (DART_VM_OPTIONS=--new_gen_semi_max_size=64 and 128) for a better p99. Over 5 runs the change was inside the noise, and memory did not move. So there is no flag to set. Dox never sets VM flags for you. DART_VM_OPTIONS is read by the AOT binary from dox build, so you can try your own.

docs.title: Database drivers
docs.text:
One find-by-id query, AOT build (dart build cli), database on the same machine (Apple M-series), one isolate:

Database One query at a time Many queries in flight App CPU time per query Postgres 14 (4 connections) 60 µs 12.5 µs each (64 in flight) MySQL 8.4 (10 connections) 67 µs 11 µs each (32 in flight) 13.5 µs MariaDB 11 (10 connections) 63 µs 9.7 µs each (32 in flight) 12.4 µs
  • The CPU time counts the Dart thread and the Rust thread. For MySQL, it is about 75,000 queries per second on one core.
  • Dart sends many queries to Rust in one call. Rust sends many results back in one message.
  • One query alone spends most of its time on the trip to the database. Many requests at the same time, like in a web server, get the most out of the driver.

docs.title: Bodies, uploads and big responses
docs.text:
These are on by default. You only need to keep them:

  • A body over maxBodySize or maxMultipartSize gets 413 before it is all read. Set the same limit in the proxy. See Size limits.
  • An upload over 1 MB streams to a temp file, so it does not fill the memory. See Request.
  • A File or Stream response is streamed, not loaded into memory. See Files and big responses.

docs.title: gzip
docs.text:
gzip in Dart is off by default.

AppConfig(compress: true);
  • It saves bandwidth, but costs CPU on every response. The native server gzips on a Rust thread. Streamed responses are not compressed.
  • A proxy (Caddy, nginx) does it better. Turn it on in Dart only when there is no proxy.
  • With compress: true, text and JSON responses are sent chunked, without Content-Length.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
LogMiddleware prints one JSON line per request. Writing to stdout blocks the isolate. So Dox collects log lines and writes them every 20 ms (or every 64 KB) in one write. If the process is killed hard, the last 20 ms of request logs can be lost. Errors from Logger are still written right away.

Turn LogMiddleware off when a proxy already writes access logs. The new project does this for you: enabled is false when APP_ENV is production.

Leave responseHandler unset when you do not need it. With no handler, a plain value (text, map, list) is sent without building a DoxResponse.

docs.title: What Dox does for you
docs.text:
• Routes are grouped by method. The regex of each route is built once, not on every request.
  • The argument types of each controller are read once at start, not on every request.
  • JSON and text responses are encoded once, straight to bytes, with Content-Length set.

docs.title: Queue
docs.text:
A queue runs slow work in the background. The request answers at once. A worker process does the work later.

Use it to send emails, call slow APIs, make reports or resize images. The dox_queue package gives you jobs, three drivers (Redis, database and sync), retries, delays and a worker.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
dart pub add dox_queue

dox_queue has a builder. Your app already runs build_runner for dox_builder, so nothing else is needed.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. You write a job class with @Job().
  2. dart run build_runner build writes lib/jobs.g.dart. It knows how to save and load each job.
  3. Your code calls dispatch(). The job is saved in Redis or in the database.
  4. A worker (dart run bin/queue.dart) takes the job and runs its handle() method.

docs.title: 1. Config
2. Service
docs.text:
The service sets up the queue in every isolate. Put it in lib/ so the generated container finds it.

lib/services/queue_service.dart
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

import '../config/queue.dart';

/// Sets up the queue. Dox finds every DoxService class,
/// see lib/container.g.dart.
class AppQueueService extends QueueService {
  AppQueueService() : super(queueConfig);
}

docs.title: 3. Worker file
4. Tables (database driver only)
docs.text:
Add a migration in db/migration. QueueTables makes the jobs and failed_jobs tables.

db/migration/2026_10_25_000000000_create_queue_tables.dart
// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

/// The jobs and failed_jobs tables of dox_queue.
class CreateQueueTables extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await QueueTables.up(schema);
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await QueueTables.down(schema);
  }
}

Then run dox migrate.

docs.title: Write a job
What is saved
docs.text:
The parameters of the unnamed constructor are saved with the job. Each parameter needs a field or getter with the same name.

These types work:

  • int, double, num, String, bool
  • DateTime
  • enums (saved by name)
  • List and Map<String, ...> of these, also nested
  • dynamic and Object (the value must be JSON)
  • nullable versions of all of them

Any other type stops the build with a clear message.

Save an id, not an object

Do not save a User. Save the userId, and load the user in handle(). The user may change between dispatch and run. The id gives you fresh data.

docs.title: Services in a job
docs.text:
A job is made again from its saved data, so it can not get services in its constructor. Get them in handle() from the Dox container:

UserService users = Dox().ioc.get<UserService>();

The worker runs registerContainer, so every @Inject() class of your app is there.

docs.title: Job names
docs.text: The class name is saved with each job. When you rename a class, queued jobs of the old name can not be found. Keep the old name with @Job(name: 'SendWelcomeEmail').

docs.title: Dispatch a job
docs.text:
await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: user.id).dispatch();

Both ways do the same:

await Queue.dispatch(SendWelcomeEmail(userId: user.id));

A delay, another queue:

await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatch(
  delay: Duration(minutes: 10),
  queue: 'emails',
);

dispatch() returns the job id.

Run a job now, in this process, with no queue:

await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchSync();

docs.title: Run the worker
docs.text:
dart run bin/queue.dart

Commands:

Command What it does work run jobs. This is the default failed list the failed jobs retry <id> put one failed job back on its queue retry all put all failed jobs back forget <id> delete one failed job flush delete all failed jobs

Flags of work:

Flag Default What it does --queue=high,default default the queues to work. The first one goes first --concurrency=4 1 jobs at once in this process --once off run one job, then stop --tries=3 1 tries of a job that does not set tries --timeout=60 60 max run time in seconds of a job that does not set timeout --sleep=3 3 seconds to wait when the queues are empty --stop-when-empty off stop when the queues are empty 
dart run bin/queue.dart work --queue=emails,default --concurrency=4

--concurrency runs jobs as async tasks on one thread. It helps for jobs that wait (email, HTTP, database). For CPU heavy jobs, run more worker processes.

docs.title: Stop the worker
docs.text:
Press Ctrl+C, or send SIGTERM (docker stop does it). The worker takes no new job. It waits for the running jobs, then it stops. A second signal stops it at once.

Restart the worker after a deploy

The worker keeps your code in memory. Restart it after each deploy, or it runs the old code.

docs.title: Keep it running
docs.text:
Run the worker as its own process, next to the web server. For example with Docker Compose:

services:
  web:
    build: .
    command: dart run bin/server.dart
  worker:
    build: .
    command: dart run bin/queue.dart work --concurrency=4

Or with systemd, Supervisor or a second Fly.io process. Set it to restart when it stops.

docs.title: Retries and failed jobs
docs.text:
When handle() throws:

  1. The worker waits the backoff time and tries again, up to tries times.
  2. After the last try, the job goes to the failed jobs, and failed() runs.

A timeout counts as a failed try.

A timeout does not stop the code

Dart can not stop a running Future. After a timeout the try counts as failed, but handle() keeps running in the background until it ends. Write jobs that are safe to run twice.

When a worker crashes, its job stays reserved. After retryAfter another worker takes it. This counts as a try. When there are no tries left, the job fails with a message that the worker did not finish.

Failed jobs are kept until you retry or delete them:

dart run bin/queue.dart failed
dart run bin/queue.dart retry 6f1c0e...
dart run bin/queue.dart retry all
dart run bin/queue.dart forget 6f1c0e...
dart run bin/queue.dart flush

docs.title: Drivers
docs.text: Driver Where jobs are Needs sync nowhere: dispatch() runs the job at once nothing database the jobs and failed_jobs tables Postgres, MySQL 8+, MariaDB 10.6+ or SQLite redis Redis lists and sorted sets Redis

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
Jobs are rows in the jobs table. Failed jobs are rows in failed_jobs.

  • On Postgres, MySQL and MariaDB a worker takes a job with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Many workers do not wait on each other.
  • On SQLite a worker takes a job with one UPDATE ... RETURNING. SQLite runs one write at a time, so this is safe. It is good for small apps.

Use another connection of config/database.dart with QueueConfig(connection: 'postgres').

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'redis',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  redis: RedisOptions(host: env.redisHost, port: 6379),
);

Each queue has a list of ready jobs, a sorted set of delayed jobs and a sorted set of reserved jobs. A Lua script takes a job, so two workers never get the same one. Failed jobs are in the hash dox_queue:failed.

docs.title: Sync
docs.text: dispatch() runs the job at once and waits for it. There is no worker, no retry and no delay. When the job throws, failed() runs and dispatch() throws the error. Use it for tests and for local work.

docs.title: Small apps: a worker in the web server
docs.text:
You can skip the worker process. Set workInProcess: true:

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'database',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  workInProcess: true,
);

The first isolate of the web server then runs jobs too. When the server stops, it waits for the running jobs.

Heavy jobs slow down your API

The jobs share the isolate with web requests. A long or CPU heavy job makes requests on that isolate slow. Use a worker process when your jobs are heavy or many.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Use the sync driver. dispatch() then runs the job at once, so you can check the result right after.

import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:dox_sample/jobs.g.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  setUp(() {
    Queue.configure(QueueConfig(driver: 'sync', jobs: jobRegistry));
  });

  test('sends the welcome email', () async {
    await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatch();
    // check the email was sent
  });
}

To test a job alone, call handle():

await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).handle();

To test the queue itself, use the database driver with SQLite :memory:, and run a worker that stops when the queue is empty:

await Worker(
  driver: Queue.driver,
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  options: WorkerOptions(stopWhenEmpty: true),
).run();

docs.title: Scheduler
docs.text:
dox_scheduler runs your tasks on a schedule, like cron.

You write the schedule in Dart, in one file. Each task is a plain function. A task runs once per tick, even when many isolates or servers run the schedule.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: dart pub add dox_scheduler

docs.title: Define tasks
docs.text:
Put the tasks in lib/config/schedule.dart.

import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';

ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig();

void schedule(Schedule s) {
  s.call('cleanup', cleanup).dailyAt('02:00');
  s.call('report', sendReport).hourly();
  s.call('ping', ping).cron('*/5 * * * *').timezone('Asia/Yangon');
}

Future<void> cleanup() async {
  // delete old rows, files, ...
}

s.call(name, function) adds a task. The name must be unique. It shows in the logs and in the lock keys. A task with no frequency runs every minute.

docs.title: Queue jobs
docs.text:
The scheduler does not know about queues. Wrap the job in a function:

s.call('report', () => SendReport().dispatch()).hourly();

The task only puts the job on the queue. A queue worker runs it.

docs.title: Frequencies
docs.text:
Method Runs everyMinute() every minute (the default) everyTwoMinutes() every 2 minutes everyFiveMinutes() every 5 minutes everyTenMinutes() every 10 minutes everyFifteenMinutes() every 15 minutes everyThirtyMinutes() at minute 0 and 30 hourly() at minute 0 of every hour hourlyAt(17) at minute 17 of every hour daily() every day at 00:00 dailyAt('13:00') every day at 13:00 twiceDaily(1, 13) every day at 01:00 and 13:00 weekly() every Sunday at 00:00 weeklyOn(DateTime.monday, '08:00') every Monday at 08:00 monthly() the 1st of every month at 00:00 monthlyOn(15, '12:00') the 15th of every month at 12:00 yearly() January 1st at 00:00 cron('*/5 9-17 * * 1-5') any 5 field cron expression

You can limit the days. The order of the calls does not matter.

Method Runs weekdays() Monday to Friday weekends() Saturday and Sunday days(<int>[DateTime.monday, DateTime.friday]) only on these days 
s.call('standup', remind).weekdays().dailyAt('09:00');

docs.title: Cron expressions
docs.text:
cron() takes the standard 5 fields: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week.

Field Values minute 0-59 hour 0-23 day of month 1-31 month 1-12 or JAN-DEC day of week 0-7 or SUN-SAT (0 and 7 are Sunday)

Each field takes *, a number 5, a range 1-5, a list 1,15, and a step */15 or 0-30/10.

When both day fields are set, a day matches when either field matches. This is the standard cron rule. 0 0 1 * MON runs on the 1st of the month and on every Monday. When one day field starts with *, both must match.

docs.title: Time zones
docs.text:
The schedule uses UTC by default. Use timezone() to read the time in another zone:

s.call('report', sendReport).dailyAt('08:00').timezone('Asia/Yangon');

The name is an IANA name, like Europe/London or America/New_York. The zone data comes from the timezone package.

With summer time (DST):

  • A time that does not exist that day (it is skipped when the clock goes forward) does not run that day.
  • A time that happens twice (when the clock goes back) runs once.
  • hourly() and other "every" frequencies keep running every real hour.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
s.call('sync', sync).everyFiveMinutes().between('09:00', '17:00');
s.call('night', night).hourly().between('22:00', '06:00'); // crosses midnight
s.call('promo', promo).daily().when(isPromoOn);
s.call('backup', backup).daily().skip(isHoliday);
Method What it does between('09:00', '17:00') runs only in this time of day, both ends included, in the task zone when(function) runs only when the function gives true skip(function) does not run when the function gives true

when and skip take a function that gives a bool or a Future<bool>.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Method What it does withoutOverlapping() does not start while the last run still runs onOneServer() runs once per tick across isolates and servers. On by default onEveryServer() runs on every process that runs the schedule runInBackground() the next task of the same minute does not wait for this one timeout(Duration(minutes: 5)) counts the run as failed when it takes longer

docs.title: withoutOverlapping
docs.text: A lock is held while the task runs. When the next minute comes and the lock is still held, the task is skipped. The lock expires after 24 hours, in case the process dies. Pass another expiry like this: withoutOverlapping(Duration(hours: 1)).

docs.title: Once per tick
docs.text:
Before a task runs, the scheduler takes a lock named after the task and the minute. The first process to take it runs the task. The others skip it. The lock is not released, so a late server can not run the same minute again.

The locks use a cache store.

Many servers need Redis

A memory store lives inside one process. It works for one work process, or for many isolates of one server. When many servers run the schedule, set a Redis store: ScheduleConfig(store: 'redis').

When the store has no locks (file, null), the scheduler uses a memory store.

docs.title: Timeout
docs.text: Dart can not stop a running function. After the timeout, the run counts as failed and the hooks run, but the work may go on.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
s
    .call('report', sendReport)
    .daily()
    .before(logStart)
    .onSuccess(logDone)
    .onFailure(alertTeam)
    .after(cleanUp);

Future<void> alertTeam(Object error, StackTrace stack) async {
  await notifyTeam('report failed: $error');
}
Hook Runs before before the task. When it throws, the task does not run and counts as failed onSuccess after the task worked onFailure after the task threw or timed out. It gets the error and the stack trace after after the task, always

An error in a task is logged and the next task still runs.

docs.title: Run the schedule
docs.text:
bin/schedule.dart runs the schedule:

import 'dart:io';

import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SchedulerRunner(
    schedule: schedule,
    app: appConfig,
    config: scheduleConfig,
  ).run(args);
}

With app, the runner starts your app services first (like the database). It stops them at the end.

Command What it does dart run bin/schedule.dart work runs due tasks at every minute until you stop it. The default dart run bin/schedule.dart run runs the tasks due this minute once, then exits dart run bin/schedule.dart list shows each task, its schedule and its next run time dart run bin/schedule.dart test cleanup runs one task now

docs.title: work
docs.text:
work is a long running process. Run it next to your server, with the same deploy tool (systemd, Docker, Kubernetes).

It wakes at each full minute and runs the due tasks. On Ctrl+C or SIGTERM it starts no new task and waits for the running ones. A second signal stops it at once.

docs.title: run
docs.text:
run is for a system cron. Add one line to the crontab:

* * * * * cd /path/to/app && dart run bin/schedule.dart run

It runs the tasks of this minute, waits for them, and exits. The exit code is 1 when a task failed.

Use a compiled binary to start faster: dart compile exe bin/schedule.dart -o build/schedule.

docs.title: list
docs.text:
Task     Schedule                   Next run
cleanup  0 2 * * *                  2026-10-26 02:00 UTC
report   0 * * * *                  2026-10-25 14:00 UTC
ping     */5 * * * * Asia/Yangon    2026-10-25 20:35 Asia/Yangon

The next run time checks the frequency and between(). It does not check when() and skip().

docs.title: test
docs.text: test <name> runs one task now, with its hooks. It does not check the schedule, the filters or the locks.

docs.title: Run inside the server
docs.text:
You can run the schedule inside your Dox server instead of a work process. Add a service that extends SchedulerService:

// lib/services/schedule_service.dart
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';

class ScheduleService extends SchedulerService {
  ScheduleService() : super(schedule: schedule, config: scheduleConfig);
}

Then turn it on in lib/config/schedule.dart:

ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig(inProcess: true);

Run dart run build_runner build. The generated container finds the service.

How it works:

  • Only the first isolate runs the tasks. The other isolates only serve requests.
  • With many servers, each server runs the loop. The once-per-tick lock makes each task run once. Use a Redis store for this.
  • When the server stops, it waits for the running tasks.

Trade-offs:

  • Tasks use the CPU of the server, so they can slow down requests on the first isolate.
  • A long task makes the server stop slower.
  • With a separate work process, you can deploy, scale and restart the scheduler on its own.

Use work for heavy tasks. Use the in-process service for small apps.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Scheduler runs the tasks. Give it a fake clock to test a schedule with no waiting:

import 'package:dox_cache/dox_cache.dart';
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

class FakeClock extends ScheduleClock {
  FakeClock(this.time);

  DateTime time;

  @override
  DateTime now() {
    return time;
  }
}

test('cleanup runs at 02:00', () async {
  Schedule s = Schedule();
  schedule(s);
  Scheduler scheduler = Scheduler(
    tasks: s.tasks,
    store: CacheStore(MemoryDriver()),
    clock: FakeClock(DateTime.utc(2026, 10, 25, 2)),
  );
  Map<String, TaskOutcome> outcomes = await scheduler.runDue();
  expect(outcomes['cleanup'], TaskOutcome.ran);
});

ScheduledTask.isDue(time) and ScheduledTask.nextRun(time) check a schedule with no run at all.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
A service is a class with a setup() method. Dox runs it at start, in every isolate.

Use it to set up things like the database or auth.

docs.title: Why services
docs.text: Dox runs your app on many isolates, and they do not share memory. Code that you run once in bin/server.dart only sets up the first isolate. The others have, for example, no database connection. A service fixes this: each isolate runs setup() itself.

docs.title: Create a service
docs.text:
Implement DoxService and put your code in setup(). setup() can be async. Dox waits for it.

lib/services/orm_service.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

class ORMService implements DoxService, DoxShutdown {
  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig);
  }

  /// Close the database connections when the server stops.
  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await SqlQueryBuilder.close();
  }
}

docs.title: Register it
docs.text:
You do not need to. Dox finds every class that implements DoxService. Run dart run build_runner build. The service is then in lib/container.g.dart. Each isolate makes its own instance from the container. Its constructor can ask for other classes of the container. See Dependency injection.

Services run in the order of their file path. To run one first, list it in AppConfig:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  container: registerContainer,
  services: <DoxService>[ORMService()], // runs before the others
);

A listed service runs first. Then the others run. No service runs twice.

You can also add a service in code, before startServer():

bin/server.dart
Dox().initialize(appConfig);
Dox().addService(MyService());
await Dox().startServer();

docs.title: Example: auth
When setup() runs
docs.text:
In each isolate, Dox runs setup() of each service, one after the other: the listed ones first, then the ones of the container. Then it registers the routes and starts the server, so routes can use what a service set up. See What each isolate does at start.

dox openapi:generate also runs setup() of every service, because it needs the routes.

docs.title: Clean up on shutdown
docs.text:
On SIGTERM or SIGINT Dox stops the server gracefully (see Deployment). After the open requests are done, it runs shutdown() of each service that also implements DoxShutdown. It runs in every isolate. Use it to close connections or flush data.

The ORMService of a new project already does this: its shutdown() calls SqlQueryBuilder.close(). Dox closes the cache stores (eg. Redis) by itself, after the services.

lib/services/redis_service.dart
class RedisService implements DoxService, DoxShutdown {
  late RedisConnection redis;

  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    redis = await RedisConnection.open();
  }

  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await redis.close();
  }
}

An error in shutdown() goes to the report method of the exception handler. The other services still run.

docs.title: Rules for a service
docs.text:
• Open connections in setup(), not in the constructor. A service listed in AppConfig is copied to each isolate. An open socket or database pool can not be copied, so the isolate fails to start.
  • Keep setup() short. It runs once per isolate. Data you load in it is kept once per isolate, so 8 isolates keep 8 copies.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: This page shows how to test a Dox app with the test package: HTTP routes, cache, storage, env and the database.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Add the test package as a dev dependency:

dart pub add dev:test

Put your tests in the test/ folder. Run them with:

dart test

docs.title: Test HTTP routes
docs.text:
DoxTestClient from package:dox_core/testing.dart starts your app inside the test and sends requests to it.

test/http_test.dart
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('GET /api/ping', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.get('/api/ping');
    res.expectStatus(200).expectBody('pong');
  });

  test('POST /api/posts', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.post(
      '/api/posts',
      body: <String, dynamic>{'title': 'Hello', 'body': 'My first post.'},
    );
    res.expectStatus(201).expectJson(containsPair('title', 'Hello'));
  });
}
  • DoxTestClient.start(appConfig) runs your services (like the ORM service) and adds your routes, the same as a real start.
  • It listens on 127.0.0.1 and a free port that the OS picks. So it does not clash with dox serve, and many test files can run at the same time.
  • It runs on one isolate. serverPort and totalIsolate of the config are not used.
  • client.close() stops the server and runs the DoxShutdown services (for example, it closes the database).
  • With one isolate, you can also add a route inside a test with Route.get(...). It works right away.

docs.title: Send requests
docs.text:
Method What it does get(path) GET. The path can have a query: '/api/users?page=2'. post(path, body: ...) POST. Also put, patch and delete. send('OPTIONS', path) any other method headers: {...} extra headers for one request withHeaders({...}) a copy of the client that sends these headers on every request withToken(token) a copy of the client that sends Authorization: Bearer <token>

A Map or List body is sent as JSON. A String or List<int> body is sent as it is. Redirects are not followed, so you can check a 302 and its Location header.

docs.title: Check the response
docs.text:
Member What it gives res.status the status code, like 200 res.body the body as text res.json the body read as JSON res.header('content-type') one header (any case) res.headers all headers, with lower case names

The expect methods fail the test when the response is not right. They return the response, so you can chain them:

res
    .expectStatus(422)
    .expectHeader('content-type', contains('application/json'))
    .expectJson(<String, dynamic>{'title': 'The title is required'});
Method Fails when expectStatus(200) the status is another one. The message shows the body. expectJson(value or matcher) the JSON body does not match. Use a Map, or a matcher like containsPair('id', 1). expectBody(value or matcher) the text body does not match expectHeader(name, value or matcher) the header does not match. Use isNull for "not there".

docs.title: Log in as a user
docs.text:
Make a token, then send it with withToken:

TestResponse login = await client.post(
  '/api/auth/login',
  body: <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com', 'password': 'secret123'},
);
DoxTestClient ann = client.withToken(login.json['token'] as String);
(await ann.get('/api/auth/me')).expectStatus(200);

docs.title: Test the cache
docs.text:
Dox().cache is the CacheManager that Cache() uses. Replace it with a memory store, so tests do not write files or need Redis:

setUp(() {
  Dox().cache = CacheManager(CacheConfig(
    defaultStore: 'memory',
    stores: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
      'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory'},
    },
  ));
});

test('caches the posts', () async {
  await Cache().put('posts', <String>['a', 'b']);
  expect(await Cache().get('posts'), <dynamic>['a', 'b']);
});

A new CacheManager in setUp gives each test an empty cache. See Cache.

docs.title: Test file storage
docs.text:
Dox().storage.fake(name) swaps one disk with an empty memory disk. restore(name) puts the real disk back.

setUpAll(() {
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);
});

test('saves the report', () async {
  Disk fake = Dox().storage.fake('s3');

  String path = await Storage()
      .disk('s3')
      .put('reports', <int>[1, 2, 3], extension: 'pdf'); // '/reports/<uuid>.pdf'

  expect(await fake.exists(path.substring(1)), isTrue);
  Dox().storage.restore('s3');
});
  • Call Dox().initialize() first. The storage disks are made from appConfig.
  • Storage() paths start with /. A Disk key does not, so remove the first / when you ask the Disk directly.

See File Storage.

docs.title: Test the env
docs.text:
Pass your own values to AppEnv.load(). Then nothing is read from the shell or the .env file:

AppEnv env = AppEnv.load(
  EnvReader(
    environment: <String, String>{'APP_KEY': 'test'},
    dotEnv: <String, String>{'DB_PORT': '5433'},
  ),
);
expect(env.dbPort, 5433);

A missing or bad key throws an EnvException. So you can also test that your app stops on a bad env. See Environment Variables.

docs.title: Test the database
docs.text:
A test that uses models needs a real database. Run the migrations once in setUpAll. Then empty the tables before each test with refreshDatabase() from package:dox_orm/testing.dart:

test/user_test.dart
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    await Migrator(
      migrations: migrations,
      config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
    ).migrate();
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig); // runs the ORM service
  });

  // every test starts with empty tables
  setUp(refreshDatabase);

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('register makes a user', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.post(
      '/api/auth/register',
      body: <String, dynamic>{
        'name': 'Ann',
        'email': 'ann@example.com',
        'password': 'secret123',
      },
    );
    res.expectStatus(201);
  });
}
  • refreshDatabase() empties every table and starts the ids at 1 again. The tables stay. It keeps the rows of the migrations table (dox_db_migration).
  • It works on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. Foreign keys are not checked while it empties the tables.
  • refreshDatabase(keep: <String>['dox_db_migration', 'countries']) keeps the rows of more tables.
  • Use a separate test database. Set its name in the env of the test run, for example DB_NAME=app_test dart test. Never run it on a database with real data.
  • A test without the server can start the ORM with SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig).

See Testing with a database for a full example with SQLite.

Run test files one by one

dart test runs test files at the same time. When two files use the same tables, run them one by one: dart test --concurrency=1.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
This page shows how to install the Dox CLI, make a new project and start the server.

3.x is alpha

Dox 3 is in alpha (3.0.0-alpha.x). It needs Dart 3.13 or newer.

docs.title: Install the CLI
docs.text:
dart pub global activate dox ^3.0.0-alpha

Check that it works:

dox version

dox: command not found

The shell can not find the CLI when the pub bin folder is not in your PATH. Add this line to ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc, then open a new terminal:

export PATH="$PATH":"$HOME/.pub-cache/bin"

docs.title: Create a new project
docs.text:
dox create new_blog

dox create downloads the newest 3.x release of dox-sample, the starter project. To get one exact version, add --version, for example dox create new_blog --version 3.0.0-alpha.5.

It also makes your .env file from .env.example, with a new random APP_KEY. Then get the packages:

cd new_blog
dart pub get

The starter project uses SQLite, so there is no database to install. The file db/dox.sqlite is created at the first start. To use Postgres or MySQL instead, change DB_CONNECTION and the DB_* values in .env. See Database.

Add Dox to an existing Dart project

Add the packages you need to pubspec.yaml. All Dox packages share one version, so use ^3.0.0-alpha for each of them. It picks the newest alpha.

pubspec.yaml
dependencies:
  dox_core: ^3.0.0-alpha
  dox_orm: ^3.0.0-alpha
  dox_migration: ^3.0.0-alpha

dev_dependencies:
  dox_builder: ^3.0.0-alpha
  build_runner: ^2.17.1

docs.title: Start the server
docs.text:
dox s

dox s does two things:

  • It runs dart run build_runner watch, so generated files stay up to date.
  • It runs dart run bin/server.dart, and restarts it when a .dart file changes.

To skip the builder, use dox s --ignore-build-runner. To start the server without the CLI, run dart run bin/server.dart.

At the first start it also runs the migrations in db/migration. The server uses the port in APP_PORT in the .env file (3000 by default). Check it:

curl localhost:3000/ping

pong

docs.title: Start the server with Docker
docs.text:
docker-compose up -d --build

Production

Do not use dox s or dart run in production. Build a native binary with dox build. See Deployment.

docs.title: Run the code generator
docs.text:
Dox makes code for models and DTOs with build_runner. dox s already runs it. To run it alone:

dox build_runner:watch   # runs again on every file change
dox build_runner:build   # runs once

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
All Dox packages use the same version.

Package What it does dox the CLI dox_core HTTP server, routing, requests, responses, validation dox_orm query builder and models dox_migration database migrations dox_auth JWT authentication dox_builder, dox_annotation code generation for models and DTOs dox_validation typed validation schemas dox_openapi OpenAPI docs dox_storage file storage: local, S3 dox_cache cache: memory, file, Redis dox_socketio Socket.IO server dox_http_native native HTTP server (Rust) dox_postgres_native, dox_mysql_native native database drivers for Postgres and MySQL/MariaDB

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
Each guide solves one job from start to end. Copy the files, run the commands, and check the result. The reference pages explain each part in more detail. The guides link to them.

The code of all guides is in one app on GitHub: examples/guides. CI builds it and runs its tests on every push, so the code on these pages keeps working.

Guide What you get File upload Accept an image, check its size and type, save it, return its URL. Pagination A list route with page and per_page, and the JSON shape it returns. JWT authentication Register, log in, protect routes, read the user, log out. Custom errors Your own exception classes, one JSON shape for every error, logging. Background work Run work after the response, use another thread for CPU work, run a timer. Docker A small production image with dox build, Postgres, env and a health check. Testing with a database Tests on SQLite or a test Postgres, with migrations and cleanup. Static files and SPA Serve a folder or a single page app, with cache headers. CORS for a browser front-end The CORS setup that works with a React, Vue or Flutter web app. Environments Dev, staging and production config, .env files, secrets and APP_KEY.

All guides use the app that dox create my_app makes. The package name is my_app. Change it to your own package name in the imports.

docs.title: API docs with OpenAPI
docs.text: Turn on OpenAPI docs for the blog API, open the docs page, and make the docs better with comments and annotations.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• The blog API from the tutorial, or any Dox app.
  • build_runner and dox_builder. A new app has both. dox_core already has dox_openapi, so you add no package.

docs.title: 1. Write the config
docs.text:
build_runner writes lib/openapi.g.dart. Its openApiRegistry holds what the builder found in your routes, controllers, DTOs and models. Pass it to an OpenApiConfig:

lib/config/openapi.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:blog/openapi.g.dart';

OpenApiConfig openApi = OpenApiConfig(
  info: Info(title: 'Blog API', version: '1.0.0'),
  registry: openApiRegistry,
);

Add it to AppConfig:

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:blog/config/openapi.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  /// OpenAPI docs (config/openapi.dart)
  openApi: openApi,
);

docs.title: 2. Build and start
docs.text:
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve

.env has APP_ENV=development, so the docs routes are on.

docs.title: 3. Open the docs page
docs.text:
Open http://localhost:3000/docs. It is a Scalar page with every route and "Try it" buttons. It loads Scalar from the jsDelivr CDN.

The app now has three new routes:

Route What it gives GET /docs the Scalar docs page (HTML) GET /openapi.json the OpenAPI 3.1 document as JSON GET /openapi.yaml the same document as YAML

docs.title: 4. Read the JSON
docs.text:
curl http://localhost:3000/openapi.json

This is the real output for the blog API, shortened. The top level:

{
  "openapi": "3.1.0",
  "info": {"title": "Blog API", "version": "1.0.0"},
  "paths": {
    "/ping": {},
    "/api/ping": {},
    "/api/posts": {},
    "/api/posts/{id}": {},
    "/api/auth/register": {},
    "/api/auth/login": {},
    "/api/auth/user": {}
  },
  "components": {
    "schemas": {"Post": {}, "SavePost": {}, "RegisterUser": {}, "LoginUser": {}, "User": {}, "ValidationError": {}},
    "securitySchemes": {
      "bearerAuth": {"type": "http", "scheme": "bearer", "bearerFormat": "JWT"}
    }
  }
}

POST /api/posts, as the builder found it. You wrote no docs code for it:

{
  "tags": ["Post"],
  "summary": "POST /api/posts",
  "operationId": "PostController.store",
  "requestBody": {
    "required": true,
    "content": {"application/json": {"schema": {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/SavePost"}}}
  },
  "responses": {
    "200": {"description": "Successful response"},
    "401": {"description": "Not logged in"},
    "422": {
      "description": "Validation failed",
      "content": {"application/json": {"schema": {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/ValidationError"}}}
    },
    "500": {"description": "Server error"}
  },
  "security": [{"bearerAuth": []}]
}

Where each part comes from:

Part Comes from tags: ["Post"] the class name PostController, without Controller summary the first line of the /// comment: /// POST /api/posts requestBody the argument SavePost body of store 401 and bearerAuth AuthMiddleware on the route 422 the route has a request class 200 with no body store returns DoxResponse, so the builder can not see the body. Step 6 fixes this

docs.title: 5. See how a DTO becomes a schema
docs.text:
This is the SavePost DTO of the tutorial:

lib/app/http/dtos/save_post.dto.dart
@Dto()
class SavePost {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 100)
  final String title;

  @Trim()
  @MinLength(10)
  final String body;

  const SavePost({required this.title, required this.body});

  static const DtoSchema<SavePost> schema = $SavePostDto;
}

And this is its schema in /openapi.json:

"SavePost": {
  "type": "object",
  "title": "SavePost",
  "properties": {
    "title": {"type": "string", "minLength": 3, "maxLength": 100},
    "body": {"type": "string", "minLength": 10}
  },
  "required": ["title", "body"]
}
In the DTO In the schema String title (not nullable) "type": "string" and title in required @Length(min: 3, max: 100) "minLength": 3, "maxLength": 100 @MinLength(10) "minLength": 10 @Email() (in RegisterUser) "format": "email" @Trim(), @Lowercase(), @Unique(...) nothing. They change or check the value on the server only

A model becomes a schema too. Post has id, the @Column fields title and body, and created_at and updated_at. Keys in hidden are left out. That is why User has no password.

When you change a rule, run build_runner again, and the docs change with it.

docs.title: 6. Make the docs better
docs.text:
Write a /// comment on a controller method. The first line is the summary. The rest is the description. Add @Tags and @Response (from dox_core) when the automatic result is not what you want.

lib/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart
@Inject()
class PostController {
  /// List all posts
  ///
  /// Newest posts are not first. There is no paging yet.
  Future<List<Post>> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Post().all();
  }

  /// Create a post
  @Tags(<String>['Posts'])
  @Response(201, Post, description: 'The new post')
  Future<DoxResponse> store(SavePost body) async {
    Post post = Post()
      ..title = body.title
      ..body = body.body;
    await post.save();
    return response(post).statusCode(201);
  }

  // ...
}

Run dart run build_runner build again and restart the app. The real result:

"get": {
  "tags": ["Post"],
  "summary": "List all posts",
  "description": "Newest posts are not first. There is no paging yet.",
  "operationId": "PostController.index"
},
"post": {
  "tags": ["Posts"],
  "summary": "Create a post",
  "operationId": "PostController.store",
  "responses": {
    "201": {
      "description": "The new post",
      "content": {"application/json": {"schema": {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/Post"}}}
    },
    "401": {},
    "422": {},
    "500": {}
  }
}
  • @Response(201, Post) replaces the empty 200. The docs now match the real status code.
  • @Tags(['Posts']) moves the route to the group "Posts" in the docs page.
  • @Summary('...') and @Description('...') set the text without a /// comment.
  • @ApiIgnore() leaves a method (or a whole controller) out of the docs.

See OpenAPI: change the docs for all annotations.

docs.title: 7. Turn it off in production
docs.text:
This is the default. enabled is null, so the docs routes are on only when APP_ENV is development or local. With APP_ENV=production all three routes give 404:

curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:3000/docs           # 404
curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:3000/openapi.json   # 404

To show the docs on staging too, but never in production, set enabled yourself:

lib/config/openapi.dart
OpenApiConfig openApi = OpenApiConfig(
  enabled: env.appEnv != 'production',
  info: Info(title: 'Blog API', version: '1.0.0'),
  registry: openApiRegistry,
);

Warning

enabled: true in production shows every route of your API to anyone. Only do it for a public API.

To give the document to a front-end team without a running server, write it to files with dox openapi:generate. See OpenAPI: write the files.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
curl -s http://localhost:3000/openapi.json | head -n 5

{
  "openapi": "3.1.0",
  "info": {
    "title": "Blog API",
    "version": "1.0.0"

Open http://localhost:3000/docs, find "Create a post" under "Posts", and send a request with "Try it".

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• OpenAPI for all options, the Scalar look, Swagger UI and login schemes
  • Validation rules for the rules and their JSON Schema keys
  • Environments for APP_ENV

docs.title: Background work
docs.text: Answer the request now and do the slow work after. Use another thread for CPU work. Run a job on a timer.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A Dox app.

docs.title: What Dox gives you
docs.text:
Dox has no job queue. It has three building blocks from Dart itself:

You want Use Runs where I/O work after the response (send an email, call an API, write rows) a Future you do not await the same isolate, between requests CPU work (resize an image, parse a big file, compute) Isolate.run() a new thread work every N minutes (cleanup, sync) Timer.periodic in a service one isolate of your choice

None of them survive a restart. See When you need a real queue.

docs.title: 1. Work after the response
docs.text:
Start the future and return. unawaited tells the linter you did this on purpose. An error in the future goes to the report method of the ExceptionHandler in AppConfig.

lib/app/http/controllers/report.controller.dart
import 'dart:async';
import 'dart:isolate';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class ReportController {
  /// POST /api/reports
  /// Answers at once. The work runs after the response, in this isolate.
  Map<String, String> store(DoxRequest req) {
    String id = DateTime.now().microsecondsSinceEpoch.toString();
    unawaited(_build(id));
    return <String, String>{'id': id, 'status': 'queued'};
  }

  /// I/O work (database, HTTP calls, email) is fine here. It shares the
  /// event loop with the requests, so it must not block the CPU.
  Future<void> _build(String id) async {
    await Future<void>.delayed(const Duration(seconds: 2));
    print('report $id is ready');
  }

  /// GET /api/primes/{limit}
  /// CPU work runs on another thread with `Isolate.run`.
  /// The request waits for the result, but other requests are not blocked.
  Future<Map<String, int>> primes(int limit) async {
    int count = await Isolate.run(() => countPrimes(limit));
    return <String, int>{'limit': limit, 'primes': count};
  }
}

/// Must be a top level or static function with plain arguments.
/// The new isolate has no Dox, no database and no services.
int countPrimes(int limit) {
  List<bool> sieve = List<bool>.filled(limit + 1, true);
  int count = 0;
  for (int i = 2; i <= limit; i++) {
    if (!sieve[i]) continue;
    count++;
    for (int j = i * i; j <= limit; j += i) {
      sieve[j] = false;
    }
  }
  return count;
}

Do not block the event loop

_build shares the thread with the requests of this isolate. A long loop makes them all wait. Put a long loop in Isolate.run.

docs.title: 2. CPU work on another thread
docs.text:
Isolate.run runs the function on a new isolate and sends the result back. Pass plain data in (an int, a String, bytes) and get plain data out. Save the result in the request isolate.

primes above waits for the result. To not wait, combine both patterns:

unawaited(Isolate.run(() => countPrimes(limit)).then(saveResult));

docs.title: 3. Work on a timer
docs.text:
setup() of a service runs in every isolate, and Dox starts one per CPU core. So start the timer on isolate 1 only.

lib/services/cleanup_service.dart
import 'dart:async';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

/// Work on a timer. `setup()` runs in every isolate, so the timer is
/// started on isolate 1 only. Otherwise 8 isolates do the same job.
class CleanupService implements DoxService {
  @override
  void setup() {
    if (Dox().isolateId != 1) return;
    Timer.periodic(const Duration(hours: 1), _run);
  }

  Future<void> _run(Timer timer) async {
    DateTime limit = DateTime.now().subtract(const Duration(days: 30));
    List<User> old = await User()
        .withTrash()
        .where('deleted_at', '<', limit)
        .get();
    for (User user in old) {
      await user.forceDelete();
    }
    print('cleanup: removed ${old.length} users');
  }
}

Dox finds CleanupService by itself. To be sure the database is ready first, list ORMService in AppConfig:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  container: registerContainer,
  services: <DoxService>[ORMService()], // runs before CleanupService
  // ...
);

When you run more than one process (two machines), each process has an isolate 1. Then the job runs twice. Use a database lock, or run the job from one place only.

docs.title: 4. Add the routes
Check it
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/reports

The answer comes at once:

{"id":"1792677668393002","status":"queued"}

Two seconds later, the server prints report 1792677668393002 is ready.

curl http://localhost:3000/api/primes/100000

{"limit":100000,"primes":9592}

docs.title: When you need a real queue
docs.text: The work above is lost when the process stops, and it does not retry. When that is not OK (payments, emails that must arrive), save the job as a row in a table first. Then a Timer.periodic service, or a second small Dart program, reads the table, does the work, and marks the row as done. A failed row stays in the table, so you can retry it.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Isolate for what each isolate shares, and what it does not
  • Services
  • Custom errors for the ExceptionHandler that gets the errors of a future nobody awaits

docs.title: CORS for a browser front-end
docs.text: Let a web app on another origin (http://localhost:5173 in development, https://my.app in production) call your API.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app.
  • A front-end that runs on its own origin, like Vite, Next.js or Flutter web.

docs.title: 1. Write the config
2. Set the origin per environment
docs.text:
CORS_ORIGIN is a new key. Add a getter for it to the AppEnv class:

lib/config/env.dart
  /// the front-end URL that may call the API
  String get corsOrigin => 'http://localhost:5173';

Run dart run build_runner build to update env.g.dart. Then set the value in .env:

.env
CORS_ORIGIN=http://localhost:5173

In staging and production, set CORS_ORIGIN as a real environment variable: https://my.app. The origin is scheme, host and port. No path, no / at the end.

docs.title: 3. Choose credentials
docs.text:
Your front-end sends origin credentials a token in Authorization: Bearer (see JWT authentication) your front-end URL false cookies (fetch(url, {credentials: 'include'})) your front-end URL, never * true nothing, a public API '*' false

Two or more front-ends

Set origin to a list, like ['https://a.com', 'https://b.com']. Dox compares the Origin header of the request with the list. It sends back only the origin that matches. If none matches, it sends no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, and the browser blocks the call.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
The browser sends a preflight OPTIONS request before a POST with JSON or a custom header. Dox answers it by itself. You do not need an OPTIONS route.

curl -i -X OPTIONS http://localhost:3000/api/users \
  -H 'Origin: http://localhost:5173' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: Authorization'

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
access-control-allow-origin: http://localhost:5173
access-control-allow-methods: GET,POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE
access-control-allow-headers: Content-Type,Authorization
access-control-expose-headers: Content-Disposition
access-control-allow-credentials: false
access-control-max-age: 600

A normal request gets the origin header too:

curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/ping -H 'Origin: http://localhost:5173' | grep -i access-control-allow-origin

access-control-allow-origin: http://localhost:5173

In the browser, open the front-end and call the API with fetch. The console shows no CORS error.

docs.title: When it still fails
docs.text: The console says The fix No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header CORS_ORIGIN does not match the page origin exactly. Check http or https, and the port. The value of ... header is 'a.com,b.com' origin is one text with commas. Use a List<String> instead. Request header field x-foo is not allowed Add the header to headers. credentials mode is 'include' with * Set origin to the front-end URL and credentials: true.

docs.title: Webhooks and server-to-server calls
docs.text:
CORS only matters for browsers. A webhook from Stripe or a call from another server ignores these headers. Turn CORS off for such routes to send fewer headers:

Route.disabledCors(() {
  Route.post<WebhookController>('/webhooks/stripe', (WebhookController c) => c.handle);
});

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• CORS for every option
  • JWT authentication

docs.title: Custom errors
docs.text: Give your app its own exception classes, send every error in one JSON shape, and log the unexpected ones.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A Dox app.

docs.title: How Dox handles an error
docs.text:
When a controller or a middleware throws:

Error Status What Dox does an IHttpException, like NotFoundHttpException its code sends its message. Does not call report a validation error (bad DTO input) 422 sends the field errors. Does not call report any other Exception or Error 500 sends Server Error (the error text only in development). Calls report

report is a method of the exception handler. The response goes through the responseHandler of AppConfig last. This guide sets the shape there.

docs.title: 1. Write your own exceptions
docs.text:
Extend IHttpException. Set code (the HTTP status), errorCode (a short text for the client) and message.

lib/app/exceptions/app_exception.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// 403. Thrown when the user may not do this.
class ForbiddenException extends IHttpException {
  ForbiddenException({String message = 'Forbidden'}) {
    super.code = HttpStatus.forbidden;
    super.errorCode = 'forbidden';
    super.message = message;
  }
}

/// 409. Thrown when the row already exists or was changed by someone else.
class ConflictException extends IHttpException {
  ConflictException({String message = 'Conflict'}) {
    super.code = HttpStatus.conflict;
    super.errorCode = 'conflict';
    super.message = message;
  }
}

Throw them anywhere in a controller, a middleware or a service:

lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/exceptions/app_exception.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class UserController {
  /// GET /api/users/{id}
  Future<User> show(int id) async {
    User? user = await User().find(id);
    if (user == null) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException(message: 'User $id not found');
    }
    return user;
  }

  /// DELETE /api/users/{id}
  Future<Map<String, bool>> destroy(int id) async {
    if (id == 1) {
      throw ForbiddenException(message: 'The first user can not be deleted');
    }
    User user = await show(id);
    await user.delete();
    return <String, bool>{'deleted': true};
  }
}

docs.title: 2. One JSON shape for every error
docs.text:
The response handler sees every response before it is sent. For an error, the content is the exception object. Turn it into your shape here.

lib/app/http/response_handler.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// Gives every error the same JSON shape:
/// `{"error": {"code": "not_found", "message": "..."}}`.
/// A validation error (422) also has `"errors": {field: message}`.
class ResponseHandler extends ResponseHandlerInterface {
  @override
  DoxResponse handle(DoxResponse res) {
    dynamic content = res.getContent();

    if (content is ValidationException) {
      return res.statusCode(content.code).content(<String, dynamic>{
        'error': <String, dynamic>{
